docs.title: Diabetes & Endocrine Emergencies (acute — very high yield)
docs.parent: Diabetes & Endocrine Emergencies (acute — very high yield)
docs.text:
**Who:** usually **type 1** (new presentation or insulin omission/illness); can occur in type 2, and **euglycaemic DKA** with SGLT2 inhibitors. Precipitants: infection, missed insulin, MI, new diagnosis.

**Pathophysiology:** absolute insulin deficiency + high counter-regulatory hormones → lipolysis → **ketone (β-hydroxybutyrate) overproduction** → **high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis**, osmotic diuresis → dehydration and total-body **potassium depletion** (despite a normal/high initial serum K⁺).

**Diagnostic criteria — note the guideline shift:** ⚑

| | UK JBDS (traditional) | 2024 international consensus |
|---|---|---|
| Glucose | >11 mmol/L (or known diabetes) | **≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dL)** or known diabetes |
| Ketones | **capillary ketones ≥3.0** mmol/L or urine ≥2+ | **β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L** (or urine ≥2+) |
| Acidosis | **bicarbonate <15** mmol/L and/or pH <7.3 | **bicarbonate <18** and/or **pH <7.3** |
| Anion gap | — | **removed** from criteria |

*Key change: β-hydroxybutyrate (not urine ketones) is the preferred measure; the anion gap has been dropped; severity is now graded by ketone/pH level. Quote the JBDS numbers for a UK/Australian exam but recognise the 2024 update.*

**Management (JBDS "fix the fluids, insulin, potassium"):**
1. **IV 0.9% saline** — restore circulating volume first (a litre stat if hypotensive; then a structured rehydration regimen).
2. **Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour.** Continue the patient's **long-acting basal insulin**. ⚑
3. **Potassium** — add to fluids once K⁺ is known and urine is flowing; insulin drives K⁺ into cells (monitor closely — hypokalaemia is the dangerous iatrogenic complication).
4. **Add glucose (e.g. 10% dextrose)** when glucose falls **<14 mmol/L** so insulin can continue clearing ketones without hypoglycaemia.
5. Monitor ketones/bicarbonate/pH to confirm **resolution** (ketones <0.6, pH >7.3, bicarbonate >15/18); convert to subcutaneous insulin only when eating and ketones cleared. Find and treat the precipitant.

**Complications:** **hypokalaemia** (commonest iatrogenic, potentially fatal), **cerebral oedema** (especially children — avoid over-rapid fluids), aspiration, VTE, ARDS.

docs.title: Diabetes & Endocrine Emergencies (acute — very high yield)
docs.parent: Diabetes & Endocrine Emergencies (acute — very high yield)
docs.text:
**Who:** older **type 2** patients, often with intercurrent illness; develops over days.

**Features/criteria:** **marked hyperglycaemia (often >30 mmol/L)**, **high osmolality (>320 mosmol/kg)**, **profound dehydration**, and **NO significant ketosis/acidosis** (pH >7.3, bicarbonate >15, ketones <3) — because residual insulin suppresses ketogenesis. Altered consciousness correlates with osmolality.

**Management — gentler than DKA:**
- **Fluid (0.9% saline) is the mainstay**; replace slowly to avoid rapid osmotic shifts (cerebral oedema, central pontine myelinolysis).
- **Insulin only after fluids** (often lower/later than in DKA; start ~**0.05 units/kg/h** if ketones present or glucose not falling with fluid alone). ⚑
- **High VTE risk → prophylactic (sometimes therapeutic) anticoagulation.** Watch potassium. Higher mortality than DKA.

**Discriminator:** **DKA = acidosis + ketones, younger/type 1, hours; HHS = hyperosmolar, minimal ketones, older/type 2, days, higher mortality, more cautious insulin/fluids.**

docs.title: Diabetes & Endocrine Emergencies (acute — very high yield)
docs.parent: Diabetes & Endocrine Emergencies (acute — very high yield)
docs.text:
**Definition:** **Whipple's triad** — low plasma glucose (**<3.0 mmol/L** clinically significant; <4.0 "treat"), consistent symptoms, and relief on correction.
- **Autonomic** (early, glucose ~3.3): sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, anxiety.
- **Neuroglycopenic** (lower glucose): confusion, drowsiness, seizures, focal deficits, coma.
- **Causes:** insulin/**sulfonylurea** excess, missed meals, alcohol, exercise, renal/liver failure, Addison's, **insulinoma** (endogenous — high insulin **and** high C-peptide).

**Treatment ladder:**
- **Conscious, able to swallow:** 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate (glucose tablets/juice), recheck in 15 min, repeat, then a long-acting carbohydrate.
- **Impaired/unable to swallow:** **IM glucagon** (won't work in alcohol/liver failure or sulfonylurea-depleted glycogen) or **IV glucose (e.g. 100 mL 20% dextrose)**.
- **Sulfonylurea overdose:** prolonged — admit, may need **octreotide**. Recheck and treat the cause.

docs.title: Diabetes & Endocrine Emergencies (acute — very high yield)
docs.parent: Diabetes & Endocrine Emergencies (acute — very high yield)
docs.text:
| Emergency | One-line recognition | Immediate action |
|---|---|---|
| **Addisonian crisis** (§7) | Shock + ↓Na⁺/↑K⁺ + pigmentation | **IV hydrocortisone + saline** |
| **Thyroid storm** (§5) | Fever, tachyarrhythmia, delirium, thyrotoxic | β-blocker + PTU + iodine (after PTU) + hydrocortisone |
| **Myxoedema coma** (§5) | Hypothermia, bradycardia, ↓GCS, hypoventilation | IV levothyroxine + hydrocortisone + rewarm |
| **Severe hypercalcaemia** (§6) | Confusion, dehydration, short QT | **IV saline** then bisphosphonate |
| **Phaeochromocytoma crisis** (§7) | Severe paroxysmal hypertension, headache/sweating | α-blockade (**never β first**) |
| **Pituitary apoplexy** (§4) | Sudden headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia | **Urgent hydrocortisone** + neurosurgery |
| **Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia** (§4) | Seizures/↓GCS, Na⁺ very low | Hypertonic (3%) saline, correct slowly |

---

Updated DKA diagnostic criteria (β-hydroxybutyrate, bicarbonate <18, anion gap removed) and HHS insulin timing flagged ⚑ and cross-checked against the 2024 consensus and JBDS guidance.

Discriminator table + sources at the end of each section. British/Australian spelling. ⚑ = point where an older textbook is out of date.*

docs.title: Diabetes Mellitus
docs.text:
| Type | Mechanism | Clues |
|---|---|---|
| **Type 1** | Autoimmune β-cell destruction → **absolute insulin deficiency** | Younger/lean, rapid onset, ketosis-prone, **GAD/IA-2/ZnT8 antibodies**, low C-peptide |
| **Type 2** | Insulin **resistance** + relative deficiency | Older/overweight, metabolic syndrome, gradual, family history |
| **LADA** | Slow autoimmune (type 1 in adults) | "Type 2" that fails oral agents fast; antibody-positive |
| **MODY** | Monogenic, autosomal dominant | Young, non-obese, strong AD family history, antibody-negative, C-peptide preserved |
| **Secondary** | Pancreatic (CF, pancreatitis, haemochromatosis), endocrine (Cushing's, acromegaly, phaeo), drug (steroids, thiazides), gestational | Context-dependent |

**Diagnostic thresholds** (WHO/NICE — confirm with a repeat unless symptomatic):

| Test | Diabetes | "Pre-diabetes" |
|---|---|---|
| **HbA1c** | **≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%)** | 42–47 mmol/mol (6.0–6.4%) |
| **Fasting glucose** | **≥7.0 mmol/L** | Impaired fasting glucose 6.1–6.9 |
| **2 h OGTT / random** | **≥11.1 mmol/L** | Impaired glucose tolerance 7.8–11.0 (OGTT) |

**Rules:** in an **asymptomatic** person you need **two abnormal results** (same or different tests); one abnormal result **plus symptoms** (osmotic symptoms, or a hyperglycaemic crisis) is enough. **HbA1c is unreliable** and should not be used when red-cell turnover is abnormal: **pregnancy, recent blood loss/transfusion, haemolysis, haemoglobinopathies, iron/B12 deficiency, CKD, recent-onset (rapid) type 1**. ⚑

docs.title: Diabetes Mellitus
docs.text:
**Structure:** lifestyle (diet, weight loss, activity, smoking cessation) + **cardiorenal risk management** (BP, statin, address albuminuria) run alongside glucose-lowering. Modern therapy is chosen for **organ protection**, not glucose alone.

**The updated drug pathway (NICE NG28, revised):** ⚑
- **First-line is now dual therapy — metformin + an SGLT2 inhibitor** — offered from diagnosis (metformin titrated first, then the SGLT2i added), even without established cardiovascular disease. SGLT2i monotherapy if metformin is not tolerated.
- **If atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or high CV risk / CKD** → ensure an **SGLT2 inhibitor** is included (proven cardiorenal benefit); a **GLP-1 receptor agonist** is added/preferred where CVD risk or weight is the priority. NICE now supports early **triple therapy (metformin + SGLT2i + semaglutide)** in ASCVD.
- **GLP-1 RA** (e.g. semaglutide) or the dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist **tirzepatide** — strong HbA1c and weight benefit; consider where BMI is high or weight is a driver.
- **Insulin** when other measures fail to control (e.g. HbA1c persistently high, or symptomatic hyperglycaemia).

*This is the single biggest change from older texts: the old "metformin alone, then add" ladder has been replaced by **early combination and organ-protective drug choice**. Glucose target is **individualised** (a common default is 48 mmol/mol on lifestyle/metformin, 53 mmol/mol if on a drug that can cause hypoglycaemia).*

**Drug one-liners (full detail in Section 11):**

| Class | Benefit | Watch for |
|---|---|---|
| **Metformin** | Weight-neutral, no hypos, first-line | GI upset; **lactic acidosis** risk in renal impairment; stop if eGFR <30 |
| **SGLT2 inhibitor** (-gliflozin) | **Cardiorenal protection**, weight loss, no hypos | **Euglycaemic DKA**, genital thrush/UTI, volume depletion; **sick-day: stop when acutely unwell** |
| **GLP-1 RA / tirzepatide** | Weight loss, CV benefit | Nausea, pancreatitis (rare); injectable (oral semaglutide exists) |
| **DPP-4 inhibitor** (-gliptin) | Weight-neutral, oral, no hypos | Modest effect; pancreatitis (rare) |
| **Sulfonylurea** (gliclazide) | Cheap, effective, rapid | **Hypoglycaemia, weight gain** |
| **Pioglitazone** | No hypos | Weight gain, **fluid retention/HF**, fractures, bladder-cancer caution |

docs.title: Diabetes Mellitus
docs.text:
- **Basal–bolus (multiple daily injections):** long-acting basal (e.g. glargine/degludec) + rapid-acting bolus with meals (carbohydrate counting), or an **insulin pump (CSII)**; increasingly **hybrid closed-loop ("artificial pancreas")** systems. ⚑
- **Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM/flash)** is now standard of care in type 1. Aim for **"time in range"** as well as HbA1c.
- Never stop basal insulin in type 1, even when not eating (fasting/illness) — omission precipitates **DKA**.

docs.title: Diabetes Mellitus
docs.text:
**Microvascular:**
- **Retinopathy** — background → pre-proliferative → **proliferative** (neovascularisation → vitreous haemorrhage/retinal detachment); **maculopathy** is the main cause of visual loss. Annual retinal screening; laser/anti-VEGF for proliferative/maculopathy.
- **Nephropathy** — **albuminuria** (screen with urine ACR) → declining eGFR. **ACE inhibitor/ARB** for albuminuria + BP; **SGLT2 inhibitors** slow progression. ⚑
- **Neuropathy** — symmetrical **glove-and-stocking** sensory loss (the basis of foot ulceration), autonomic (gastroparesis, postural hypotension, erectile dysfunction), mononeuropathy.

**Macrovascular:** accelerated atherosclerosis → **IHD, stroke, peripheral arterial disease** — the leading cause of death; manage BP, lipids (statin), antiplatelet where indicated, smoking.

**Diabetic foot:** the interaction of **neuropathy + ischaemia + infection**; annual foot risk assessment; multidisciplinary foot team for ulcers/**Charcot** arthropathy.

---

docs.text:

##### Sources
**NICE NG28** (type 2 diabetes management — updated first-line dual therapy); ADA *Standards of Care in Diabetes*; WHO diagnostic criteria; NICE NG17 (type 1). Updated first-line dual therapy, SGLT2i cardiorenal role and closed-loop technology flagged ⚑ and cross-checked against current NICE/ADA guidance.

docs.title: Endocrine Anatomy
docs.text: *Written out as prose + tables (not image-only) — pair with `endocrine_anatomy_sheet.svg`.*

docs.title: Endocrine Anatomy
docs.text:
The **pituitary (hypophysis)** sits in the **sella turcica** of the sphenoid bone, connected to the hypothalamus by the **infundibulum (stalk)**. Two critical neighbours make pituitary pathology a clinical emergency of *location*:
- **Optic chiasm** sits directly **above** the gland → an expanding pituitary mass compresses the crossing nasal fibres → **bitemporal hemianopia** (a superior-quadrant "upper temporal" defect first, as the chiasm is pushed from below).
- **Cavernous sinuses** flank it, carrying the **internal carotid** and cranial nerves **III, IV, V1, V2, VI** → lateral extension or apoplexy causes **ophthalmoplegia** (CN III palsy classic).

Two functionally and embryologically distinct lobes:

| Lobe | Origin | Nature | Blood supply | Hormones |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Anterior (adenohypophysis)** | Rathke's pouch (oral ectoderm) | Glandular | **Hypophyseal portal veins** (not direct arterial) | GH, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH, prolactin |
| **Posterior (neurohypophysis)** | Neuroectoderm (downgrowth of hypothalamus) | Neural | Direct arterial | **Stores** ADH, oxytocin (made in hypothalamus) |

**Discriminator:** the anterior pituitary's **portal (not arterial) blood supply** is why it is vulnerable to ischaemia after post-partum haemorrhage → **Sheehan syndrome** (the gland enlarges in pregnancy, then infarcts when perfusion drops).

docs.title: Endocrine Anatomy
docs.text:
The **thyroid** has two lobes joined by an **isthmus** (over the 2nd–4th tracheal rings), invested in pretracheal fascia so it **moves up with swallowing** — the exam sign that a neck lump is thyroid. Key surgical relations:
- **Recurrent laryngeal nerves** run in the tracheo-oesophageal groove behind the gland → damage in thyroidectomy → **hoarse voice** (unilateral) or airway compromise (bilateral).
- **External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve** (to cricothyroid) runs with the superior thyroid artery → injury changes voice pitch (the "opera-singer" nerve).

**Embryology:** the thyroid descends from the **foramen caecum** at the tongue base down the **thyroglossal duct** → a persistent duct gives a midline **thyroglossal cyst** (moves up on tongue protrusion) and failed descent gives a **lingual thyroid**. *Memory: thyroglossal cyst rises with tongue protrusion; thyroid lump rises with swallowing.*

**Parathyroids** — usually **four** (two superior, two inferior), tiny, on the posterior thyroid. Embryology explains their variable position and a common exam trap:
- **Superior** parathyroids ← **4th pharyngeal pouch** (more constant position).
- **Inferior** parathyroids ← **3rd pharyngeal pouch**, migrating **with the thymus** → can end up ectopic in the mediastinum/thymus (relevant when a missing adenoma is hunted at surgery).

docs.title: Endocrine Anatomy
docs.text:
The **adrenal (suprarenal) glands** cap the kidneys. Cortex and medulla have separate origins (cortex = mesoderm; medulla = neural crest) and separate jobs:

| Layer | Zone | Product | Regulator | Memory hook |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cortex** (outer) | **Glomerulosa** | **Aldosterone** (mineralocorticoid) | RAAS / K⁺ | **"Salt"** |
| | **Fasciculata** | **Cortisol** (glucocorticoid) | ACTH | **"Sugar"** |
| | **Reticularis** | **Androgens** (DHEA) | ACTH | **"Sex"** |
| **Medulla** (inner) | — | **Catecholamines** (adrenaline > noradrenaline) | Sympathetic (splanchnic) | **"The deeper you go, the sweeter it gets"** |

*Memory: **G-F-R = Salt, Sugar, Sex; the deeper you go, the sweeter (more valued) it gets.*** The medulla is effectively a modified sympathetic ganglion — hence phaeochromocytoma behaves like sympathetic overdrive. Adrenal **venous drainage is asymmetric**: right adrenal vein → IVC directly (short); left → left renal vein — relevant to **adrenal vein sampling**.

**Endocrine pancreas — islets of Langerhans** (~1–2% of pancreatic mass):

| Cell | Product | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **β (beta)** — central, most numerous | **Insulin** (+ C-peptide, amylin) | Lowers glucose |
| **α (alpha)** — peripheral | **Glucagon** | Raises glucose |
| **δ (delta)** | **Somatostatin** | Inhibits insulin, glucagon, GH, gut hormones |
| **PP/F cells** | Pancreatic polypeptide | Regulates pancreatic secretion |

**Discriminator:** **C-peptide** is co-secreted 1:1 with endogenous insulin — so it separates endogenous hyperinsulinism (insulinoma → **high** C-peptide) from **exogenous insulin** administration (suppressed C-peptide). Sulfonylurea abuse raises both (measure the drug screen).

docs.title: Endocrine Anatomy
docs.text:
The **ovaries** (theca/granulosa cells → oestrogen, progesterone; regulated by LH/FSH) and **testes** (Leydig cells → testosterone under LH; Sertoli cells → inhibin/sperm under FSH) are endocrine as well as reproductive organs. The **pineal gland** secretes **melatonin** (circadian rhythm).

**Diffuse neuroendocrine system:** scattered **enterochromaffin/neuroendocrine cells** in the gut and bronchi are the origin of **carcinoid/neuroendocrine tumours** (serotonin and other peptides) and are the conceptual link to **MEN syndromes** (Section 10) — multiple neuroendocrine tissues sharing a genetic driver.

---

docs.title: Endocrine Anatomy
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Visual defect from a pituitary mass | **Bitemporal hemianopia** (chiasm compression) |
| Cranial nerve palsy in pituitary apoplexy | **CN III** (cavernous sinus) |
| Anterior pituitary blood supply | **Hypophyseal portal veins** (why Sheehan's occurs) |
| Neck lump that moves on **swallowing** | Thyroid |
| Neck lump that moves on **tongue protrusion** | Thyroglossal cyst |
| Nerve at risk in thyroidectomy → hoarse voice | **Recurrent laryngeal** nerve |
| Adrenal cortex zones & products | **G-F-R = aldosterone, cortisol, androgens** ("Salt, Sugar, Sex") |
| Adrenal medulla product & origin | Catecholamines; **neural crest** |
| Superior vs inferior parathyroid origin | Superior = **4th** pouch; inferior = **3rd** pouch (migrates with thymus) |
| Distinguishes endogenous from injected insulin | **C-peptide** (high vs suppressed) |
| Islet cell secreting glucagon | **α cells** |
| Right adrenal vein drains into | **IVC directly** |

##### Sources
Gray's Anatomy for Students; Moore's *Clinically Oriented Anatomy*; Langman's *Medical Embryology* (pharyngeal pouches, thyroglossal duct); Merck Manual Professional (adrenal and pituitary anatomy). Zona/product mapping and parathyroid embryology are standard anatomical facts, cross-checked across the above.

docs.title: Endocrine Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.h: Endocrine Master Notes — Endocrine Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text: *Consolidated drug section — the guaranteed pharmacology part of the spine. Mechanisms + the exam-critical adverse effects and prescribing rules.*

docs.title: Endocrine Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
| Drug / class | Mechanism | Key benefits | Key adverse effects / rules |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Metformin** (biguanide) | ↓hepatic gluconeogenesis, ↑insulin sensitivity | First-line, weight-neutral, **no hypoglycaemia**, CV-safe | GI upset, B12 deficiency; **lactic acidosis** — stop if eGFR <30 and during acute illness/contrast |
| **SGLT2 inhibitors** (-gliflozin) | Block renal glucose reabsorption (glycosuria) | **Cardiorenal protection**, weight loss, BP↓, no hypos | **Euglycaemic DKA**, genital/urinary infection, volume depletion, (rare) Fournier's; **sick-day: withhold when acutely unwell** ⚑ |
| **GLP-1 receptor agonists** (-tide: semaglutide, dulaglutide) | Incretin — ↑glucose-dependent insulin, ↓glucagon, ↓gastric emptying, satiety | **Weight loss**, CV benefit | Nausea/vomiting, (rare) pancreatitis; injectable (oral semaglutide exists); withhold peri-op per guidance |
| **Tirzepatide** | **Dual GIP/GLP-1** agonist | Greatest HbA1c + weight reduction ⚑ | As GLP-1 RA |
| **DPP-4 inhibitors** (-gliptin) | Prolong endogenous incretins | Oral, weight-neutral, no hypos | Modest; (rare) pancreatitis; avoid combining with GLP-1 RA |
| **Sulfonylureas** (gliclazide) | Close β-cell K-ATP channel → insulin release | Cheap, rapid, effective | **Hypoglycaemia** (prolonged), **weight gain** |
| **Pioglitazone** (TZD) | PPAR-γ → ↑insulin sensitivity | No hypos, durable | **Fluid retention/heart failure**, weight gain, fractures, bladder-cancer caution |
| **Insulin** | Replaces/augments insulin | Universally effective | **Hypoglycaemia**, weight gain; never omit basal in T1DM |

**Insulin types:** rapid (aspart/lispro), short (soluble/regular), intermediate (NPH/isophane), long-acting analogues (glargine, detemir, **degludec** ultra-long); pre-mixed. Regimens: basal–bolus, twice-daily mixed, basal-only (often added to orals in T2DM).

docs.title: Endocrine Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
**Glucocorticoids** — relative potency (learn the ladder):

| Steroid | Approx. equivalent dose | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Hydrocortisone | 20 mg | Physiological replacement; used IV in crises |
| Prednisolone | 5 mg | Standard oral anti-inflammatory |
| Dexamethasone | 0.75 mg | Long-acting, minimal mineralocorticoid; used in tests/cerebral oedema |

*Adverse effects (Cushingoid): hyperglycaemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, weight gain, thin skin/bruising, cataracts/glaucoma, proximal myopathy, mood change, immunosuppression, peptic ulcer, adrenal suppression.* **Never stop long-term steroids abruptly** (risk of adrenal crisis) — taper; **sick-day rules** (double the dose in illness).

**Thyroid drugs:**
- **Carbimazole** (first-line antithyroid) — blocks thyroid peroxidase; **agranulocytosis** warning; teratogenic (aplasia cutis) → **use PTU in first trimester**. ⚑
- **Propylthiouracil (PTU)** — also blocks peripheral T4→T3; first-trimester and thyroid-storm agent; rare **hepatotoxicity**.
- **Levothyroxine** — titrate to TSH; interactions (iron/calcium/PPIs reduce absorption — separate dosing); dose **rises in pregnancy**.

**Pituitary/posterior drugs:** **dopamine agonists** (cabergoline/bromocriptine — prolactinoma; adverse: nausea, postural hypotension, impulse-control disorders, fibrosis); **somatostatin analogues** (octreotide/lanreotide — acromegaly, NETs; adverse: gallstones, GI upset); **pegvisomant** (GH-receptor antagonist); **desmopressin** (cranial DI — watch hyponatraemia); **GH** replacement.

docs.title: Endocrine Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
- **Bisphosphonates** (alendronate/risedronate/zoledronate) — inhibit osteoclasts; take upright/fasting; **oesophagitis, osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fractures, acute-phase reaction (IV)**; correct vitamin D/calcium first.
- **Denosumab** (RANKL monoclonal) — 6-monthly SC; **do not stop abruptly** (rebound vertebral fractures). ⚑
- **Romosozumab** (sclerostin antibody), **teriparatide/abaloparatide** (PTH analogues, anabolic) — very-high-risk osteoporosis; teriparatide contraindicated in Paget's/prior skeletal radiotherapy.
- **Mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists**: **spironolactone** (Conn's, also causes gynaecomastia) and the more selective **eplerenone**.
- **Phaeochromocytoma blockade**: **α-blocker first** (phenoxybenzamine/doxazosin) **then β-blocker** — never the reverse.
- **Cortisol-synthesis inhibitors**: **metyrapone, ketoconazole** (medical control of Cushing's).
- **Fludrocortisone** — mineralocorticoid replacement in Addison's.

docs.title: Endocrine Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
- **Steroid sick-day rules & withdrawal:** double glucocorticoid in intercurrent illness, parenteral if vomiting, never stop long-term steroids suddenly, steroid emergency card.
- **Drug-induced endocrine disease (common exam links):** steroids → Cushing's/diabetes; **amiodarone/lithium** → thyroid dysfunction; **thiazides** → hyperglycaemia/hyponatraemia/hypercalcaemia; antipsychotics/metoclopramide → hyperprolactinaemia; **checkpoint inhibitors** → autoimmune endocrinopathies (hypophysitis, thyroiditis, adrenalitis, type 1 diabetes). ⚑
- **Peri-operative endocrine management:** stress-dose steroids for adrenal insufficiency/long-term steroid users; euglycaemia and a variable-rate insulin infusion for insulin-dependent diabetics; α-blockade optimisation before phaeochromocytoma surgery; euthyroid before elective thyroid surgery.

---

docs.title: Endocrine Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| First-line T2DM drugs ⚑ | **Metformin + SGLT2 inhibitor** |
| Metformin stop threshold | **eGFR <30** (and acute illness/contrast) |
| SGLT2i emergency to remember | **Euglycaemic DKA** |
| Sulfonylurea main harms | **Hypoglycaemia, weight gain** |

| Steroid equivalence: prednisolone 5 mg ≈ hydrocortisone | **20 mg** (dexamethasone 0.75 mg) |

##### Sources
BNF and NICE (glucose-lowering drugs, corticosteroids, antithyroid drugs, bisphosphonates); Endocrine Society guidelines; NICE NG28; NOGG 2024 (bone agents). Updated first-line dual diabetes therapy, SGLT2i sick-day rules, denosumab rebound and checkpoint-inhibitor endocrinopathies flagged ⚑ and cross-checked against current BNF/NICE guidance.

docs.title: Endocrine Physiology
docs.text:
Hormones fall into **three chemical classes**, and the class predicts almost everything about how the hormone behaves:

| Class | Examples | Storage | Transport | Receptor | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Peptide/protein** | Insulin, GH, PTH, ADH, most pituitary hormones | Pre-formed in vesicles | Dissolved (water-soluble) | **Cell-surface** | Fast (seconds–minutes) |
| **Steroid** | Cortisol, aldosterone, sex steroids, vitamin D | Made **on demand** (not stored) | Bound to carrier proteins (lipophilic) | **Intracellular/nuclear** | Slow (hours — needs gene transcription) |
| **Amine** | Thyroid hormones, catecholamines | Thyroid: stored in colloid; catecholamines: vesicles | Thyroid bound (TBG); catecholamines free | Thyroid = **nuclear**; catecholamines = **surface** | Thyroid slow; catecholamines fast |

**Discriminator:** thyroid hormone is an amine but behaves like a **steroid** (lipophilic, carrier-bound, **nuclear receptor**, slow genomic action). Catecholamines are amines that behave like **peptides** (surface receptor, fast). *Memory: the receptor location tells you the speed — surface = fast/second-messenger, nuclear = slow/gene transcription.*

**Second-messenger systems** (surface receptors):
- **cAMP (Gs)** — ACTH, LH/FSH, TSH, PTH, glucagon, ADH (V2), β-adrenergic. *Memory: "FLAT ChAMP" hormones use cAMP.*
- **IP₃/DAG (Gq)** — GnRH, TRH, ADH (V1), angiotensin II, α₁-adrenergic. *Memory: "GGOAT" → the ones that raise intracellular calcium.*
- **Receptor tyrosine kinase** — **insulin**, IGF-1 (also growth factors).
- **JAK/STAT** — GH, prolactin, leptin, cytokines.

docs.title: Endocrine Physiology
docs.text:
The **hypothalamus** releases factors into the hypophyseal **portal system** to control the **anterior pituitary**, which in turn drives peripheral endocrine glands. The **posterior pituitary** is different — it is neural tissue storing hormones made in the hypothalamus.

| Hypothalamic factor | Anterior pituitary hormone | Target/effect |
|---|---|---|
| GHRH (+) / somatostatin (−) | **GH** | Liver IGF-1, growth, metabolism |
| TRH (+) | **TSH** (also stimulates prolactin) | Thyroid → T4/T3 |
| CRH (+) | **ACTH** | Adrenal cortex → cortisol |
| GnRH (+, pulsatile) | **LH/FSH** | Gonads → sex steroids, gametes |
| **Dopamine (−, tonic)** | **Prolactin** | Lactation |

**Two high-yield consequences of this wiring:**
- **Prolactin is under tonic *inhibition* by dopamine.** Anything that removes dopamine (stalk compression by a pituitary mass, dopamine-antagonist drugs like antipsychotics/metoclopramide) → **hyperprolactinaemia**. *This is why a big non-functioning pituitary tumour can still raise prolactin — the "stalk effect."*
- **TRH stimulates prolactin too**, so **primary hypothyroidism (high TRH)** can cause a modestly raised prolactin.

**Posterior pituitary** stores/releases two hypothalamic hormones:
- **ADH (vasopressin)** — from supraoptic/paraventricular nuclei; acts on renal collecting-duct **V2 receptors** (aquaporin-2 insertion → water reabsorption) and vascular **V1** (vasoconstriction).
- **Oxytocin** — uterine contraction, milk ejection.

docs.title: Endocrine Physiology
docs.text:
**Insulin vs glucagon** — the fed/fasted switch:

| | Insulin (fed) | Glucagon (fasted) |
|---|---|---|
| Source | β cells (islet) | α cells |
| Trigger | ↑glucose, incretins (GLP-1/GIP) | ↓glucose |
| Net effect | **Anabolic** — glycogenesis, lipogenesis, protein synthesis; drives K⁺ **into** cells | **Catabolic** — glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis |

**Counter-regulatory (stress/hyperglycaemic) hormones:** glucagon, **cortisol, growth hormone, adrenaline**. They all oppose insulin — which is why **stress, steroids and infection worsen glycaemic control** and can precipitate DKA/HHS.

**Calcium homeostasis** — the three-organ loop (learn this cold, it explains every calcium disorder):

| Hormone | Source | Bone | Kidney | Gut | Net serum Ca²⁺ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PTH** | Parathyroids (low Ca²⁺ trigger) | ↑resorption | ↑Ca²⁺ reabsorption, ↑phosphate excretion, **↑1α-hydroxylase** | ↑ (indirectly via vit D) | **↑** (↓ phosphate) |
| **1,25-vitamin D (calcitriol)** | Skin→liver→kidney activation | ↑resorption (permissive) | ↑Ca²⁺ + phosphate reabsorption | **↑Ca²⁺ + phosphate absorption** | **↑** (↑ phosphate) |
| **Calcitonin** | Thyroid C-cells | ↓resorption | ↑excretion | — | ↓ (minor in humans) |

**Discriminator:** **PTH raises calcium but *lowers* phosphate**; **vitamin D raises both**. This phosphate split is how you read the calcium panel (see Section 6). Vitamin D activation: skin (7-dehydrocholesterol → cholecalciferol) → **liver (25-hydroxylation)** → **kidney (1α-hydroxylation, PTH-driven)** to active **1,25-(OH)₂-D**.

**Cortisol** (glucocorticoid) actions: ↑gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance (**diabetogenic**), protein catabolism, immunosuppression/anti-inflammatory, permissive for catecholamine vascular tone (why cortisol deficiency → shock), ↑appetite, mineralocorticoid effect at high levels. Secreted with a **diurnal rhythm** (peak ~waking, trough ~midnight) — the basis of **midnight/late-night cortisol testing**.

**RAAS:** ↓renal perfusion/↓Na⁺ → **renin** (JG cells) → angiotensinogen → **angiotensin I** → (ACE, lung) → **angiotensin II** (vasoconstriction + ↑aldosterone). **Aldosterone** (zona glomerulosa) → renal Na⁺ retention and **K⁺/H⁺ excretion** → this is why aldosterone excess causes **hypertension + hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis**, and deficiency causes the reverse.

docs.title: Endocrine Physiology
docs.text:
One rule governs every endocrine dynamic test:

> **Suspect excess → try to SUPPRESS it (a normal axis suppresses; autonomous secretion does not).**
> **Suspect deficiency → try to STIMULATE it (a normal axis responds; a failed gland does not).**

| Suspected problem | Test | Normal (excludes disease) |
|---|---|---|
| Cushing's (cortisol **excess**) | **Dexamethasone suppression** | Cortisol suppresses |
| Acromegaly (GH **excess**) | **OGTT** (glucose should suppress GH) | GH suppresses <1 µg/L |
| Conn's (aldosterone **excess**) | Saline/fludrocortisone **suppression** | Aldosterone suppresses |
| Adrenal insufficiency (**deficiency**) | **Short Synacthen** (ACTH stimulation) | Cortisol rises |
| GH/ACTH reserve (**deficiency**) | Insulin tolerance test | GH/cortisol rise to hypoglycaemia |
| Diabetes insipidus (ADH **deficiency/resistance**) | **Water deprivation** ± desmopressin | Urine concentrates |

---

docs.title: Endocrine Physiology
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Steroid vs peptide receptor location | Steroid = **intracellular/nuclear**; peptide = **cell-surface** |
| Amine that acts like a steroid | **Thyroid hormone** (nuclear, carrier-bound, slow) |
| Insulin receptor type | **Receptor tyrosine kinase** |
| GH & prolactin signal via | **JAK/STAT** |
| Prolactin's dominant control | **Tonic inhibition by dopamine** |
| Why a pituitary mass raises prolactin | Stalk effect (loss of dopamine inhibition) |
| PTH effect on phosphate | **Lowers** it (raises calcium) |
| Vitamin D effect on phosphate | **Raises** it (raises calcium) |
| Final activation step of vitamin D | **1α-hydroxylation in the kidney** (PTH-driven) |
| Aldosterone excess electrolyte triad | ↑BP, **↓K⁺, metabolic alkalosis** |
| Counter-regulatory hormones | Glucagon, cortisol, GH, adrenaline |
| Suspect hormone **excess** → which test? | **Suppression** |
| Suspect hormone **deficiency** → which test? | **Stimulation** |

##### Sources
Guyton & Hall *Textbook of Medical Physiology* (endocrinology chapters); Greenspan's *Basic & Clinical Endocrinology*; Robbins & Cotran *Pathologic Basis of Disease* (endocrine system); Merck Manual Professional (principles of endocrinology). Second-messenger groupings and the calcium loop are standard physiology, cross-checked across the above.

docs.title: Key Differentials Quick-Reference
docs.h: Endocrine Master Notes — Key Differentials Quick-Reference
docs.text: *A **view** of `endocrine_recognition_summary.md` (the source of truth) — for fast lookup. Do not edit here independently; update the recognition summary and regenerate.*

docs.title: Key Differentials Quick-Reference
docs.text:
- **Hyponatraemia** → volume status first: euvolaemic + concentrated urine = SIADH; hypovolaemic + ↑K⁺ + pigment = Addison's.
- **Hypercalcaemia** → ↑PTH = primary hyperparathyroidism; suppressed PTH = malignancy; low urine Ca = FHH.
- **Secondary hypertension** → ↓K⁺/alkalosis = Conn's; paroxysmal headache/sweating = phaeochromocytoma; Cushingoid = Cushing's.
- **Polyuria/polydipsia** → glycosuria = diabetes mellitus; dilute urine, no glucose = diabetes insipidus (DDAVP splits cranial/nephrogenic).
- **Weight loss + sweats** → thyrotoxicosis, phaeo, new diabetes, Addison's, carcinoid.
- **Weight gain + lethargy** → hypothyroidism, Cushing's, PCOS/metabolic syndrome.

docs.title: Key Differentials Quick-Reference
docs.text:
- **Antibodies:** TRAb → Graves'; anti-TPO → Hashimoto's; GAD/IA-2 → type 1 diabetes; 17-OHP → CAH; calcitonin → medullary thyroid cancer; metanephrines → phaeo; 5-HIAA → carcinoid.
- **Dynamic tests:** fails to suppress on dexamethasone = Cushing's; GH fails to suppress on OGTT = acromegaly; fails to rise on Synacthen = adrenal insufficiency; ARR high = Conn's.
- **Which is high/low:** primary failure = trophic hormone opposite to target; PTH suppressed in malignancy hypercalcaemia; C-peptide low = exogenous insulin.

docs.title: Key Differentials Quick-Reference
docs.text:
- Cushing's disease vs ectopic ACTH → high-dose dexamethasone suppresses the pituitary only.
- Primary vs secondary adrenal insufficiency → pigmentation + hyperkalaemia = primary.
- Cranial vs nephrogenic DI → cranial responds to DDAVP.
- Primary hyperparathyroidism vs FHH → low urinary calcium in FHH.
- DKA vs HHS → ketoacidosis (young/T1) vs hyperosmolar, minimal ketones (old/T2).
- Insulinoma vs exogenous insulin → C-peptide high vs suppressed.
- Graves' vs toxic MNG → diffuse uptake + eye signs vs patchy uptake.
- MEN 1 (3 Ps) vs MEN 2 (medullary thyroid + phaeo, RET); 2B adds mucosal neuromas/marfanoid.
- Phaeochromocytoma → α-blockade before β (β-first precipitates crisis).

*Full tables, buzzwords and biochemical patterns: see `endocrine_recognition_summary.md`.*

docs.title: Pituitary & Hypothalamic Disorders
docs.h: Endocrine Master Notes — Pituitary & Hypothalamic Disorders

docs.title: Pituitary & Hypothalamic Disorders
docs.text:
**Mass effect** of any sellar lesion: **bitemporal hemianopia** (chiasm), headache, cavernous-sinus cranial nerve palsies (III), and disruption of normal secretion. A **macroadenoma** is ≥10 mm; a **microadenoma** <10 mm.

**Order of anterior hormone loss** in progressive compression — a classic exam fact: **GH → FSH/LH → TSH → ACTH → prolactin** *(memory: "Go Look For The Adenoma" — Growth, LH/FSH, TSH, ACTH; **Prolactin rises**, doesn't fall, because of stalk disconnection)*. So the earliest deficits are growth failure/hypogonadism and the last, most dangerous, is **ACTH/cortisol deficiency**.

**Replacement in hypopituitarism** (learn the safety rule): give **hydrocortisone BEFORE levothyroxine** — starting thyroxine first in someone who is also cortisol-deficient increases metabolic demand and can precipitate an **adrenal crisis**.

**Pituitary apoplexy** *(emergency)* — haemorrhage/infarction of a (usually pre-existing) adenoma: **sudden severe headache, visual loss/ophthalmoplegia, and acute hypopituitarism** → treat with **urgent hydrocortisone** and neurosurgical/endocrine input. **Sheehan syndrome** is post-partum pituitary infarction (failure of lactation and other deficits after major PPH — see the portal-supply point in Section 2).

docs.title: Pituitary & Hypothalamic Disorders
docs.text:
##### Prolactinoma (commonest functioning pituitary tumour)
- **Presentation:** women — galactorrhoea, oligo/amenorrhoea, infertility (present early, small tumours); men — hypogonadism, low libido, erectile dysfunction, often a larger tumour with mass effect at diagnosis.
- **Discriminator:** distinguish a true prolactinoma (prolactin often **>5000 mU/L**, roughly scaling with tumour size) from the modest rise of the **"stalk effect"** (a non-functioning macroadenoma disconnecting dopamine, prolactin usually <2000–3000). Always exclude **pregnancy, hypothyroidism (high TRH), antipsychotics/metoclopramide, and renal failure** first.
- **Management:** **dopamine agonist first-line — cabergoline** (or bromocriptine) — even for macroprolactinomas, because they shrink medically. Surgery is second-line. *This is the pituitary tumour treated with drugs, not surgery.*

##### Acromegaly (GH excess, usually a somatotroph adenoma)
- **Presentation:** enlarging hands/feet (ring/shoe size), coarse facial features, prognathism, macroglossia, sweating, headache, carpal tunnel, **hypertension, impaired glucose tolerance/diabetes**, and premature cardiovascular disease. In children (before physes fuse) → **gigantism**.
- **Diagnosis:** **IGF-1** (screening; stable integrated marker) → confirm with **failure of GH to suppress on OGTT**. MRI to localise.
- **Management:** **transsphenoidal surgery** is first-line. Medical adjuncts: **somatostatin analogues** (octreotide/lanreotide), the GH-receptor antagonist **pegvisomant**, dopamine agonists; radiotherapy for residual disease.

##### Cushing's disease
Pituitary ACTH excess — covered with the adrenal Cushing's workup in Section 7.

docs.title: Pituitary & Hypothalamic Disorders
docs.text:
##### Diabetes insipidus (DI)
Deficiency of ADH (**cranial**) or renal resistance to it (**nephrogenic**) → **dilute polyuria, polydipsia**, and **hypernatraemia** if water access is limited.

| | Cranial DI | Nephrogenic DI |
|---|---|---|
| Problem | No ADH (pituitary/hypothalamus) | Kidney unresponsive to ADH |
| Causes | Tumour, surgery, trauma, infiltration | **Lithium**, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, genetic |
| **Water deprivation** | Fails to concentrate | Fails to concentrate |
| **After DDAVP** | **Concentrates (>50%)** | **No response** |
| Treatment | **Desmopressin** | Treat cause; thiazide, low-salt/protein diet |

##### SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis)
- **Euvolaemic hyponatraemia** with **inappropriately concentrated urine** (urine osmolality >100, often > plasma) and **high urinary sodium (>30–40)**, with **low plasma osmolality** — in a clinically **euvolaemic** patient, with **normal thyroid, adrenal and renal function** (all must be excluded first).
- **Causes** — the four groups: **CNS** (stroke, meningitis, haemorrhage), **lung** (pneumonia, small-cell carcinoma — ectopic ADH), **drugs** (SSRIs, carbamazepine, chemotherapy, PPIs), and **malignancy**.
- **Management:** treat the cause; **fluid restriction** first-line; consider vasopressin-receptor antagonists (**tolvaptan**) or demeclocycline in resistant cases. **Correct sodium slowly** (≤8–10 mmol/L per 24 h) to avoid **osmotic demyelination**.

---

docs.title: Pituitary & Hypothalamic Disorders
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Order of pituitary hormone loss | **GH → LH/FSH → TSH → ACTH** (prolactin rises) |
| Replace which hormone first in panhypopituitarism | **Hydrocortisone before levothyroxine** |
| Sudden headache + visual loss + known pituitary tumour | **Pituitary apoplexy** → urgent hydrocortisone |
| Failure of lactation post-PPH | **Sheehan syndrome** |
| Commonest functioning pituitary tumour | **Prolactinoma** |
| First-line treatment of prolactinoma | **Dopamine agonist (cabergoline)** — even if macro |
| Prolactin very high (>5000) vs modest rise | True prolactinoma vs **stalk effect** |
| Confirms acromegaly | **GH fails to suppress on OGTT** (IGF-1 screens) |
| First-line treatment of acromegaly | **Transsphenoidal surgery** |
| DI that responds to DDAVP | **Cranial** |
| DI caused by lithium/hypercalcaemia | **Nephrogenic** |
| Euvolaemic hyponatraemia + concentrated urine | **SIADH** |
| Risk of correcting hyponatraemia too fast | **Osmotic demyelination** (≤8–10 mmol/L/24 h) |

##### Sources
Greenspan's *Basic & Clinical Endocrinology*; Endocrine Society guidelines (acromegaly, hyperprolactinaemia, hyponatraemia); NICE CKS; Merck Manual Professional. The order of hormone loss and DDAVP responses are standard, cross-checked across the above.

docs.title: Reproductive, Metabolic & Multi-Gland Endocrinology
docs.h: Endocrine Master Notes — Reproductive, Metabolic & Multi-Gland Endocrinology

docs.title: Reproductive, Metabolic & Multi-Gland Endocrinology
docs.text:
##### Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
Commonest endocrine disorder in women of reproductive age; a state of **hyperandrogenism + insulin resistance**.
- **Rotterdam criteria** — diagnosis needs **2 of 3**: (1) **oligo/anovulation**, (2) **clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism** (hirsutism, acne; raised free testosterone), (3) **polycystic ovaries on ultrasound** — after excluding mimics (CAH, Cushing's, androgen-secreting tumour, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease). ⚑
- **Associated:** obesity, insulin resistance/impaired glucose tolerance/T2DM, dyslipidaemia, subfertility, **endometrial hyperplasia** risk (from unopposed oestrogen).
- **Biochemistry clue:** raised **LH:FSH ratio** (classic but not required), raised free testosterone with **normal/low SHBG**, normal/mildly raised androgens (a *very* high testosterone suggests a tumour instead).
- **Management:** weight loss/lifestyle first; **combined oral contraceptive** for menstrual regulation/hyperandrogenism; **metformin** for metabolic features; **letrozole** (first-line) or clomifene for ovulation induction; ensure endometrial protection (regular withdrawal bleeds).

##### Amenorrhoea and hirsutism
- **Primary amenorrhoea** (no menarche): Turner's, constitutional delay, imperforate hymen, androgen insensitivity, GnRH deficiency (Kallmann's — with anosmia).
- **Secondary amenorrhoea:** **pregnancy first**, then hypothalamic (low weight/stress/exercise), **hyperprolactinaemia**, PCOS, thyroid disease, premature ovarian insufficiency, Sheehan's, Asherman's.
- **Rapid virilisation** (deep voice, clitoromegaly, rapid hirsutism) → **androgen-secreting tumour or CAH**, not PCOS.

##### Menopause
Cessation of ovarian function → oestrogen deficiency: vasomotor symptoms, urogenital atrophy, mood/sleep change, accelerated bone loss. **HRT** relieves symptoms (weigh VTE/breast-cancer risk; give a progestogen with oestrogen if the uterus is present).

docs.title: Reproductive, Metabolic & Multi-Gland Endocrinology
docs.text:
| | Primary (hypergonadotrophic) | Secondary (hypogonadotrophic) |
|---|---|---|
| Problem | Testis | Pituitary/hypothalamus |
| Testosterone | Low | Low |
| **LH/FSH** | **High** | **Low/normal** |
| Causes | **Klinefelter's (47,XXY)**, mumps orchitis, trauma, chemo | Hypopituitarism, **Kallmann's** (+anosmia), hyperprolactinaemia, obesity, opioids, steroids |

**Gynaecomastia** = benign glandular breast tissue in a male from a **raised oestrogen:androgen ratio**: physiological (neonatal, puberty, elderly), drugs (**spironolactone, digoxin, cimetidine, antipsychotics, cannabis, anti-androgens**), liver disease, hyperthyroidism, hypogonadism, and — important not to miss — **testicular/hCG-secreting tumours**. Distinguish from fatty pseudogynaecomastia and exclude malignancy if unilateral/hard/fixed.

docs.title: Reproductive, Metabolic & Multi-Gland Endocrinology
docs.h: 10.3 Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia and Neuroendocrine Tumours
docs.text:
**MEN syndromes** — autosomal dominant; learn the components (very high yield):

| Syndrome | Gene | Components |
|---|---|---|
| **MEN 1** ("**3 Ps**") | **MEN1** (menin) | **Parathyroid** hyperplasia (commonest/first), **Pancreatic** islet tumours (gastrinoma/insulinoma), **Pituitary** adenoma |
| **MEN 2A** | **RET** | **Medullary thyroid carcinoma**, **Phaeochromocytoma**, **Parathyroid** hyperplasia |
| **MEN 2B** | **RET** | Medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma, **mucosal neuromas + marfanoid habitus** (no parathyroid disease) |

*Memory: MEN1 = "3 Ps" (Parathyroid, Pancreas, Pituitary); MEN2A = medullary + phaeo + parathyroid; MEN2B = medullary + phaeo + **mucosal neuromas/marfanoid** (Ps become "2 Ms").* **All MEN2 subtypes → medullary thyroid carcinoma** — RET-positive relatives are offered **prophylactic thyroidectomy**; always **exclude phaeochromocytoma before any surgery**.

**Carcinoid / neuroendocrine tumours:**
- **Carcinoid syndrome** (flushing, diarrhoea, wheeze, right-sided valvular heart disease) occurs when a serotonin-secreting NET **metastasises to the liver** (bypassing first-pass metabolism) or is bronchial. Diagnose with **urinary 5-HIAA** and chromogranin A; localise with somatostatin-receptor imaging (Ga-DOTATATE). Treat with **somatostatin analogues (octreotide)**; **carcinoid crisis** is precipitated by handling/anaesthesia → octreotide cover.
- Other functional pancreatic NETs: **insulinoma** (hypoglycaemia), **gastrinoma** (Zollinger–Ellison → refractory peptic ulcers/diarrhoea), **VIPoma** (watery diarrhoea), **glucagonoma** (necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes).

docs.title: Reproductive, Metabolic & Multi-Gland Endocrinology
docs.text:
- **Metabolic syndrome:** clustering of **central obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia (high triglycerides/low HDL), and dysglycaemia/insulin resistance** — a cardiovascular and diabetes risk state.
- **Obesity management:** lifestyle first; **incretin-based pharmacotherapy** (GLP-1 RA **semaglutide**, GIP/GLP-1 **tirzepatide**) now has a major role and substantial weight-loss efficacy ⚑; **bariatric surgery** for higher BMI thresholds (typically BMI ≥40, or ≥35 with comorbidity; lower thresholds considered in certain groups) with durable weight loss and diabetes remission.

---

docs.title: Reproductive, Metabolic & Multi-Gland Endocrinology
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| PCOS diagnostic framework | **Rotterdam — 2 of 3** (oligo-ovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries) |
| First-line ovulation induction in PCOS | **Letrozole** |
| Very high testosterone + rapid virilisation | **Androgen-secreting tumour** (not PCOS) |
| First test in secondary amenorrhoea | **Pregnancy test** |
| Hypogonadism + anosmia | **Kallmann syndrome** |
| Male hypogonadism with **high** LH/FSH | **Primary** (e.g. Klinefelter's 47,XXY) |
| Drug causes of gynaecomastia | Spironolactone, digoxin, cimetidine, antipsychotics, cannabis |
| MEN 1 components | **Parathyroid, Pancreas, Pituitary (3 Ps)** |
| MEN 2A components | Medullary thyroid ca, phaeochromocytoma, parathyroid |
| MEN 2B distinguishing feature | **Mucosal neuromas + marfanoid** (no parathyroid) |
| Gene in MEN 2 | **RET** |
| Always exclude before MEN2 surgery | **Phaeochromocytoma** |
| Carcinoid syndrome needs | **Liver metastases** (or bronchial primary) |
| Test for carcinoid | **Urinary 5-HIAA** (+ chromogranin A) |
| Refractory peptic ulcers + diarrhoea | **Gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison)** |

##### Sources
Endocrine Society/relevant guidelines (PCOS Rotterdam criteria, MEN, neuroendocrine tumours); NICE CKS (amenorrhoea, menopause, obesity); Merck Manual Professional; BNF (drug causes of gynaecomastia). Incretin obesity pharmacotherapy flagged ⚑ and cross-checked against current NICE/guideline positions.

---

docs.title: Thyroid Disorders
docs.text:
**Common features:** weight loss despite good appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, tremor, palpitations/AF, anxiety, loose stools, oligomenorrhoea, proximal myopathy, lid lag/stare. **Biochemistry: ↑free T4/T3 with ↓TSH** (primary).

**Separate the causes — the key is the uptake scan + eye signs + antibodies:**

| Cause | Uptake scan | Distinctive features |
|---|---|---|
| **Graves' disease** (autoimmune, commonest) | **Diffuse ↑uptake** | **TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb)**; **eye disease** (proptosis, ophthalmoplegia), **pretibial myxoedema**, thyroid acropachy; diffuse goitre with bruit |
| **Toxic multinodular goitre** | **Patchy/multifocal uptake** | Older patient, nodular gland, often AF |
| **Toxic adenoma** | **Single hot nodule** | Solitary autonomous nodule |
| **Thyroiditis** (de Quervain's, postpartum, silent) | **Absent/low uptake** | Transient, painful (de Quervain's) or painless; raised ESR (de Quervain's) |
| **Exogenous thyroxine** | **Absent uptake, low thyroglobulin** | Factitious/over-replacement |

**Discriminator:** **eye signs (Graves' orbitopathy) and pretibial myxoedema occur only in Graves'** — they are extrathyroidal autoimmune features, so their presence makes the diagnosis clinically. **Absent uptake = thyroiditis or exogenous hormone**, not a hyperfunctioning gland.

**Management of Graves'/thyrotoxicosis:**
- **Symptom control:** **β-blocker (propranolol)** for tremor/palpitations.
- **Antithyroid drugs — carbimazole** (or **propylthiouracil, PTU**): either **titration** or **"block-and-replace"** (block with carbimazole + add levothyroxine). Key adverse effect: **agranulocytosis** — warn the patient to seek an urgent FBC if sore throat/fever. **PTU preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy** (carbimazole is teratogenic — aplasia cutis); switch back to carbimazole later. ⚑
- **Definitive:** **radioiodine** (avoid in pregnancy/active eye disease; can worsen orbitopathy) or **surgery** (for large goitre, compressive symptoms, suspected malignancy, pregnancy where drugs fail).
- **Graves' ophthalmopathy:** smoking cessation (strongly worsens it), selenium in mild disease, glucocorticoids/orbital radiotherapy/decompression in severe; the anti-IGF-1R antibody **teprotumumab** is a newer option for active disease. ⚑

**Thyroid storm** *(emergency)* — decompensated thyrotoxicosis with fever, tachyarrhythmia, agitation/delirium, vomiting: treat with **β-blocker + high-dose antithyroid drug (PTU) + iodine (given ≥1 h after the antithyroid drug — Wolff–Chaikoff) + hydrocortisone**, plus supportive cooling and treat the precipitant.

docs.title: Thyroid Disorders
docs.text:
**Common features:** fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin/hair, hoarseness, bradycardia, delayed-relaxing reflexes, menorrhagia, low mood; goitre (Hashimoto's) or none.

- **Primary (95%)**: gland failure. **↑TSH with ↓free T4.** Causes: **Hashimoto's (autoimmune, anti-TPO antibodies)** — commonest in iodine-replete regions; iodine deficiency (commonest worldwide); iatrogenic (post-radioiodine/surgery, amiodarone, lithium); transient after thyroiditis.
- **Central/secondary**: pituitary/hypothalamic. **↓free T4 with low/inappropriately normal TSH.**
- **Subclinical hypothyroidism**: **↑TSH with normal free T4.** Treat if TSH persistently **>10 mU/L**, or if symptomatic/antibody-positive/pregnant/planning pregnancy at lower levels. ⚑

**Levothyroxine replacement:** titrate to **normalise TSH** (in primary disease); recheck ~6–8 weeks after a dose change. Start **low and slow in the elderly/ischaemic heart disease**. In pregnancy, requirements **rise (~25–50%)** — increase the dose promptly and aim for trimester-specific TSH targets.

**Myxoedema coma** *(emergency)* — severe decompensated hypothyroidism: hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation (hypercapnia), hyponatraemia, reduced consciousness. Treat with **IV levothyroxine (± T3), IV hydrocortisone (cover possible coexisting adrenal insufficiency), and supportive rewarming/ventilation.**

docs.title: Thyroid Disorders
docs.text:
- **De Quervain's (subacute granulomatous) thyroiditis:** **painful** tender goitre after a viral illness, **raised ESR/CRP**, **absent uptake**; classically **biphasic** — an early thyrotoxic phase (release of stored hormone) → hypothyroid phase → recovery. Treat with NSAIDs/steroids; β-blocker for symptoms. Self-limiting.
- **Postpartum and silent (painless) thyroiditis:** autoimmune, painless, biphasic; usually resolve but may leave permanent hypothyroidism.
- **Pregnancy:** hCG (a weak TSH agonist) can cause mild **gestational thyrotoxicosis**; requirements for levothyroxine **rise** in treated hypothyroidism; PTU in the first trimester, carbimazole later, for hyperthyroidism.

docs.title: Thyroid Disorders
docs.text:
**Solitary nodule pathway:** check **TSH first** — a suppressed TSH suggests an autonomous ("hot", usually benign) nodule → uptake scan; a **normal/high TSH** → **ultrasound risk stratification → FNA** of suspicious nodules. Features raising concern: rapid growth, hard/fixed nodule, cervical lymphadenopathy, hoarseness, microcalcification/irregular margins on US, prior neck irradiation.

**Thyroid cancers:**

| Type | Frequency/behaviour | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **Papillary** | Commonest (~80%), young, good prognosis | **Lymphatic** spread; psammoma bodies, Orphan-Annie nuclei; associated with **radiation** |
| **Follicular** | ~10%, older | **Haematogenous** spread (lung/bone); diagnosis needs histology (capsular invasion) — **FNA can't distinguish** follicular adenoma from carcinoma |
| **Medullary** | Parafollicular **C-cells** → **calcitonin** | Sporadic or **MEN 2** (RET); screen with calcitonin/CEA; not iodine-avid |
| **Anaplastic** | Elderly, aggressive | Rapidly enlarging fixed mass, poor prognosis, airway compromise |
| **Lymphoma** | Rare | Arises in a background of **Hashimoto's** |

**Discriminator:** **medullary carcinoma secretes calcitonin and is part of MEN 2** — think of it when there's a thyroid mass plus phaeochromocytoma/hyperparathyroidism (MEN 2A) or a marfanoid/mucosal-neuroma habitus (MEN 2B). Differentiated (papillary/follicular) cancers are treated with **thyroidectomy ± radioiodine**, and monitored with **thyroglobulin** as a tumour marker.

---

docs.title: Thyroid Disorders
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| ↑T4, ↓TSH, diffuse uptake, eye signs | **Graves' disease** |
| Thyrotoxicosis with **absent** uptake | **Thyroiditis** or exogenous thyroxine |
| Antibody in Graves' | **TSH-receptor antibody (TRAb)** |
| Antibody in Hashimoto's | **Anti-TPO** (anti-thyroid peroxidase) |
| Antithyroid drug in first-trimester pregnancy | **PTU** (carbimazole teratogenic) |
| Antithyroid drug adverse effect to warn about | **Agranulocytosis** (sore throat → urgent FBC) |
| ↑TSH, normal T4 | **Subclinical hypothyroidism** (treat if TSH >10 / symptomatic / pregnant) |
| Painful goitre + ↑ESR post-viral, biphasic | **De Quervain's thyroiditis** |
| Commonest thyroid cancer, lymphatic spread | **Papillary** |
| Thyroid cancer spreading haematogenously | **Follicular** |
| Thyroid cancer secreting calcitonin / MEN 2 | **Medullary** |
| Tumour marker after differentiated-cancer surgery | **Thyroglobulin** |
| Severe decompensated hypothyroidism | **Myxoedema coma** (IV T4 + hydrocortisone) |

##### Sources
American/British Thyroid Association guidance (thyrotoxicosis, hypothyroidism, thyroid nodules and cancer); NICE CKS thyroid disease; Greenspan's *Basic & Clinical Endocrinology*; Merck Manual Professional. Subclinical-hypothyroidism treatment thresholds and PTU-first-trimester guidance flagged as ⚑ and cross-checked against current ATA/NICE positions.

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.h: Gastroenterology Master Notes — Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
**Gallstones** — mostly **cholesterol** (or mixed); pigment stones with haemolysis. **Risk = the 5 Fs: Female, Fat, Forty, Fertile, Family history** (± rapid weight loss, ileal disease/bile-salt loss). Most are **asymptomatic** (leave alone).

**The spectrum — separate them by the presence of pain, fever, and jaundice (high yield):**

| Condition | Where the stone is | Pain | Fever/WCC | Jaundice | Key sign/test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Biliary colic** | Neck/cystic duct (transient) | RUQ, post-fatty meal, **<6 h, no fever** | No | No | US stones; settles |
| **Acute cholecystitis** | Impacted in cystic duct → inflamed GB | RUQ, **constant >6 h** | **Yes** | Usually no | **Murphy's sign +**; US: thick wall, pericholecystic fluid |
| **Choledocholithiasis** | **CBD** | RUQ | ± | **Yes (obstructive)** | ↑bilirubin/ALP; dilated CBD; **MRCP → ERCP** |
| **Ascending cholangitis** | CBD + **infection** | RUQ | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Charcot's triad** (RUQ pain + fever + jaundice); emergency |

*Discriminators: **biliary colic = pain only**; **cholecystitis = pain + fever + Murphy's** (but no jaundice); **cholangitis = pain + fever + jaundice (Charcot's triad)** — add **hypotension + confusion = Reynolds' pentad** (severe, needs urgent biliary drainage/ERCP).*

**Management:** cholecystitis → analgesia, IV antibiotics, and **laparoscopic cholecystectomy** (ideally within 1 week / same admission ⚑). CBD stones → **ERCP** clearance ± cholecystectomy. Ascending cholangitis → resuscitate, IV antibiotics, **urgent biliary decompression (ERCP)**.

**Other biliary:**
- **Murphy's sign:** arrest of inspiration on RUQ palpation (cholecystitis).
- **Mirizzi syndrome** — stone in the cystic duct compressing the CBD → obstructive jaundice.
- **Gallstone ileus** — a large stone erodes into the bowel (cholecysto-enteric fistula) → small-bowel obstruction; **Rigler's triad** (pneumobilia, obstruction, ectopic stone).
- **Courvoisier's law:** a **palpable, painless** gallbladder with jaundice is **unlikely to be gallstones** — think **malignant obstruction** (pancreatic/biliary cancer), because a chronically stone-diseased gallbladder is fibrotic and won't distend.
- **Cholangiocarcinoma** (PSC-associated, ↑CA19-9) and **gallbladder cancer** (porcelain gallbladder) — late, poor prognosis.

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
**Acute inflammation from premature enzyme activation** → autodigestion. **Causes — "I GET SMASHED"**: **I**diopathic, **G**allstones, **E**thanol, **T**rauma, **S**teroids, **M**umps, **A**utoimmune, **S**corpion, **H**yperlipidaemia/hypercalcaemia, **E**RCP, **D**rugs. **Gallstones and alcohol account for ~80%.**

**Diagnosis (2 of 3):** characteristic **epigastric pain radiating to the back**, **serum lipase (or amylase) >3× upper limit** (lipase more specific/sensitive), and/or characteristic **imaging** (CT/US). *Amylase can be normal if late-presenting or in alcoholic pancreatitis — lipase is better.*

Signs: epigastric tenderness, and (in severe/haemorrhagic disease) **Cullen's sign** (periumbilical bruising) and **Grey Turner's sign** (flank bruising).

**⚑ Severity assessment:**
- **Glasgow–Imrie score (PANCREAS)** at 48 h — **PaO₂ <8 kPa, Age >55, Neutrophils (WCC >15), Calcium <2, Renal (urea >16), Enzymes (LDH/AST high), Albumin <32, Sugar (glucose >10)**. **≥3 = severe** → HDU/ITU. (Ranson's and **APACHE II** and **CRP >150** are also used.)
- **Revised Atlanta classification** grades severity by **organ failure and complications**: **mild** (no organ failure/complications), **moderately severe** (transient organ failure <48 h and/or local complications), **severe** (**persistent organ failure >48 h**).

**Management:** **aggressive IV fluid resuscitation**, analgesia, oxygen, **early enteral nutrition** (NBM only if not tolerated; parenteral is last resort), treat the cause (**ERCP/cholecystectomy for gallstone pancreatitis**; alcohol withdrawal). **Antibiotics are not routine** — only for proven infected necrosis. Complications: **pancreatic necrosis** (± infection), **pseudocyst** (fluid collection weeks later — amylase-rich; drain if symptomatic), abscess, haemorrhage, **ARDS**, and later chronic pancreatitis/diabetes.

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
**Chronic pancreatitis** — irreversible fibrosis (commonest cause **alcohol**; also genetic, autoimmune/IgG4, obstruction). Presents with **chronic epigastric pain radiating to the back**, and the two failures: **exocrine** (steatorrhoea, weight loss, **low faecal elastase** → **pancreatic enzyme replacement, Creon**) and **endocrine** (diabetes). Imaging: **pancreatic calcification** on CT/AXR. Manage pain, alcohol cessation, enzyme/insulin replacement.

**Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma** — usually **head of pancreas**; classically **painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss** (**Courvoisier-positive** — palpable painless gallbladder), later epigastric/back pain, new-onset diabetes, thrombophlebitis migrans (Trousseau's sign). Risk: **smoking**, chronic pancreatitis, age, hereditary. Tumour marker **CA19-9**. Diagnose with **CT (pancreatic protocol) + EUS ± biopsy**. Most present **late/unresectable**; only ~20% are candidates for **Whipple's (pancreaticoduodenectomy)**; overall **poor prognosis**.

---

docs.title: Biliary Tract & Pancreatic Disease
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Gallstone risk factors | **5 Fs: Female, Fat, Forty, Fertile, Family history** |
| RUQ pain <6 h, no fever, settles | **Biliary colic** |
| RUQ pain + fever + Murphy's, no jaundice | **Acute cholecystitis** |
| RUQ pain + fever + **jaundice** | **Ascending cholangitis (Charcot's triad)** |
| Charcot's triad + hypotension + confusion | **Reynolds' pentad** (severe cholangitis) |
| Definitive treatment of cholecystitis | **Laparoscopic cholecystectomy** |
| Emergency treatment of cholangitis | **Urgent biliary drainage (ERCP)** |
| Palpable **painless** gallbladder + jaundice | **Malignant obstruction** (Courvoisier's law) |
| Stone eroding into bowel → obstruction | **Gallstone ileus** (Rigler's triad) |
| Pancreatitis causes mnemonic | **I GET SMASHED** (gallstones + alcohol ~80%) |
| Best diagnostic enzyme in pancreatitis | **Lipase** (>3× ULN) |
| Periumbilical / flank bruising | **Cullen's / Grey Turner's sign** |
| Severity score at 48 h | **Glasgow–Imrie (PANCREAS), ≥3 = severe** |
| Atlanta "severe" pancreatitis | **Persistent organ failure >48 h** |
| Antibiotics in acute pancreatitis | **Only for infected necrosis** (not routine) |
| Fluid collection weeks after pancreatitis | **Pseudocyst** |
| Low faecal elastase + calcification + steatorrhoea | **Chronic pancreatitis** (give Creon) |
| Painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss + CA19-9 | **Pancreatic head cancer** |
| Curative pancreatic cancer operation | **Whipple's (pancreaticoduodenectomy)** |

##### Sources
Robbins & Cotran (biliary/pancreatic pathology); NICE NG118 (gallstone disease), NG104 (pancreatitis); IAP/APA and BSG pancreatitis guidance (revised Atlanta severity, no routine antibiotics, early enteral nutrition ⚑); Oxford Handbook of Clinical Surgery; Merck Manual Professional. Early-cholecystectomy timing, Atlanta severity, and pancreatitis antibiotic/nutrition practice flagged ⚑ and cross-checked against NICE/IAP-APA.

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.h: Gastroenterology Master Notes — Clinical Assessment & Investigation

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.text:
**Cardinal symptoms and what they localise:**

| Symptom | Key discriminators |
|---|---|
| **Dysphagia** | Solids-then-liquids progressive = **mechanical** (stricture/cancer); solids **and** liquids from the start = **motility** (achalasia). Painful swallowing (odynophagia) = oesophagitis/candida. |
| **Dyspepsia** | Epigastric pain/burning; relation to meals (duodenal ulcer often *relieved* by food; gastric ulcer *worsened*). Screen for **ALARM** features. |
| **Abdominal pain** | Site (map to foregut/midgut/hindgut), character (colicky = obstruction/biliary; constant = inflammation/peritonism), radiation (epigastric → back = pancreatitis/AAA). |
| **Altered bowel habit** | New change >6 weeks in >50s = red flag; alternating = IBS/obstruction; nocturnal/weight loss = organic. |
| **Rectal bleeding** | Bright red on paper/coating stool = anorectal; mixed in/darker = higher; **melaena** (black tarry) = upper GI. |
| **Jaundice** | Pale stool + dark urine + itch = obstructive; painless = malignancy until proven otherwise (Courvoisier). |

**⚑ ALARM / red-flag symptoms** mandating **urgent upper GI endoscopy / 2-week-wait referral**: **A**naemia (iron-deficiency), **L**oss of weight, **A**norexia, **R**ecent onset/progressive symptoms, **M**elaena/haematemesis, **S**wallowing difficulty (dysphagia). Add **new dyspepsia in anyone ≥55** with weight loss, and any upper-abdominal mass. (NICE NG12.)

**Signs of chronic liver disease** (worth a systematic hand-to-abdomen sweep): palmar erythema, **Dupuytren's**, leuconychia, clubbing, **spider naevi** (>5, SVC distribution), gynaecomastia, **caput medusae**, splenomegaly, ascites, testicular atrophy. **Signs of decompensation:** jaundice, **asterixis** (flap) + encephalopathy, ascites, variceal bleeding, easy bruising (coagulopathy).

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.h: 3.2 Liver Function Tests and Their Interpretation
docs.text:
**First split every abnormal LFT into a *pattern*, not a list of numbers:**

| | **Hepatocellular** | **Cholestatic (obstructive)** |
|---|---|---|
| Dominant rise | **ALT/AST** (transaminases) | **ALP + γGT + bilirubin** |
| Meaning | Hepatocyte injury | Bile-flow obstruction (intra- or extra-hepatic) |
| Examples | Viral/alcoholic/autoimmune hepatitis, ischaemia, drugs, MASH | Gallstone, pancreatic/biliary cancer, PBC, PSC, drugs |

**Reading the enzymes:**
- **ALT** is more liver-specific than AST. **AST:ALT ratio >2** suggests **alcoholic** liver disease (and advanced fibrosis); **ALT > AST** is typical of viral hepatitis and MASLD.
- **Transaminases in the thousands** = a narrow differential: **ischaemia ("shock liver"), paracetamol/toxins, acute viral hepatitis** (± autoimmune).
- **Raised ALP** — is it liver or bone? Check **γGT**: **↑ALP + ↑γGT = hepatobiliary**; ↑ALP with **normal** γGT = **bone** (Paget's, mets, growth) or placenta (pregnancy).
- **Bilirubin** — see the pre-/intra-/post-hepatic split (Section 1.4).

**⚑ True tests of hepatic *function* (not just damage)** — these tell you how sick the liver actually is:
- **Albumin** (low = chronic synthetic failure, but also sepsis/nutrition) — long half-life.
- **Prothrombin time / INR** — the **most useful acute marker of synthetic function** (clotting factors have a short half-life, so PT/INR rises early in acute liver failure). *ALT/ALP tell you there is injury; INR and bilirubin tell you the liver is failing.*

**Non-invasive fibrosis assessment (⚑ replaces routine biopsy for staging in many settings):** simple scores (**FIB-4**, NAFLD fibrosis score), the **Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF)** blood test, and **transient elastography (FibroScan)**. A "**non-invasive liver screen**" for unexplained abnormal LFTs = viral serology (Hep B/C), autoantibodies + immunoglobulins (AIH, PBC), ferritin/transferrin saturation (haemochromatosis), caeruloplasmin (Wilson's, if <40y), α₁-antitrypsin, coeliac serology, lipids/glucose (MASLD), and an **ultrasound**.

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.text:
**Endoscopy:**
- **OGD (gastroscopy)** — dyspepsia with ALARM features, dysphagia, haematemesis/melaena, surveillance (Barrett's, varices), biopsy (coeliac, *H. pylori*).
- **Colonoscopy** — the gold standard for colorectal assessment; investigation of altered bowel habit/rectal bleeding/iron-deficiency anaemia, IBD assessment, polyp/cancer diagnosis and removal, surveillance.
- **Flexible sigmoidoscopy** — left colon/rectum (e.g. acute UC where full colonoscopy risks perforation).
- **Capsule endoscopy** — obscure small-bowel bleeding/Crohn's (contraindicated if stricturing — risk of capsule retention).

**Imaging:**

| Modality | Best for |
|---|---|
| **Ultrasound** | First-line for gallstones, biliary dilatation, liver texture/ascites, portal flow |
| **CT** | Acute abdomen (obstruction, perforation, ischaemia, collections), cancer staging |
| **MRCP** | **Non-invasive** imaging of the biliary/pancreatic ducts (stones, strictures, PSC beading) |
| **ERCP** | **Therapeutic** biliary intervention (stone extraction, stenting, sphincterotomy) — not first-line diagnostic (risk of pancreatitis) |
| **EUS** | Staging oesophageal/pancreatic tumours; sampling; assessing CBD stones |
| **Erect CXR / AXR** | Free air under the diaphragm (perforation); dilated loops/obstruction |

*Discriminator: **MRCP looks, ERCP acts.** Use MRCP to diagnose, ERCP to treat.*

**Stool and serology (know the "one test" for each disease):**

| Test | Points to |
|---|---|
| **Faecal calprotectin** | **Organic bowel inflammation** — distinguishes **IBD from IBS** (raised in IBD, normal in IBS) |
| **Faecal immunochemical test (FIT)** | Occult blood — bowel-cancer **screening** and symptomatic triage |
| **Faecal elastase** (low) | **Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency** (chronic pancreatitis) |
| ***C. difficile* toxin/GDH** | Antibiotic-associated / pseudomembranous colitis |
| **Anti-tTG (IgA) + total IgA** | **Coeliac disease** (must be **on a gluten-containing diet**) |
| **Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA)** | **Primary biliary cholangitis** |
| **ASMA / anti-LKM1, ↑IgG** | **Autoimmune hepatitis** |
| **pANCA + MRCP beading (+ IBD)** | **Primary sclerosing cholangitis** |
| **Ferritin ↑, transferrin sat ↑** | **Haemochromatosis** |
| **Caeruloplasmin ↓** (<40y) | **Wilson's disease** |

---

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigation
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Solids-then-liquids progressive dysphagia | **Mechanical** (stricture/cancer) |
| Solids **and** liquids dysphagia from the outset | **Motility disorder** (achalasia) |
| ALARM features (upper GI) | Anaemia, Loss of weight, Anorexia, Recent/progressive, Melaena/haematemesis, Swallowing difficulty |
| Duodenal ulcer pain vs meals | **Relieved** by food (gastric ulcer worsened) |
| Hepatocellular LFT pattern | **↑↑ALT/AST** |
| Cholestatic LFT pattern | **↑ALP + ↑γGT + ↑bilirubin** |
| AST:ALT ratio **>2** | **Alcoholic** liver disease |
| Transaminases in the thousands | Ischaemia, paracetamol/toxin, acute viral hepatitis |
| ↑ALP, **normal** γGT | **Bone** (or placental) source |
| Best acute marker of synthetic function | **PT/INR** |
| Distinguishes IBD from IBS | **Faecal calprotectin** (↑ in IBD) |
| Low faecal elastase | **Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency** |
| "Looks vs acts" on the biliary tree | **MRCP diagnoses, ERCP treats** |
| Free air under diaphragm | **Perforation** (erect CXR) |
| Coeliac serology caveat | Must be tested **on gluten** (+ check total IgA) |

##### Sources
NICE NG12 (suspected cancer referral / ALARM features) and CG184 (dyspepsia); Kumar & Clark and Oxford Handbook (LFT interpretation, examination); BSG guidance (non-invasive liver screen, fibrosis assessment); Merck Manual Professional. Fibrosis-assessment and referral thresholds ⚑ cross-checked against current NICE/BSG guidance.
