docs.title: Anaemias & Red Cell Disorders
docs.h: Haematology & Oncology Notes — Anaemias & Red Cell Disorders
docs.text:
*Sources: Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology; BSH guidelines (iron deficiency, sickle cell, AIHA); NICE CKS (anaemia, B12/folate); StatPearls; Robbins. Scope: the MCV/reticulocyte framework and every red-cell disorder a finals student is expected to recognise and manage. Frame throughout is clue → diagnosis.*

---

docs.title: Anaemias & Red Cell Disorders
docs.text:
Anaemia = Hb below the reference range (roughly **<130 g/L men, <120 g/L non-pregnant women**; WHO thresholds). Two orthogonal frameworks together crack almost any case:

1. **By MCV** — microcytic (<80), normocytic (80–100), macrocytic (>100 fL).
2. **By reticulocytes** — high (haemolysis/blood loss = marrow responding) vs low (production failure).

```
              MICROCYTIC (<80)          NORMOCYTIC (80–100)         MACROCYTIC (>100)
              Iron deficiency           Acute blood loss             Megaloblastic:
              Thalassaemia              Anaemia of chronic disease     B12 / folate deficiency
              Anaemia of chronic dis.   Haemolysis (retics high)     Non-megaloblastic:
              Sideroblastic             Marrow failure/infiltration    alcohol, liver, hypothyroid,
              (Lead poisoning)          CKD (↓EPO)                     myelodysplasia, reticulocytosis
```

docs.title: Anaemias & Red Cell Disorders
docs.text:
**Iron deficiency anaemia (IDA)** — the commonest anaemia worldwide. Film: **microcytic, hypochromic, pencil (elliptocyte) cells, anisopoikilocytosis.** Iron studies: **↓ferritin, ↓iron, ↑TIBC, ↓transferrin saturation.** Causes by age/sex: menstrual/pregnancy loss in premenopausal women; **GI blood loss in men and postmenopausal women — colorectal/gastric cancer until proven otherwise** (a 2-week-wait scope). Malabsorption (coeliac) is an under-tested cause — **check coeliac serology** in unexplained IDA. Treat the cause + oral ferrous sulfate (or IV iron if intolerant/malabsorbing); expect a reticulocyte rise within a week and Hb rise of ~20 g/L per month.

**Anaemia of chronic disease (ACD)** — usually normocytic but can be mildly microcytic; driven by **hepcidin** (inflammation traps iron in stores). **↑/normal ferritin, ↓TIBC.** Treat the underlying disease. The IDA-vs-ACD split turns on **TIBC (high in IDA, low/normal in ACD)** and ferritin.

**Thalassaemia trait** — microcytosis **out of proportion to the mild anaemia** (very low MCV with near-normal Hb and normal/raised red cell count); ferritin normal. β-thalassaemia trait → **raised HbA₂** on electrophoresis. Don't iron-load these patients.

**Sideroblastic anaemia** — defective haem synthesis; **ring sideroblasts** in marrow, raised ferritin/iron. Congenital (X-linked) or acquired (alcohol, lead, isoniazid, myelodysplasia). **Lead poisoning** gives **basophilic stippling** + microcytosis.

docs.title: Anaemias & Red Cell Disorders
docs.text:
**Megaloblastic** (impaired DNA synthesis → large cells + **hypersegmented neutrophils**, mild pancytopenia):
- **B12 deficiency** — pernicious anaemia (autoimmune, anti-intrinsic-factor/parietal-cell antibodies, atrophic gastritis), ileal disease/resection, veganism, metformin. **Neurological features are the danger:** peripheral neuropathy, and **subacute combined degeneration of the cord** (dorsal columns + corticospinal tracts → sensory ataxia, spasticity, absent ankle jerks with upgoing plantars). **Replace B12 before/with folate** — giving folate alone can precipitate/worsen neurological damage.
- **Folate deficiency** — poor diet, alcohol, pregnancy, malabsorption, methotrexate/anti-folate drugs, haemolysis (increased demand). No neurology.

**Non-megaloblastic macrocytosis** — **alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia**, and **reticulocytosis** (young red cells are large — so brisk haemolysis raises MCV without B12/folate deficiency).

docs.title: Anaemias & Red Cell Disorders
docs.text:
Normocytic anaemia = acute blood loss, ACD, CKD (↓EPO — treat with EPO analogues once iron-replete), marrow failure, or **haemolysis**. The **haemolysis framework** is two questions:

**(a) Inherited vs acquired?** **(b) Intravascular vs extravascular?**

- **Extravascular** (spleen/liver macrophages destroy cells): **spherocytes**, splenomegaly, ↑unconjugated bilirubin, ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin (milder). Examples: hereditary spherocytosis, warm AIHA.
- **Intravascular** (lysis in circulation): **haemoglobinuria, haemoglobinaemia, marked ↓haptoglobin, ↑LDH**, urinary haemosiderin. Examples: G6PD crisis, ABO transfusion reaction, PNH, MAHA, mechanical valve.

**Inherited:**
- **Hereditary spherocytosis** — autosomal dominant membrane defect (spectrin/ankyrin); spherocytes, **↑MCHC**, negative DAT, **osmotic fragility / EMA-binding** test; splenomegaly, pigment gallstones; folate ± splenectomy.
- **G6PD deficiency** — X-linked; **episodic** oxidative intravascular haemolysis triggered by **infection, fava beans, drugs** (dapsone, primaquine, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin); film shows **bite cells + Heinz bodies**; enzyme assay (delay testing until after the acute episode). Manage by removing the trigger.

**Acquired:**
- **Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA)** — **DAT-positive**:
  - **Warm (IgG)** — extravascular, spherocytes; idiopathic or secondary (**CLL, lymphoma, SLE, drugs**); first-line **steroids**.
  - **Cold (IgM)** — agglutination in cold peripheries; secondary to **Mycoplasma, EBV**, lymphoma; **avoid cold**, treat underlying cause (steroids less effective; rituximab).
- **Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH)** — acquired PIGA mutation → loss of GPI-anchored complement regulators → **complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis, thrombosis (esp. intra-abdominal), pancytopenia**; diagnose by **flow cytometry (CD55/CD59 loss)**; treat with **eculizumab** (complement C5 inhibitor).
- **Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA)** — **schistocytes** from mechanical shearing across fibrin/platelet thrombi: **DIC, TTP, HUS**, malignant hypertension, mechanical valve, HELLP (covered in Section 5).

docs.title: Anaemias & Red Cell Disorders
docs.text:
**Sickle cell disease (HbSS)** — autosomal recessive **β-globin point mutation (Glu→Val)**; HbS polymerises when deoxygenated → sickling, haemolysis, vaso-occlusion. Screening: **Guthrie/newborn** and antenatal. Diagnosis: **Hb electrophoresis/HPLC**.

- **Crises:** **vaso-occlusive/painful** (bones, chest), **acute chest syndrome** (dyspnoea/infiltrates/hypoxia — a leading cause of death, needs urgent transfusion), **aplastic** (**parvovirus B19** shuts off erythropoiesis), **sequestration** (splenic pooling → shock, in children), **haemolytic**.
- **Chronic complications:** **hyposplenism** (autosplenectomy → encapsulated-organism sepsis; vaccinate + penicillin prophylaxis), stroke, retinopathy, avascular necrosis (femoral head), priapism, leg ulcers, pulmonary hypertension, gallstones, chronic kidney disease.
- **Management:** hydration, analgesia (often opioids), oxygen, treat infection, transfusion/exchange for severe crises. **⚑ Hydroxycarbamide (hydroxyurea)** raises **HbF** and reduces crisis frequency — a cornerstone of long-term care; newer agents include **crizanlizumab** and **voxelotor** (availability varies ⚑), and curative options are **allogeneic stem cell transplant** and, increasingly, **gene therapy**.

**Thalassaemias** — reduced globin-chain synthesis → ineffective erythropoiesis + haemolysis, microcytic:
- **α-thalassaemia** — deletions of the 4 α-globin genes. 1–2 genes = trait/asymptomatic; 3 genes = **HbH disease** (moderate anaemia); 4 genes = **Hb Barts / hydrops fetalis** (fatal in utero).
- **β-thalassaemia** — **trait** (raised HbA₂, mild microcytosis, no treatment) vs **major** (transfusion-dependent from infancy, **skeletal/facial bone expansion, hepatosplenomegaly from extramedullary haematopoiesis**). Regular transfusion → **iron overload** → treat with **iron chelation** (desferrioxamine, deferasirox); definitive cure by transplant.

docs.title: Anaemias & Red Cell Disorders
docs.text:
**Aplastic anaemia** — **pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow** and no infiltrate/fibrosis; immune-mediated, drugs (chloramphenicol, carbimazole, chemotherapy), viral (hepatitis, parvovirus), or inherited (**Fanconi anaemia**). Treat with supportive care, immunosuppression (ATG + ciclosporin), or transplant. **Pure red cell aplasia** (isolated anaemia, absent reticulocytes) — parvovirus B19, thymoma, drugs.

**Polycythaemia** (raised Hb/Hct):
- **Relative** (plasma volume ↓) — dehydration, "Gaisböck's."
- **Absolute primary — polycythaemia vera** — a myeloproliferative neoplasm; **⚑ JAK2 V617F mutation in >95%**; low EPO; itch after hot baths (aquagenic pruritus), plethora, thrombosis, splenomegaly; risk of transformation to myelofibrosis/AML. Treat with **venesection ± hydroxycarbamide + aspirin.** (Covered further in Section 7.)
- **Absolute secondary** — appropriate ↑EPO (chronic hypoxia — COPD, altitude, cyanotic heart disease) or inappropriate ↑EPO (renal/hepatic tumours). High EPO here, unlike PV.

---

docs.title: Anaemias & Red Cell Disorders
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Microcytic + pencil cells + low ferritin | Iron deficiency |
| IDA vs ACD single discriminator | TIBC (high IDA, low/normal ACD) |
| Very low MCV, near-normal Hb, high RBC count | Thalassaemia trait |
| Raised HbA₂ | β-thalassaemia trait |
| Basophilic stippling + microcytosis | Lead poisoning / sideroblastic |
| Macrocytic + hypersegmented neutrophils | Megaloblastic (B12/folate) |
| Macrocytic anaemia + neuro signs (dorsal columns) | B12 deficiency / SACD |
| Why treat B12 before folate | Folate alone can precipitate SACD |
| Bite cells + Heinz bodies, X-linked, fava beans | G6PD deficiency |
| Spherocytes + negative DAT + ↑MCHC | Hereditary spherocytosis |
| Spherocytes + positive DAT | Warm AIHA |
| Cold agglutinins after Mycoplasma/EBV | Cold AIHA (IgM) |
| Intravascular haemolysis + thrombosis + pancytopenia, CD55/CD59 loss | PNH |
| Schistocytes | MAHA (DIC/TTP/HUS/valve) |
| Sickle + sudden aplastic crisis | Parvovirus B19 |
| Sickle drug that raises HbF | Hydroxycarbamide ⚑ |
| Pancytopenia + hypocellular marrow, no infiltrate | Aplastic anaemia |
| Polycythaemia + JAK2 + low EPO + aquagenic pruritus | Polycythaemia vera ⚑ |
| Secondary polycythaemia EPO level | High (unlike PV, where EPO is low) |

##### Sources
Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology (MCV/reticulocyte framework, haemolysis, haemoglobinopathies); BSH guidelines on iron deficiency, sickle cell disease and AIHA; NICE CKS anaemia/B12–folate; StatPearls (G6PD, hereditary spherocytosis, PNH, aplastic anaemia); Robbins (thalassaemia genetics). Hb diagnostic cut-offs follow WHO (men <130, women <120 g/L); labs vary slightly. ⚑ Hydroxycarbamide and JAK2 testing reflect current practice not in older textbooks.

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.h: Haematology & Oncology Notes — Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
*Sources: Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology; BSH (British Society for Haematology) laboratory guidance; NICE suspected-cancer referral guidance (NG12); StatPearls; Robbins. Scope: how to take the history, read the FBC/film, interpret haematinics and the haemolysis screen, run a coagulation/thrombophilia work-up sensibly, and structure an oncology diagnosis. This is the interpretation scaffolding every later section reuses.*

---

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
**The symptom clusters that matter:**

- **Anaemia:** fatigue, dyspnoea, palpitations, pallor, angina.
- **Neutropenia:** recurrent/severe infections, mouth ulcers.
- **Thrombocytopenia/bleeding:** bruising, petechiae, epistaxis, menorrhagia, gum bleeding.
- **B symptoms** (lymphoma/leukaemia staging & prognosis): **fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, weight loss >10% over 6 months.** *Alcohol-induced nodal pain* is a rare but classic Hodgkin clue.
- **Hyperviscosity** (myeloma, Waldenström, high WCC leukaemia): headache, visual disturbance, confusion, mucosal bleeding.
- **Red-flag "cancer" symptoms:** unexplained weight loss, night sweats, bone pain, new lymphadenopathy, unexplained bruising/bleeding.

**Examination:** pallor, jaundice (haemolysis), bruising/petechiae, **lymphadenopathy** (all node groups + character), **hepatosplenomegaly**, bony tenderness (sternal tenderness in leukaemia), fundoscopy (hyperviscosity), and a full systems survey for a primary tumour.

**Performance status** drives every oncology treatment decision — learn the **ECOG/WHO** scale:

| ECOG | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Fully active |
| 1 | Restricted in strenuous activity, ambulatory, light work |
| 2 | Ambulatory, self-caring, **up >50% of waking hours**, no work |
| 3 | Limited self-care, in bed/chair **>50%** of waking hours |
| 4 | Completely disabled, bedbound |
| 5 | Dead |

Rule of thumb: **ECOG ≥3 usually precludes intensive chemotherapy.**

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.h: 3.2 The full blood count & blood film
docs.text:
**Reading an FBC** — go line by line, then think in patterns:

- **Anaemia** → classify by **MCV** (micro <80, normo 80–100, macro >100 fL) — the master framework of Section 4.
- **Pancytopenia** (all three lineages down) → think **marrow failure/infiltration** (aplasia, leukaemia, myeloma, myelofibrosis, megaloblastic anaemia), **hypersplenism**, or **peripheral destruction**. Always a bone marrow question.
- **High WCC** → is it a reactive **neutrophilia** (left shift, toxic granulation, infection), a **leukaemoid reaction** (very high neutrophils with left shift — infection/inflammation; **high LAP score**), or **leukaemia** (blasts; basophilia and **low LAP** point to CML)?
- **Thrombocytosis** → reactive (infection, inflammation, iron deficiency, post-splenectomy, malignancy) vs clonal (essential thrombocythaemia, other MPN).

**Blood-film morphology — the single highest-yield recognition table in haematology:**

| Film finding | Points to |
|---|---|
| **Microcytic hypochromic + pencil cells** | Iron deficiency |
| **Target cells** | Liver disease, thalassaemia, hyposplenism |
| **Spherocytes** | Hereditary spherocytosis or **autoimmune haemolysis** (DAT distinguishes) |
| **Schistocytes (fragments)** | **Microangiopathic haemolysis** — DIC, TTP/HUS, mechanical valve |
| **Bite cells / Heinz bodies** | G6PD deficiency (oxidative haemolysis) |
| **Sickle cells** | Sickle cell disease |
| **Tear-drop cells (dacrocytes)** | Myelofibrosis, marrow infiltration |
| **Rouleaux** (stacked coins) | High paraprotein — **myeloma**, chronic inflammation |
| **Howell–Jolly bodies** | Hyposplenism/post-splenectomy |
| **Blast cells** | Acute leukaemia |
| **Auer rods** | **AML** (pathognomonic) |
| **Smear/smudge cells** | **CLL** |
| **Hypersegmented neutrophils** | Megaloblastic anaemia (B12/folate) |
| **"Left shift" + toxic granulation** | Bacterial infection |

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
**Iron studies — read them as a set, not in isolation:**

| Test | Iron deficiency | Anaemia of chronic disease | Iron overload |
|---|---|---|---|
| Serum iron | ↓ | ↓ | ↑ |
| **Ferritin** | **↓** | **↑ or normal** ⚑ | ↑↑ |
| **TIBC / transferrin** | **↑** | ↓ or normal | ↓ |
| Transferrin saturation | ↓ | ↓/normal | ↑ |

⚑ **Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant** — it rises in infection, inflammation and malignancy, so a "normal" ferritin does **not** exclude iron deficiency in an unwell patient. If in doubt, **transferrin saturation and the film** help; a very low ferritin (<15–30 µg/L) is specific for deficiency. The discriminating pair: **iron deficiency has a *high* TIBC; ACD has a *low/normal* TIBC.**

**B12 & folate** → macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils; low B12 with neurological signs = pernicious anaemia/subacute combined degeneration (**check anti-intrinsic-factor antibodies**; treat B12 before/with folate to avoid precipitating cord degeneration).

**Reticulocyte count** — the "is the marrow responding?" test. **High retics** = appropriate marrow response → **haemolysis or blood loss**. **Low/inappropriately normal retics** with anaemia = a production problem (deficiency, marrow failure, ACD).

**The haemolysis screen** — order these together whenever haemolysis is suspected:

| Test | Haemolysis pattern |
|---|---|
| **LDH** | ↑ (released from lysed cells) |
| **Haptoglobin** | ↓ (consumed mopping up free Hb) — most marked in **intravascular** haemolysis |
| **Unconjugated bilirubin** | ↑ |
| **Reticulocytes** | ↑ |
| **DAT (Coombs)** | **Positive → immune** haemolysis; negative → non-immune (hereditary, mechanical, G6PD) |
| Urinary haemosiderin / haemoglobinuria | Present in intravascular haemolysis |

**Bone marrow examination** — **aspirate** (cell morphology, cytogenetics, flow cytometry, iron stores) vs **trephine** (architecture, cellularity, fibrosis, infiltration). A **dry tap** suggests fibrosis or a packed marrow.

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
**Interpret the coagulation screen by which arm is prolonged:**

| Pattern | Suggests |
|---|---|
| **↑ PT (INR), normal APTT** | Factor VII deficiency; **warfarin**; early liver disease; vitamin K deficiency |
| **Normal PT, ↑ APTT** | **Haemophilia A/B**, **von Willebrand disease**, **heparin**, lupus anticoagulant (paradoxically thrombotic) |
| **Both ↑ (PT + APTT)** | Common-pathway problem: **DIC**, liver failure, vitamin K deficiency, warfarin overdose, massive transfusion |
| **Both normal, but bleeding** | Platelet-type problem (thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction) or mild VWD |

**Mixing study** — mix patient plasma 1:1 with normal plasma. **Corrects → factor deficiency.** **Fails to correct → an inhibitor** (e.g. lupus anticoagulant, factor VIII inhibitor).

**D-dimer** — a fibrin degradation product; **sensitive, not specific.** Useful to *rule out* VTE in a low-probability patient (a negative D-dimer excludes); a positive result has many non-thrombotic causes (infection, malignancy, pregnancy, surgery, age).

**Thrombophilia screen** — factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C, protein S, antithrombin, antiphospholipid antibodies. **Test sparingly and at the right time:** many results are unreliable during acute thrombosis, on anticoagulation, or in pregnancy; it rarely changes management for a first *provoked* VTE. **Antiphospholipid syndrome** is the one worth actively seeking in unexplained arterial/venous thrombosis, recurrent miscarriage, or a prolonged APTT that fails to correct.

**Protein studies** — serum **electrophoresis** (detects a monoclonal band/paraprotein), **immunofixation** (types it — e.g. IgG kappa), **serum free light chains** (κ/λ ratio — key for myeloma diagnosis and light-chain disease), and **urinary Bence Jones protein** (free light chains in urine).

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
**Tumour markers** are aids, not diagnoses — most are neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose or screen (with narrow exceptions). Their real value is **monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence** in a known cancer. Learn the map:

| Marker | Cancer | Caveats / other causes of rise |
|---|---|---|
| **PSA** | Prostate | BPH, prostatitis, catheter, DRE, ejaculation |
| **CA-125** | Ovarian (epithelial) | Endometriosis, ascites, menstruation, any peritoneal irritation |
| **CA 19-9** | Pancreatic, biliary | Cholestasis; absent in Lewis-negative people |
| **CEA** | Colorectal (monitoring) | Smoking, IBD, other GI |
| **AFP** | Hepatocellular, non-seminomatous germ cell | Pregnancy, hepatitis |
| **β-hCG** | Germ cell (choriocarcinoma, non-seminoma), gestational trophoblastic | Pregnancy |
| **AFP + β-hCG** | Testicular (non-seminoma) | Seminoma: β-hCG may rise, **AFP does not** |
| **Calcitonin** | Medullary thyroid | — |
| **Thyroglobulin** | Differentiated thyroid (monitoring) | — |

**Staging investigation set:** **CT** (chest/abdo/pelvis for most solid tumours), **MRI** (local soft-tissue/CNS/rectal/prostate staging), **PET-CT** (metabolically active disease — lymphoma staging, occult mets), **bone scan** (osteoblastic mets — prostate, breast), and site-specific endoscopy.

**Biopsy principles:** **FNA** (cytology only — cells, no architecture; good for confirming a node is malignant), **core biopsy** (histology + receptor/molecular tests — the workhorse for solid tumours), **excisional biopsy** (whole node — needed to diagnose and subtype **lymphoma**, because architecture matters). Always get tissue *before* systemic therapy.

**TNM staging** (Tumour size/depth, Node involvement, Metastasis) + **histological grade** (differentiation) together give prognosis; the **multidisciplinary team (MDT)** integrates radiology, pathology, surgery, oncology and specialist nursing to agree a plan. **NICE NG12** defines the **2-week-wait urgent referral** thresholds by symptom cluster (e.g. iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult, dysphagia, PR bleeding with change in bowel habit, post-menopausal bleeding, haematuria).

---

docs.title: Clinical Assessment & Investigations
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| B symptoms | Fever >38, drenching night sweats, weight loss >10%/6 months |
| ECOG cut-off that usually precludes intensive chemo | ≥3 (bed/chair >50% of waking hours) |
| Iron deficiency vs ACD single best discriminator | **TIBC/transferrin high in deficiency, low/normal in ACD** |
| Why a normal ferritin doesn't exclude iron deficiency | Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant ⚑ |
| Reticulocytes high in anaemia | Haemolysis or blood loss (marrow responding) |
| DAT positive | Immune haemolysis |
| Haptoglobin low + haemoglobinuria | Intravascular haemolysis |
| Isolated ↑APTT that fails to correct on mixing | Inhibitor — think lupus anticoagulant/factor inhibitor |
| Mixing study corrects | Factor deficiency |
| ↑PT + ↑APTT + ↓platelets + ↓fibrinogen + ↑D-dimer | DIC |
| Rouleaux on film | Paraprotein (myeloma) |
| Auer rods | AML |
| Smear cells | CLL |
| Tumour marker for testicular non-seminoma | AFP + β-hCG (AFP not raised in pure seminoma) |
| Biopsy needed to diagnose lymphoma | Excisional (architecture) — not FNA |
| Osteoblastic mets imaging | Bone scan (prostate, breast) |

##### Sources
Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology (FBC/film, haematinics, coagulation interpretation); BSH laboratory and thrombophilia-testing guidance (when to test); NICE NG12 (suspected-cancer referral, 2-week-wait); StatPearls (tumour markers, DAT/haemolysis screen); Robbins (staging/grading principles). Note: ferritin reference cut-offs for iron deficiency vary by assay/lab and by inflammatory state — the film and transferrin saturation resolve borderline cases.

docs.title: Haematological Malignancies
docs.text:
*Sources: Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology; WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours (5th ed, 2022) & ICC; BSH guidelines; IMWG criteria (myeloma); Robbins; StatPearls; NICE. Scope: the leukaemias, lymphomas, plasma-cell disorders and myeloproliferative/myelodysplastic neoplasms — recognition, key cytogenetics, staging, and outline management. Cytogenetic translocations and film clues are the highest-yield content; drilled in the recognition summary.*

---

docs.title: Haematological Malignancies
docs.text:
Two axes classify blood cancers: **acute vs chronic** (acute = immature **blasts**, rapid, marrow failure; chronic = more mature cells, indolent) and **myeloid vs lymphoid** (lineage). The four-box grid — **AML, ALL, CML, CLL** — plus lymphomas, myeloma and the MPN/MDS group covers finals.

**The acute-leukaemia presentation** = **marrow failure**: anaemia (fatigue/pallor), neutropenia (infection), thrombocytopenia (bleeding/bruising), ± infiltration (bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, gum hypertrophy in monocytic AML, CNS/testicular in ALL). **Blasts on the film** + a **hypercellular marrow packed with blasts (≥20%)** clinch acute leukaemia.

docs.title: Haematological Malignancies
docs.text:
**Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)** — mainly **older adults**. Myeloid blasts; **Auer rods are pathognomonic**; myeloperoxidase-positive. Associated with prior MDS, chemo/radiotherapy, Down syndrome. Diagnosis by marrow (≥20% blasts), flow cytometry, cytogenetics/molecular (prognostic: NPM1, FLT3, core-binding-factor translocations).

- **⚑ Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL, AML-M3)** is the can't-miss subtype: **t(15;17) PML–RARA**, presents with **DIC and life-threatening bleeding**. Treatment is a haematological emergency: **all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) + arsenic trioxide** (differentiation therapy), started on clinical suspicion before genetics confirm, plus aggressive DIC support. APL is now highly curable — recognising it early saves lives.

**Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL)** — the **commonest childhood cancer** (peak 2–5 years). Lymphoid blasts (usually B-lineage, TdT-positive). Features: marrow failure + **CNS and testicular involvement** (sanctuary sites needing dedicated prophylaxis), bone pain, lymphadenopathy. High **tumour-lysis** risk on starting treatment. **Philadelphia-positive ALL** [t(9;22)] carries worse prognosis and gets a **TKI** added. Long, phased chemotherapy (induction → consolidation → CNS prophylaxis → maintenance); good paediatric cure rates.

docs.title: Haematological Malignancies
docs.text:
**Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML)** — a myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by the **Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) → BCR-ABL1 fusion** (a constitutively active tyrosine kinase). Middle age; often incidental **marked leucocytosis with the whole granulocyte series + basophilia**, massive splenomegaly, low **LAP score** (distinguishes from a leukaemoid reaction, which has high LAP). Three phases: **chronic → accelerated → blast crisis** (transforms to acute leukaemia). **⚑ Treatment revolutionised by TKIs** — first-line **imatinib** (or a second-generation TKI: dasatinib/nilotinib/bosutinib), with molecular monitoring of *BCR-ABL1* transcripts; life expectancy now approaches normal. Ponatinib for the resistant **T315I** mutation.

**Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL)** — commonest leukaemia in **older adults in the West**; clonal mature **B lymphocytes**. Often an incidental **lymphocytosis**; **smear/smudge cells** on film; lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly. Complications: **autoimmune haemolytic anaemia/ITP**, hypogammaglobulinaemia (infections), and **Richter's transformation** to aggressive lymphoma (rapid nodal enlargement, systemic symptoms). Stage by **Binet/Rai**; many need only watchful waiting. Treatment when progressive: **BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib) and BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax** have largely replaced chemoimmunotherapy ⚑; prognosis stratified by **del(17p)/TP53, IGHV mutation status**.

docs.title: Haematological Malignancies
docs.text:
Lymphomas are solid tumours of lymphoid tissue, split into **Hodgkin** and **non-Hodgkin**. Both present with **painless lymphadenopathy ± B symptoms**; diagnosis needs an **excisional node biopsy** (architecture). Staged by **Ann Arbor** (I–IV; suffix **A** = no B symptoms, **B** = B symptoms present) with PET-CT.

**Hodgkin lymphoma (HL)** — **Reed–Sternberg cells** ("owl-eye" binucleate cells, CD15+/CD30+) in an inflammatory background. **Bimodal age** (young adults + elderly), EBV-associated. Clues: **contiguous nodal spread from the neck**, **alcohol-induced nodal pain**, "**B symptoms**", mediastinal mass. Nodular sclerosing is commonest. **Highly curable** with chemotherapy (ABVD) ± radiotherapy; long-term survivorship issues (secondary cancers, cardiac, infertility) drive de-escalation.

**Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL)** — a heterogeneous group, mostly **B-cell**; often **non-contiguous/extranodal** spread:

| Type | Pace | Key feature |
|---|---|---|
| **Diffuse large B-cell (DLBCL)** | Aggressive | Commonest NHL; rapidly enlarging mass; curable with **R-CHOP** |
| **Follicular** | Indolent | **t(14;18) → BCL-2**; waxing/waning; often incurable but long survival |
| **Burkitt** | Highly aggressive | **t(8;14) → MYC**; "starry-sky" histology; **jaw mass (endemic/EBV)** or abdominal; extreme **tumour-lysis** risk |
| **MALT / marginal zone** | Indolent | Gastric MALT linked to ***H. pylori*** (may regress with eradication) |
| **Mantle cell** | Aggressive | **t(11;14) → cyclin D1** |

docs.title: Haematological Malignancies
docs.text:
**Multiple myeloma** — malignant clonal **plasma cells** producing a **monoclonal paraprotein (M-protein)**. Remember the end-organ damage as **CRAB**, with three added **SLiM** biomarkers that now define myeloma even without CRAB:

**⚑ IMWG diagnostic criteria** — clonal bone-marrow plasma cells **≥10%** (or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) **plus ≥1** of:
- **CRAB:** **C**alcium raised (>2.75 mmol/L or >0.25 above ULN); **R**enal (creatinine >177 µmol/L or creatinine clearance <40 mL/min); **A**naemia (Hb <100 g/L or >20 below normal); **B**one lesions (≥1 lytic lesion on X-ray/CT/PET).
- **SLiM:** **S**ixty percent — clonal marrow plasma cells **≥60%**; **Li**ght chains — involved:uninvolved serum free light-chain ratio **≥100** (involved ≥100 mg/L); **M**RI — **>1 focal lesion ≥5 mm**.

Clinical: bone pain (lytic lesions, **"pepper-pot" skull**, fractures), hypercalcaemia, renal failure (light-chain/cast nephropathy), anaemia, recurrent infection (immunoparesis), hyperviscosity, cord compression. Investigations: **serum/urine electrophoresis + immunofixation, serum free light chains, β2-microglobulin (prognosis), skeletal survey/whole-body MRI or CT, marrow.** Film: **rouleaux**. Treatment (incurable but very treatable): proteasome inhibitors (bortezomib), immunomodulators (lenalidomide), **anti-CD38 (daratumumab)**, steroids, ± autologous stem-cell transplant; bisphosphonates for bone disease. **⚑ Note: modern imaging is whole-body CT/MRI/PET, not the old plain skeletal survey alone; a bone scan is *not* used (lesions are lytic, not osteoblastic).**

**MGUS** (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance) — paraprotein **<30 g/L**, marrow plasma cells **<10%**, **no CRAB/SLiM**; a common, asymptomatic precursor with ~1%/year progression to myeloma — monitor.

**Smouldering myeloma** — between MGUS and myeloma (paraprotein ≥30 g/L or 10–60% plasma cells) but **no myeloma-defining event**; higher progression rate, observed closely.

**Waldenström macroglobulinaemia** — a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma making **IgM** → **hyperviscosity** (visual disturbance, mucosal bleeding, neuro) without lytic bone lesions; MYD88 mutation; plasmapheresis for hyperviscosity.

**Amyloidosis (AL)** — light-chain deposition → nephrotic syndrome, restrictive cardiomyopathy, macroglossia, neuropathy; **Congo red apple-green birefringence** on biopsy.

docs.title: Haematological Malignancies
docs.text:
**Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN)** — clonal overproduction of mature myeloid cells; **JAK2/CALR/MPL** driver mutations ⚑; risk of thrombosis and marrow-failure transformation:

| MPN | Cell overproduced | Hallmark | Key point |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Polycythaemia vera** | Red cells | **JAK2 V617F (>95%)**, low EPO, aquagenic pruritus | Venesect + aspirin ± hydroxycarbamide |
| **Essential thrombocythaemia** | Platelets | Platelets ↑↑ (>450), JAK2/CALR | Thrombosis/bleeding; aspirin ± cytoreduction |
| **Primary myelofibrosis** | Fibrosis of marrow | **Tear-drop cells, leukoerythroblastic film, massive splenomegaly, dry tap** | JAK inhibitor (ruxolitinib); worst prognosis |
| **CML** | Granulocytes | **BCR-ABL1** (see 7.3) | The Philadelphia MPN |

**Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS)** — clonal marrow **dysplasia with ineffective haematopoiesis** → **cytopenias despite a cellular marrow**, in older adults. Blasts <20% (≥20% = AML). Risk stratify (IPSS-R); risk of transformation to AML. Supportive care/transfusion, hypomethylating agents (azacitidine), transplant in selected fit patients.

---

docs.title: Haematological Malignancies
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Auer rods | AML |
| **t(15;17) / PML–RARA + DIC** | APL — ATRA emergency ⚑ |
| Commonest childhood cancer, blasts + CNS/testicular | ALL |
| **Philadelphia t(9;22) BCR-ABL1** | CML (also Ph+ ALL) |
| Basophilia + massive spleen + low LAP score | CML |
| High LAP score, very high neutrophils, infection | Leukaemoid reaction (not CML) |
| Smear/smudge cells + lymphocytosis, older adult | CLL |
| CLL + rapid nodal growth + systemic symptoms | Richter's transformation |
| CLL + AAT / ITP | Autoimmune cytopenia of CLL |
| Reed–Sternberg (owl-eye) cells | Hodgkin lymphoma |
| Alcohol-induced nodal pain / contiguous neck spread | Hodgkin lymphoma |
| Commonest NHL, aggressive, R-CHOP | DLBCL |
| **t(14;18) BCL-2** | Follicular lymphoma |
| **t(8;14) MYC**, starry sky, jaw mass | Burkitt lymphoma (huge TLS risk) |
| Gastric lymphoma linked to *H. pylori* | MALT lymphoma |
| **t(11;14) cyclin D1** | Mantle cell lymphoma |
| CRAB + paraprotein + rouleaux + lytic lesions | Multiple myeloma |
| Myeloma SLiM: plasma cells / FLC ratio / MRI ⚑ | ≥60% / ≥100 / >1 focal lesion |
| Paraprotein <30, marrow PC <10%, no CRAB | MGUS |
| IgM paraprotein + hyperviscosity, no bone lesions | Waldenström macroglobulinaemia |
| Congo red apple-green birefringence | AL amyloidosis |
| JAK2 V617F + low EPO + itch after hot bath | Polycythaemia vera ⚑ |
| Tear-drop cells + dry tap + massive spleen | Myelofibrosis |
| Cytopenias with a cellular dysplastic marrow, blasts <20% | Myelodysplastic syndrome |

##### Sources
Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology; WHO 5th-edition classification of haematolymphoid tumours (2022); BSH guidelines (AML/APL, CLL, myeloma); **IMWG diagnostic criteria (SLiM-CRAB, myeloma.org / IMWG 2014 update)**; Robbins (lymphoma cytogenetics); StatPearls; NICE. Blast threshold for acute leukaemia (≥20%) per WHO. ⚑ TKI-first CML, BTKi/venetoclax in CLL, JAK2/CALR MPN drivers, and whole-body imaging (not skeletal survey) in myeloma reflect current practice beyond older textbooks.

docs.title: Haematology–Oncology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.h: Haematology & Oncology Notes — Haematology–Oncology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
*Sources: BNF; Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology; NICE; StatPearls; Martindale. Scope: the drugs a finalist must recognise, dose safely, and monitor — haematinics, anticoagulants, cytotoxics and their signature toxicities, targeted/immune agents, and supportive drugs. Emphasis on the toxicities and prescribing-safety traps that come up in written papers and OSCEs.*

---

docs.title: Haematology–Oncology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
| Drug | Use | Watch |
|---|---|---|
| **Ferrous sulfate/fumarate (oral iron)** | Iron deficiency | GI upset, black stools, constipation; take with vitamin C, avoid with tea/PPIs; Hb rise ~20 g/L/month |
| **IV iron** (ferric carboxymaltose) | Intolerance/malabsorption, CKD, rapid need | Anaphylaxis (rare), staining at site |
| **Hydroxocobalamin (B12)** | B12 deficiency/PA | IM loading; treat **before/with** folate (avoid SACD) |
| **Folic acid** | Folate deficiency, pregnancy | Exclude B12 deficiency first |
| **Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents** (epoetin, darbepoetin) | Renal anaemia, some chemo anaemia | Ensure iron-replete; hypertension, thrombosis; avoid over-correcting Hb |
| **G-CSF (filgrastim)** | Post-chemo neutropenia, stem-cell mobilisation | Bone pain |
| **Iron chelators** (desferrioxamine, deferasirox) | Transfusional iron overload (thalassaemia) | Visual/auditory (desferrioxamine), renal (deferasirox) |

docs.title: Haematology–Oncology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
*(Mechanisms/reversal detailed in Section 5.5 — summarised here.)*

- **Unfractionated heparin** — IV, monitor **APTT**, reversed by **protamine**; use when rapid on/off needed (renal failure, peri-procedure).
- **LMWH (enoxaparin, dalteparin)** — subcut, predictable, no routine monitoring (anti-Xa in renal impairment/pregnancy/extremes of weight); VTE treatment/prophylaxis, ACS.
- **Warfarin** — vitamin K antagonist, **INR** monitoring, many interactions, **teratogenic**, initial procoagulant effect (bridge with heparin); reversal **vitamin K/PCC**. Still first-line for **mechanical valves and antiphospholipid syndrome** ⚑.
- **DOACs** — **dabigatran** (direct thrombin; reversal **idarucizumab**) and **apixaban/rivaroxaban/edoxaban** (direct Xa; reversal **andexanet alfa/PCC**). No routine monitoring; **renally cleared** (caution/avoid in severe renal impairment); now first-line for most VTE/AF and much cancer-associated thrombosis ⚑; **avoid in mechanical valves and triple-positive APS**.
- **Fondaparinux** — synthetic Xa inhibitor (used in ACS, HIT).
- **Antiplatelets** — **aspirin** (COX-1 → ↓thromboxane), **P2Y12 inhibitors** (clopidogrel/ticagrelor/prasugrel); bleeding risk.
- **Thrombolytics** (alteplase/tenecteplase) — massive PE, stroke, STEMI; major bleeding risk.

docs.title: Haematology–Oncology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
Cytotoxics damage rapidly dividing cells → **shared toxicities: myelosuppression (nadir ~7–14 days), mucositis, alopecia, nausea/vomiting, infertility, second malignancy, tumour lysis.** Learn the **class-specific signature toxicities** (a favourite written-paper item):

| Class | Examples | Mechanism | Signature toxicity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Alkylating agents** | Cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide | Cross-link DNA | **Haemorrhagic cystitis** (give **mesna**); infertility, secondary leukaemia |
| **Platinum agents** | Cisplatin, carboplatin, oxaliplatin | DNA cross-links | **Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, peripheral neuropathy** (cisplatin); **cold-induced neuropathy** (oxaliplatin) |
| **Antimetabolites** | Methotrexate, 5-FU, capecitabine, gemcitabine | Block DNA synthesis | MTX: mucositis, myelosuppression, hepatic/pulmonary — **folinic acid rescue**; 5-FU: mucositis, diarrhoea, coronary spasm |
| **Anthracyclines** | Doxorubicin, daunorubicin | Topoisomerase II, free radicals | **Cardiotoxicity** (cumulative, dose-limiting — monitor LVEF); red urine |
| **Vinca alkaloids** | Vincristine, vinblastine | Inhibit microtubule assembly | **Peripheral neuropathy** (vincristine); **vincristine is fatal if given intrathecally** ⚑ |
| **Taxanes** | Paclitaxel, docetaxel | Stabilise microtubules | Peripheral neuropathy, hypersensitivity, myelosuppression |
| **Topoisomerase inhibitors** | Etoposide, irinotecan | Block topoisomerase | Irinotecan: diarrhoea; myelosuppression |
| **Bleomycin** | — | DNA strand breaks | **Pulmonary fibrosis**; minimal myelosuppression |

⚑ **Vincristine intrathecal error** is a never-event that has killed patients — vinca alkaloids are IV only.

docs.title: Haematology–Oncology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
| Agent / class | Target | Key toxicity / note |
|---|---|---|
| **Imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib** | BCR-ABL1 (CML), c-KIT (GIST) | Oedema, cytopenias; transformed CML prognosis ⚑ |
| **Osimertinib/erlotinib** | EGFR (NSCLC) | Rash, diarrhoea |
| **Rituximab** | CD20 (B-cell lymphoma/CLL, autoimmune) | Infusion reactions, hepatitis B reactivation, infection |
| **Trastuzumab (Herceptin)** | HER2 (breast, gastric) | **Cardiotoxicity** (esp. with anthracyclines) — monitor LVEF |
| **Bevacizumab** | VEGF | Hypertension, bleeding, poor wound healing, GI perforation |
| **Cetuximab** | EGFR (RAS-WT colorectal, H&N) | Acneiform rash, hypomagnesaemia |
| **Checkpoint inhibitors** (pembrolizumab/nivolumab PD-1; atezolizumab PD-L1; ipilimumab CTLA-4) | Immune checkpoints | **Immune-related adverse events** — colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis/hypophysitis — treat with **steroids** ⚑ |
| **CAR-T cell therapy** | CD19 (refractory B-cell) | **Cytokine release syndrome** (fever/hypotension — tocilizumab), neurotoxicity ⚑ |
| **Endocrine — tamoxifen** | ER antagonist (breast tissue) | VTE, endometrial cancer, hot flushes (pre-menopausal) |
| **Endocrine — aromatase inhibitors** (anastrozole/letrozole) | Block peripheral oestrogen synthesis | Osteoporosis, arthralgia (**post**-menopausal breast) |
| **Androgen deprivation** (GnRH agonists — goserelin; anti-androgens) | Testosterone suppression (prostate) | Hot flushes, bone loss, metabolic; **initial tumour flare** with GnRH agonists |

docs.title: Haematology–Oncology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
- **Antiemetics by emetogenic risk:** low → metoclopramide/domperidone; moderate–high → **5-HT₃ antagonists (ondansetron)** + **dexamethasone** ± **NK1 antagonist (aprepitant)**; anticipatory → lorazepam.
- **Tumour-lysis prophylaxis:** **allopurinol** (xanthine oxidase inhibitor — prevents urate formation) or **rasburicase** (recombinant urate oxidase — breaks down existing urate; **avoid in G6PD deficiency**), with IV hydration.
- **Bone-targeted:** **bisphosphonates** (zoledronic acid — hypercalcaemia of malignancy, myeloma/metastatic bone disease; watch osteonecrosis of the jaw, renal) and **denosumab** (RANKL antibody).
- **Growth factors:** G-CSF (neutropenia), ESAs (anaemia), TPO agonists (ITP).
- **Analgesia:** WHO ladder (Section 8.5); **allopurinol interacts with azathioprine/6-MP** (blocks their metabolism → toxicity — reduce dose).

docs.title: Haematology–Oncology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
High-yield safety points, each an exam favourite:
- **Neutropenic sepsis:** never delay broad-spectrum antibiotics for the blood count. ⚑
- **Methotrexate is dosed WEEKLY, not daily** — daily dosing is a fatal error; co-prescribe **folic acid** (on a different day) and monitor FBC/LFTs; **folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue** for high-dose/toxicity.
- **Vincristine is intravenous only** — intrathecal administration is fatal. ⚑
- **Warfarin** — check interactions and INR; **teratogenic**.
- **Chemotherapy is dosed by body-surface area / AUC (carboplatin)** — verify calculations; cytotoxics need safe handling.
- **Allopurinol + azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine** — dangerous interaction (reduce thiopurine dose).
- **Trastuzumab/anthracyclines** — monitor cardiac function.
- **ESAs** — do not over-correct Hb (thrombosis risk); ensure iron-replete first.

---

docs.title: Haematology–Oncology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Cyclophosphamide bladder toxicity + antidote | Haemorrhagic cystitis — mesna |
| Cisplatin triad of toxicity | Nephro-, oto-, neurotoxicity |
| Oxaliplatin neuropathy trigger | Cold |
| Doxorubicin dose-limiting toxicity | Cardiotoxicity (monitor LVEF) |
| Bleomycin signature toxicity | Pulmonary fibrosis |
| Vincristine fatal error | Intrathecal administration ⚑ |
| Methotrexate dosing trap + rescue | Weekly (not daily); folinic acid rescue |
| Trastuzumab toxicity | Cardiotoxicity |
| Bevacizumab toxicities | HTN, bleeding, poor wound healing, GI perforation |
| Checkpoint inhibitor toxicity + treatment | irAEs (colitis/pneumonitis/endocrine) — steroids ⚑ |
| CAR-T acute toxicity | Cytokine release syndrome (tocilizumab) ⚑ |
| Tamoxifen serious risks | VTE, endometrial cancer |
| Aromatase inhibitor use + toxicity | Post-menopausal breast; osteoporosis/arthralgia |
| GnRH agonist prostate caution | Initial testosterone flare |
| Allopurinol vs rasburicase mechanism | Prevents urate formation vs breaks down urate |
| Rasburicase contraindication | G6PD deficiency |
| Bisphosphonate long-term risk | Osteonecrosis of jaw, renal |
| Allopurinol + azathioprine | Reduce thiopurine (toxicity) |
| Warfarin still first-line over DOAC | Mechanical valve, triple-positive APS ⚑ |
| Rituximab pre-treatment check | Hepatitis B status (reactivation) |

##### Sources
BNF (dosing, interactions, monitoring); Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology; NICE (anticoagulation, chemotherapy safety, antiemetics); StatPearls; Martindale. ⚑ TKI/immunotherapy/CAR-T agents and their toxicities, DOAC-first anticoagulation, and the vincristine-intrathecal and methotrexate-weekly never-events reflect current safety guidance emphasised beyond older textbooks.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.h: Haematology & Oncology Notes — Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
*Sources: Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology; BSH guidelines (ITP, TTP, VTE, DIC, massive haemorrhage, transfusion); NICE NG158 (VTE), NG89; AABB 2023/2025 red-cell transfusion guidelines; SHOT (Serious Hazards of Transfusion) reports; StatPearls. Scope: the bleeding and clotting disorders, anticoagulation, and the transfusion medicine a finalist must manage acutely. TTP and the ABO transfusion reaction are emergencies — flagged throughout.*

---

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
Distinguish two bleeding phenotypes at the bedside — it points straight at the mechanism:

| Feature | **Platelet-type** (primary haemostasis) | **Coagulation-type** (secondary haemostasis) |
|---|---|---|
| Bleeding site | **Mucocutaneous** — petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, menorrhagia, gums | **Deep** — haemarthroses, muscle haematoma, retroperitoneal |
| Timing | Immediate after injury | **Delayed** (plug forms then fails) |
| Causes | Thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, VWD | Haemophilia, DIC, warfarin, liver disease |

Then read the **coagulation screen** (PT/APTT/fibrinogen/platelets — see Section 3.4) to localise the defect.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
Low platelets arise from **reduced production** (marrow failure/infiltration, drugs, alcohol, B12/folate), **increased destruction** (immune/consumption), or **sequestration** (hypersplenism).

**Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)** — isolated thrombocytopenia, autoantibody-mediated. Children: post-viral, acute, self-limiting. Adults: chronic; secondary to SLE, CLL, HIV, *H. pylori*. Diagnosis of exclusion (normal film otherwise, no other cause). **Treat only if bleeding or platelets very low** — first-line **corticosteroids ± IVIG**; second-line TPO-receptor agonists (eltrombopag/romiplostim), rituximab, splenectomy.

**Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)** ⚑ — **a haematological emergency.** Deficiency of **ADAMTS13** (the VWF-cleaving protease; autoantibody in acquired form) → ultra-large VWF multimers → platelet-rich microthrombi → **microangiopathic haemolysis**. The **pentad** (rarely all present): **MAHA (schistocytes) + thrombocytopenia + neurological signs + renal impairment + fever.** **Coagulation screen is normal** (unlike DIC). **Do NOT give platelet transfusions** (fuels thrombosis) unless life-threatening haemorrhage. Treatment is **urgent plasma exchange** + steroids (± caplacizumab, rituximab).

**Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)** — MAHA + thrombocytopenia + **acute kidney injury**, predominantly in **children after Shiga-toxin *E. coli* O157 (bloody diarrhoea)**; renal-dominant, neurology usually milder. Mainly supportive; **avoid antibiotics** in typical STEC-HUS (may increase toxin release). Atypical HUS (complement dysregulation) → eculizumab.

**Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)** — IgG antibodies to **platelet factor 4–heparin** complexes, 5–10 days after starting heparin (sooner if re-exposed); a **fall in platelets >50% + paradoxical thrombosis** (not bleeding). Use the **4Ts score**. Management: **stop all heparin, start a non-heparin anticoagulant** (argatroban, danaparoid, fondaparinux); **do not give platelets**; warfarin only once platelets recover.

**Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)** — systemic activation of coagulation (sepsis, malignancy — esp. **APL**, obstetric, trauma) consuming clotting factors and platelets → simultaneous **bleeding and thrombosis**. Labs: **↓platelets, ↑PT + ↑APTT, ↓fibrinogen, ↑↑D-dimer, schistocytes.** Treat the **cause**; supportive component replacement (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate) only if bleeding.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
**Haemophilia** — **X-linked recessive**, so affects males; deep bleeding (haemarthroses, muscle bleeds). **A** = factor **VIII** deficiency (commoner); **B** ("Christmas disease") = factor **IX**. **Isolated prolonged APTT, normal PT/platelets/VWF.** Severity tracks factor level (<1% severe). Treat with **factor concentrate/recombinant factor** (or emicizumab prophylaxis for haemophilia A); desmopressin for mild A. Avoid IM injections/NSAIDs.

**Von Willebrand disease (VWD)** — **the commonest inherited bleeding disorder**; autosomal (usually dominant). VWF does two jobs — platelet adhesion **and** carrying factor VIII — so it causes **mucocutaneous (platelet-type) bleeding** and can prolong the APTT (low factor VIII). Type 1 (partial quantitative, commonest), 2 (qualitative), 3 (complete). Treat with **desmopressin (DDAVP)** ± VWF-containing concentrate; tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeds.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
**Virchow's triad** underlies venous thromboembolism (**DVT/PE**). Risk factors: surgery/immobility, malignancy, pregnancy/oestrogen, previous VTE, and **inherited/acquired thrombophilias**:

| Inherited | Acquired |
|---|---|
| **Factor V Leiden** (commonest; APC resistance) | **Antiphospholipid syndrome** |
| Prothrombin G20210A | Malignancy |
| Protein C / protein S / antithrombin deficiency | Pregnancy, oestrogens, nephrotic syndrome |

**Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)** — arterial **and** venous thrombosis, **recurrent miscarriage**, thrombocytopenia; antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein-I). Paradox: **prolonged APTT in vitro but thrombotic in vivo.** Long-term **warfarin** (DOACs are inferior in triple-positive/arterial APS ⚑); aspirin + LMWH in pregnancy.

**Diagnosis of VTE:** risk-stratify (Wells score) → **D-dimer** to exclude if low probability → **Doppler USS** (DVT) or **CTPA** (PE; V/Q if contrast contraindicated). **Provoked** (transient risk factor) vs **unprovoked** VTE guides duration. **Cancer-associated thrombosis** — historically LMWH; **⚑ DOACs (edoxaban, apixaban, rivaroxaban) are now first-line for most, with caution in GI/GU tumours** (bleeding).

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
| Drug | Target | Monitoring | Reversal ⚑ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Unfractionated heparin** | Antithrombin → IIa & Xa | **APTT** (or anti-Xa) | **Protamine sulfate** |
| **LMWH** (enoxaparin) | Antithrombin → mainly Xa | Usually none (anti-Xa if renal/pregnancy/extremes of weight) | Protamine (partial) |
| **Warfarin** | Vitamin-K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X | **INR** | **Vitamin K**; **PCC** (Prothrombin Complex Concentrate) for major bleeding; FFP if PCC unavailable |
| **Dabigatran** | Direct thrombin (IIa) | None routine | **Idarucizumab** |
| **Apixaban/rivaroxaban/edoxaban** | Direct factor **Xa** | None routine | **Andexanet alfa** (or PCC) |

Key safety points: **warfarin is teratogenic** (use LMWH in pregnancy); it has an **initial procoagulant effect** (protein C falls first) → bridge with heparin/LMWH when starting for acute thrombosis; countless interactions (CYP450). **DOACs** are renally cleared (avoid/reduce in severe renal impairment) and are **contraindicated in antiphospholipid syndrome (triple-positive) and mechanical heart valves** ⚑ (warfarin only there).

---

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
**ABO** is the critical system — antibodies are **naturally occurring IgM** and cause immediate intravascular haemolysis if mismatched. **Group O = universal red-cell donor; group AB = universal recipient. Group AB plasma is the universal plasma (FFP) donor** (opposite of red cells). **RhD**: RhD-negative patients can form anti-D after exposure → matters in transfusion and in **pregnancy (haemolytic disease of the newborn; give anti-D prophylaxis).**

**Pre-transfusion testing:** **Group & save** (ABO/RhD + antibody screen, no unit assigned) for possible need; **crossmatch** (units physically/electronically matched) when transfusion is likely. Emergency: **O-negative** (or group-specific) blood before crossmatch completes.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
| Component | Contains | Main indication |
|---|---|---|
| **Red cells** | RBCs | Symptomatic anaemia / significant blood loss |
| **Platelets** | Platelets | Thrombocytopenic bleeding or prophylaxis (e.g. <10 ×10⁹/L, or pre-procedure) |
| **Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)** | All clotting factors | Bleeding + coagulopathy (↑PT/APTT), DIC, warfarin reversal only if PCC unavailable |
| **Cryoprecipitate** | Fibrinogen, VWF, VIII, XIII | **Low fibrinogen** (<1.5 g/L, or <2 in obstetric haemorrhage), DIC |

**Restrictive transfusion is the default.** For **most haemodynamically stable inpatients, transfuse at Hb <70 g/L**, aiming for **70–90 g/L**; use **<80 g/L** for patients with **chronic cardiovascular disease** or post-cardiac surgery. **⚑ Exception — acute coronary syndrome/acute MI:** the **2025 AABB guideline now suggests a more liberal strategy (transfuse to keep Hb around 80–100 g/L)**, a shift from the older uniform restrictive threshold, based on the MINT trial and meta-analyses; this remains an area where sources differ, so state both the general restrictive rule and the acute-MI exception. Transfuse **one unit at a time and reassess** in non-bleeding patients.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
**Acute (within 24 h):**

| Reaction | Mechanism | Recognition | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Acute haemolytic (ABO incompatibility)** ⚑ | IgM against wrong ABO group — usually a **clerical error** | Fever, loin/back pain, hypotension, dark urine, DIC — **during** transfusion | **STOP immediately**, resuscitate (fluids), check identity, inform lab; can be fatal |
| **Febrile non-haemolytic** | Anti-leucocyte antibodies/cytokines | Isolated fever/rigors | Slow/stop, antipyretic; usually continue cautiously |
| **Allergic / urticarial** | Antibodies to donor plasma proteins | Itch, urticaria | Antihistamine, slow rate |
| **Anaphylaxis** | Often **IgA deficiency** with anti-IgA | Hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema | STOP, adrenaline, resuscitate |
| **TACO** (circulatory overload) | Volume overload | **Hypertension**, dyspnoea, raised JVP, pulmonary oedema | Slow/stop, **diuretics, O₂**, sit up |
| **TRALI** | Donor anti-leucocyte antibodies → pulmonary capillary leak | **Hypotension**, dyspnoea, bilateral infiltrates within 6 h | STOP, respiratory support; report |
| **Bacterial contamination** | Contaminated unit (esp. platelets, stored at room temp) | High fever, rigors, shock | STOP, cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics |

**TACO vs TRALI** — both cause acute dyspnoea/pulmonary oedema during/after transfusion; **TACO is hypertensive and fluid-overloaded (responds to diuretics); TRALI is hypotensive with normal filling pressures (do not diurese, support ventilation).**

**Delayed:** delayed haemolytic reaction (days later, falling Hb, positive DAT), transfusion-associated GvHD (irradiate products for at-risk patients), iron overload (chronic transfusion), post-transfusion purpura.

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
**Major haemorrhage protocol** — activate for loss of one blood volume in ~24 h or rapid ongoing loss. Give **red cells, FFP and platelets in a balanced ratio** (empirically ~1:1:1 until guided by results), replace **fibrinogen (cryoprecipitate) if <1.5 g/L**, give **tranexamic acid** (early, especially in trauma — CRASH-2), keep the patient warm, and correct calcium (citrate chelation), acidosis and coagulopathy (the "lethal triad": hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy). Reverse anticoagulants (PCC for warfarin, specific agents for DOACs). Obstetric and trauma haemorrhage have dedicated pathways.

---

docs.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis & Transfusion
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Mucocutaneous bleeding + immediate | Platelet-type (thrombocytopenia/VWD) |
| Deep/delayed bleeding (haemarthrosis) | Coagulation-type (haemophilia) |
| MAHA + thrombocytopenia + neuro + renal + fever, **normal clotting** | TTP (ADAMTS13) — plasma exchange, **no platelets** ⚑ |
| MAHA + AKI in a child after bloody diarrhoea | HUS (STEC O157) |
| Platelets ↓>50% + thrombosis 5–10 days into heparin | HIT — stop heparin, non-heparin anticoagulant |
| ↓platelets + ↑PT/APTT + ↓fibrinogen + ↑↑D-dimer | DIC |
| Commonest inherited bleeding disorder | Von Willebrand disease |
| Isolated ↑APTT, X-linked, haemarthrosis | Haemophilia (A = VIII, B = IX) |
| Thrombosis + miscarriage + ↑APTT that won't correct | Antiphospholipid syndrome — warfarin (not DOAC) ⚑ |
| Universal red cell donor / universal plasma donor | O red cells / AB plasma |
| Default restrictive transfusion threshold | Hb <70 (80 if cardiac disease) |
| Acute-MI transfusion target ⚑ | More liberal (~80–100 g/L) per 2025 AABB |
| Fever + loin pain + shock during transfusion | Acute haemolytic (ABO) — STOP, resuscitate |
| Hypertensive pulmonary oedema post-transfusion | TACO — diurese |
| Hypotensive bilateral infiltrates <6 h | TRALI — support, don't diurese |
| Anaphylaxis to transfusion | Consider IgA deficiency |
| Warfarin major-bleed reversal | Vitamin K + PCC |
| Dabigatran / factor Xa DOAC reversal | Idarucizumab / andexanet alfa |
| Antidote to heparin | Protamine sulfate |

##### Sources
Hoffbrand's Essential Haematology; BSH guidelines (ITP, TTP/ADAMTS13, HIT, DIC, VTE, transfusion, massive haemorrhage); NICE NG158 (VTE) and NG89; **AABB 2023 red-cell transfusion thresholds and 2025 AABB acute-MI guideline** (the liberal-threshold shift, MINT trial); SHOT reports (reaction epidemiology); StatPearls. ⚑ The acute-MI transfusion target and DOAC-first cancer-associated thrombosis reflect changes from older textbooks; sources still differ on the MI target (restrictive vs liberal), so both are stated.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.h: Section 8 — Principles of Oncology & Systemic Therapy
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
The commonest cancers (UK/Australia): **breast, prostate, lung, bowel** dominate incidence; **lung** remains a leading cause of cancer death. **Screening** targets common cancers with a detectable pre-clinical phase and effective early treatment:

| Programme (UK) ⚑ | Population | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **Breast** | Women ~50–71, every 3 years | Mammography |
| **Bowel** | ~50/60–74 (varies by nation) | **FIT (faecal immunochemical test)** home kit ± colonoscopy |
| **Cervical** | Women 25–64 | **Primary HPV testing** (cytology if HPV+) ⚑ |

(Australia mirrors these: **BreastScreen** 50–74, **National Bowel Cancer Screening** with iFOBT 50–74, **Cervical Screening** 25–74 with 5-yearly primary HPV.) **Prostate has no national screening programme** (PSA's poor specificity). **Lung-cancer low-dose CT screening** for high-risk ever-smokers is being rolled out ⚑.

**Prevention:** smoking cessation (lung, bladder, head & neck, oesophagus), HPV vaccination (cervical, anal, oropharyngeal), hepatitis B vaccination (HCC), alcohol/obesity reduction, sun protection (melanoma). **Hereditary predisposition** worth recognising: **BRCA1/2** (breast, ovarian, prostate, pancreatic), **Lynch/HNPCC** (colorectal, endometrial — MMR genes), **FAP** (APC — colorectal), **Li–Fraumeni** (TP53 — sarcoma, breast, brain), **MEN** syndromes, **retinoblastoma (RB1)**.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: Diagnosis needs **tissue** (Section 3.5). **Staging** describes extent — **TNM** (Tumour, Node, Metastasis) → stage groups I–IV — while **grade** describes differentiation (how abnormal the cells look). Both feed prognosis alongside **performance status** and molecular markers. **Urgent (2-week-wait) referral** pathways (NICE NG12) route red-flag presentations quickly.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
- **Surgery** — the main curative modality for localised solid tumours; also diagnostic, palliative (bypass, fixation), and reconstructive.
- **Radiotherapy** — ionising radiation damaging tumour DNA. **Radical** (curative), **adjuvant** (post-op), **neoadjuvant** (shrink pre-op), **palliative** (bone pain, cord compression, SVCO, bleeding). Toxicity is **acute** (mucositis, skin erythema, diarrhoea — inflammation of the irradiated field) vs **late** (fibrosis, stricture, second malignancy). Brachytherapy = internal source.
- **Systemic anticancer therapy** — reaches disseminated disease (see 8.4).

**Treatment intent:** **neoadjuvant** (before primary treatment), **adjuvant** (after, to kill micrometastases), **radical/curative**, or **palliative** (symptom control, prolong life). Naming the intent is expected in every oncology answer.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
| Class | Examples | Mechanism | Signature toxicity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cytotoxic chemotherapy** | (see Section 11) | Damage DNA/mitosis of dividing cells | Myelosuppression, alopecia, mucositis, N&V, infertility |
| **Targeted small molecules** | Imatinib, erlotinib/osimertinib (EGFR), TKIs | Block specific driver kinases | Rash, diarrhoea (mechanism-specific) |
| **Monoclonal antibodies** | Rituximab (CD20), trastuzumab (HER2), bevacizumab (VEGF), cetuximab (EGFR) | Block surface targets/ligands | Infusion reactions; trastuzumab cardiotoxicity; bevacizumab bleeding/HTN |
| **Immunotherapy — checkpoint inhibitors** ⚑ | Pembrolizumab/nivolumab (PD-1), atezolizumab (PD-L1), ipilimumab (CTLA-4) | Release the brakes on T cells | **Immune-related adverse events (irAEs)** — colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies |
| **CAR-T cell therapy** ⚑ | For refractory B-cell malignancies | Engineered autologous T cells | **Cytokine release syndrome (CRS)**, neurotoxicity |
| **Hormonal therapy** | Tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors, GnRH agonists, anti-androgens | Block hormone-driven growth | Menopausal symptoms, bone loss, thromboembolism (tamoxifen) |

**Immunotherapy is the major recent shift** — checkpoint inhibitors have transformed melanoma, lung, renal and many other cancers, but their toxicity is **autoimmune** and can affect any organ; management is steroids/immunosuppression and holding the drug, not the usual chemo supportive care. ⚑

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
**Cancer pain — WHO analgesic ladder:** non-opioid (paracetamol/NSAID) → weak opioid (codeine) → strong opioid (morphine), with adjuvants (dexamethasone, gabapentinoids for neuropathic pain, bisphosphonates for bone pain). Anticipate and prescribe for **constipation** (co-prescribe laxatives with opioids), **nausea**, and breakthrough pain (~1/6 of the 24-h dose). Learn basic **opioid conversion** (e.g. oral→subcut morphine divide by 2; morphine→oxycodone roughly divide by 1.5–2). **Anticipatory/end-of-life prescribing:** subcut morphine (pain/dyspnoea), midazolam (agitation), haloperidol/levomepromazine (nausea/agitation), hyoscine/glycopyrronium (secretions). Involve palliative care early; recognise the dying patient and address holistic (psychological, spiritual, family) needs.

---

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
Commonest cancer in women. Presentation: painless lump, nipple change/discharge, skin tethering/peau d'orange, axillary node. **Triple assessment** = **clinical exam + imaging (mammography/USS) + core biopsy** — the exam mantra. Types: **ductal (commonest) vs lobular**; in-situ (DCIS) vs invasive. **Receptor subtypes drive treatment ⚑:**

| Subtype | Marker | Treatment lever |
|---|---|---|
| **ER/PR positive** | Hormone receptor + | **Endocrine therapy** (tamoxifen pre-menopause; aromatase inhibitor post-menopause) |
| **HER2 positive** | HER2 amplified | **Anti-HER2** (trastuzumab, pertuzumab) |
| **Triple-negative** | ER−/PR−/HER2− | Chemotherapy (± immunotherapy/PARP inhibitor if BRCA); worst prognosis |

Management combines **surgery** (wide local excision + radiotherapy, or mastectomy) with **sentinel lymph node biopsy**, ± adjuvant chemo/radio/endocrine/anti-HER2. **BRCA1/2** carriers: earlier onset, higher risk, consider risk-reducing surgery and **PARP inhibitors**. Spread: bone, lung, liver, brain.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
Leading cancer killer; strongly smoking-related. Presentation: cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, recurrent pneumonia, or a paraneoplastic/metastatic syndrome. **Two big groups:**

**Non-small cell (NSCLC, ~85%)** — adenocarcinoma (commonest, including non-smokers), squamous (central, cavitating, **PTHrP → hypercalcaemia**), large cell. **⚑ Molecular panel guides targeted therapy in adenocarcinoma:** **EGFR** (osimertinib), **ALK** and **ROS1** rearrangements (targeted TKIs), **KRAS G12C** (sotorasib/adagrasib), **BRAF, MET, RET, NTRK**; **PD-L1** expression guides immunotherapy. Test every advanced non-squamous NSCLC.

**Small cell (SCLC, ~15%)** — central, aggressive, early metastasis, strongly smoking-related; **neuroendocrine** origin → **paraneoplastic syndromes** (SIADH, ectopic ACTH → Cushing's, **Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome**). Rarely surgical; chemo ± immunotherapy ± radiotherapy.

**Paraneoplastic map (high-yield):** **squamous → PTHrP (hypercalcaemia)**; **small cell → SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert–Eaton**; any → clubbing/HPOA, hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy. **Pancoast tumour** (apex) → Horner's syndrome + arm/brachial-plexus symptoms. **Mesothelioma** — pleural malignancy from **asbestos** (long latency); pleural plaques, effusion.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: Third commonest cancer. Adenocarcinoma via the **adenoma–carcinoma sequence** (APC → KRAS → TP53). Risk: age, IBD, diet, **FAP** (hundreds of polyps, APC — near-100% cancer risk, prophylactic colectomy) and **Lynch/HNPCC** (MMR genes; also endometrial). Presentation by side: **left/rectal** → change in bowel habit, PR bleeding, tenesmus, obstruction; **right** → occult bleeding/**iron-deficiency anaemia**, mass. **Screening: FIT** (see 8.1). Diagnosis: colonoscopy + biopsy; staging CT + MRI rectum + **CEA** baseline. Treatment: surgical resection ± adjuvant chemo (FOLFOX); rectal cancer often neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy. **⚑ Molecular:** **RAS/BRAF** status (anti-EGFR **cetuximab** only works in **RAS wild-type**); **MMR/microsatellite-instability (MSI-high)** predicts immunotherapy response and flags Lynch. Spread: **liver** (portal drainage) → lung.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
**Prostate** — commonest male cancer; adenocarcinoma of the peripheral zone. Often asymptomatic (screen-detected) or LUTS/bone pain (**osteoblastic** mets → bone scan). **PSA** raised but non-specific (BPH, prostatitis, catheter, DRE). **Gleason score / ISUP grade groups** grade aggressiveness; risk stratification guides active surveillance vs radical prostatectomy/radiotherapy vs **androgen deprivation therapy (ADT)** for advanced disease.

**Renal cell carcinoma** — "internist's tumour": haematuria, flank pain, mass (triad is late); **paraneoplastic** (polycythaemia via EPO, hypercalcaemia, hypertension, Stauffer's syndrome); left varicocele (renal vein). Surgery; TKIs/immunotherapy for advanced.

**Bladder** — **painless visible haematuria** is bladder cancer until proven otherwise (cystoscopy). Mostly **transitional cell (urothelial) carcinoma** (smoking, aromatic amines/dye/rubber; squamous with schistosomiasis). TURBT ± intravesical BCG/chemo, or cystectomy.

**Testicular** — commonest solid cancer in **young men (20–40)**; painless testicular lump. **Seminoma** vs **non-seminomatous germ cell tumours**. **Markers:** **AFP + β-hCG** (raised in NSGCT; **AFP is NOT raised in pure seminoma**), LDH. Spreads to **para-aortic nodes**. Highly curable (orchidectomy + platinum-based chemo).

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
- **Oesophageal** — **adenocarcinoma** (lower third; GORD/Barrett's/obesity — rising ⚑) vs **squamous** (upper two-thirds; smoking, alcohol). Progressive dysphagia + weight loss. Poor prognosis.
- **Gastric** — adenocarcinoma; *H. pylori*, smoking, diet, pernicious anaemia; **Virchow's node**, Sister Mary Joseph nodule, Krukenberg (transcoelomic to ovary). Signet-ring/linitis plastica.
- **Pancreatic** — ductal adenocarcinoma (head): **painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss** (Courvoisier: palpable non-tender gallbladder + jaundice → not gallstones), new diabetes, thrombophlebitis migrans (Trousseau). **CA 19-9**. Usually advanced at diagnosis; Whipple if resectable.
- **Hepatocellular carcinoma** — on a background of **cirrhosis (hepatitis B/C, alcohol, NAFLD)**; **AFP**; surveillance USS in cirrhosis. Treatment by liver function/stage (resection, transplant, ablation, TACE, systemic).

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
- **Ovarian** — presents **late** with vague bloating/abdominal distension/early satiety; **CA-125**; **epithelial** (commonest), linked to **BRCA**; risk with age, nulliparity, ovulation. Surgery + platinum chemo ± PARP inhibitors (BRCA).
- **Endometrial** — **post-menopausal bleeding** is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise (TV-USS endometrial thickness → hysteroscopy + biopsy); oestrogen-driven (obesity, unopposed oestrogen, tamoxifen, PCOS, Lynch). Usually early-stage, good prognosis.
- **Cervical** — **HPV (16/18)**-driven squamous (and adeno); post-coital/intermenstrual bleeding; prevented by **HPV vaccination + screening** ⚑.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.h: 9.7 Skin, CNS, head & neck, unknown primary
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
- **Melanoma** — UV/sun exposure; the **ABCDE** rule (Asymmetry, Border, Colour, Diameter >6 mm, Evolving). Prognosis by **Breslow thickness** (depth). **⚑ BRAF V600 mutation** → BRAF/MEK inhibitors; checkpoint immunotherapy has transformed advanced disease. Spreads widely (including brain).
- **Non-melanoma skin cancer** — **basal cell carcinoma** (commonest, "rodent ulcer", rolled pearly edge, rarely metastasises) vs **squamous cell carcinoma** (can metastasise; arises in sun-damaged skin/actinic keratosis).
- **CNS** — primary **gliomas** (glioblastoma — poor prognosis) and meningiomas, but **metastases are the commonest brain tumours** (lung, breast, melanoma, renal, colorectal); present with headache (worse in morning/on lying), seizures, focal deficit, raised ICP.
- **Head & neck** — squamous cell; smoking/alcohol, and rising **HPV-positive oropharyngeal** cancer (better prognosis).
- **Carcinoma of unknown primary** — metastatic cancer with no identifiable primary despite workup; treat by immunohistochemistry-guided likely origin.

---

docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: **The most important oncology emergency.** Definition (NICE CG151): a patient on anticancer treatment with **neutrophils ≤0.5 ×10⁹/L** (some use ≤1.0 with expected fall) **and either temperature >38°C or other signs/symptoms of clinically significant sepsis.** **Management is time-critical: broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam) within 1 hour — the "door-to-needle" rule — BEFORE waiting for the neutrophil count or imaging.** Full sepsis-six/cultures, assess with the **MASCC score** to identify low-risk patients. Never delay antibiotics. ⚑

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: Massive tumour-cell breakdown (spontaneous or on starting treatment) in **high-turnover cancers — Burkitt lymphoma, ALL, high-grade lymphomas, bulky disease**. The metabolic quartet: **↑potassium, ↑phosphate, ↑urate → ↓calcium** (and AKI from urate/phosphate crystals). **Cairo–Bishop** criteria classify laboratory vs clinical TLS. **Prevent** in at-risk patients: **IV hydration** + **allopurinol** (lower risk) or **rasburicase** (higher risk/established TLS — recombinant urate oxidase; **contraindicated in G6PD deficiency**). Treat hyperkalaemia; avoid calcium unless symptomatic; renal support if needed.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: Vertebral metastasis/collapse compressing the cord — **breast, lung, prostate, myeloma, renal**. Red flags: **new/progressive back pain (worse lying/coughing), a sensory level, limb weakness, bladder/bowel dysfunction.** **⚑ Management (NICE NG234): give dexamethasone 16 mg immediately, arrange whole-spine MRI as soon as possible and within 24 hours, and deliver definitive treatment (surgical decompression or radiotherapy) as soon as possible and within 24 hours.** Nurse flat with neutral spine alignment until stability assessed. Outcome depends on treating **before** paraplegia is established — act on suspicion.

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: Obstruction of SVC flow — commonly **lung cancer, lymphoma**. Facial/neck/arm swelling, distended veins, plethora, dyspnoea, headache; **Pemberton's sign** (facial congestion on raising the arms). Usually subacute but can be an emergency (airway/cerebral oedema). Investigate with CT; treat with corticosteroids, **endovascular stenting** (fast relief), and treat the underlying tumour (radiotherapy/chemo depending on histology — get tissue if feasible first).

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text: Commonest life-threatening metabolic complication of cancer. Mechanisms: **PTHrP** (squamous lung/head-neck, renal, breast — humoral), **osteolytic** bone metastases/myeloma, and **calcitriol** production (lymphoma). "**Bones, stones, groans, psychic moans**" + polyuria/dehydration. Management: **aggressive IV 0.9% saline rehydration** first, then an **IV bisphosphonate** (zoledronic acid) — or **denosumab** if refractory/renal impairment; treat the cancer. (Calcium-axis physiology cross-referenced from the endocrine build.)

docs.title: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.parent: Oncology Principles, Solid Tumours & Oncological Emergencies
docs.text:
- **Raised ICP / brain metastases** — headache, vomiting, papilloedema, focal signs, seizures; **dexamethasone** for vasogenic oedema, urgent imaging, neurosurgery/radiotherapy.
- **Catastrophic haemorrhage** (e.g. carotid blowout, tumour erosion) — often a palliative event; crisis medication.
- **Chemotherapy extravasation** — a vesicant leaking into tissue; stop infusion, aspirate, agent-specific antidote/cold or warm compress.
- **Immunotherapy toxicity (irAEs)** ⚑ — checkpoint-inhibitor colitis/pneumonitis/hepatitis/hypophysitis; recognise and treat with **corticosteroids** (not standard anti-infective/supportive care), hold the drug.
