docs.title: Connective Tissue Disease, Vasculitis & Multisystem Rheumatology
docs.parent: Connective Tissue Disease, Vasculitis & Multisystem Rheumatology
docs.text:
##### SLE
A **multisystem autoimmune immune-complex disease**, classically a **young woman of reproductive age** (higher prevalence and severity in Afro-Caribbean and Asian populations).

**Clinical (any system):** constitutional (fatigue, fever, weight loss); **malar "butterfly" rash** (spares nasolabial folds), photosensitivity, discoid lesions, oral ulcers, non-scarring alopecia; **non-erosive arthritis** (small joints — vs RA which erodes); serositis (pleuritis, pericarditis); **lupus nephritis** (the major prognostic determinant); neuropsychiatric lupus; haematological (haemolytic anaemia, leucopenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia); Raynaud's.

**Immunology (see also Section 3):** **ANA** (sensitive screen — the **entry criterion**), **anti-dsDNA** (specific, tracks activity/nephritis), **anti-Sm** (specific), anti-Ro/La, **low C3/C4 in active disease**.

⚑ **2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria:** **entry criterion = ANA ≥1:80** (must be positive to classify), then **weighted additive criteria** across clinical and immunological domains (only the highest-weighted item per domain counts; a criterion doesn't count if better explained by another cause); **≥10 points** classifies SLE. High-weight items include **lupus nephritis on biopsy** and **anti-dsDNA/anti-Sm**. (Classification, not a diagnostic checklist — but ANA-as-entry is the examinable change.)

**Lupus nephritis:** class determined by **renal biopsy** (ISN/RPS I–VI; **class III/IV proliferative** is the aggressive form needing immunosuppression). Screen everyone with **urinalysis + urine protein:creatinine ratio + BP**.

**Management:** ⚑ **hydroxychloroquine for essentially all patients** (reduces flares, organ damage, thrombosis, mortality — needs annual retinal screening); glucocorticoids for flares (minimise long-term); immunosuppression for organ disease (**mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide + steroids** for proliferative lupus nephritis, increasingly **plus belimumab or voclosporin** ⚑); sun protection; cardiovascular risk management.

**Drug-induced lupus:** **anti-histone antibodies**; culprits **hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline**; spares kidney/CNS, resolves on stopping the drug.

##### Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)
Autoantibody-mediated **hypercoagulable state** — primary or secondary to SLE.
- **Clinical: arterial and venous Thrombosis + pregnancy morbidity** (recurrent miscarriage, late fetal loss), thrombocytopenia, livedo reticularis. **Memory hook — "CLOT":** **C**oagulation defect, **L**ivedo reticularis, **O**bstetric loss, **T**hrombocytopenia.
- **Antibodies:** **lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein-I** (need persistence ≥12 weeks apart).
- ⚑ **Paradox:** the lupus anticoagulant **prolongs the APTT in vitro** but causes **thrombosis in vivo**.
- **Management:** long-term **warfarin** for thrombosis (⚑ **DOACs are inferior/avoided, especially in triple-positive/arterial APS**); **aspirin + LMWH** in pregnancy.

---

docs.title: Connective Tissue Disease, Vasculitis & Multisystem Rheumatology
docs.parent: Connective Tissue Disease, Vasculitis & Multisystem Rheumatology
docs.text:
##### Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)
Excess collagen → skin and internal-organ **fibrosis** + **vasculopathy**. Two forms — the split is high-yield:

| | **Limited cutaneous** (incl. **CREST**) | **Diffuse cutaneous** |
|---|---|---|
| Skin | Face + distal to elbows/knees | Proximal + trunk |
| Antibody | **Anti-centromere** | **Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase)** (also anti-RNA-pol III) |
| Onset | Long-standing Raynaud's first | Rapid |
| Big risk | **Pulmonary arterial hypertension** | **Interstitial lung disease; scleroderma renal crisis** |

**CREST = C**alcinosis, **R**aynaud's, o**E**sophageal dysmotility, **S**clerodactyly, **T**elangiectasia.
⚑ **Scleroderma renal crisis** — acute severe hypertension + AKI (diffuse disease, worsened by high-dose steroids) → **ACE inhibitor** is the treatment (one of the few times you push ACEi in an AKI). ILD → screen with PFTs/HRCT; treat with mycophenolate ± nintedanib.

##### Sjögren's syndrome
**Lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands** → **sicca (dry eyes = keratoconjunctivitis sicca, dry mouth = xerostomia)**, parotid swelling; primary or secondary (to RA/SLE).
- **Antibodies: anti-Ro (SSA), anti-La (SSB)**, RF, ANA; **Schirmer's test**, salivary gland biopsy.
- ⚑ **Increased risk of B-cell non-Hodgkin (MALT) lymphoma** — new persistent parotid swelling warrants investigation.

##### Inflammatory myopathies (polymyositis / dermatomyositis)
- **Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness** (difficulty rising from a chair, combing hair), **markedly raised CK**, EMG/muscle biopsy changes, **anti-Jo-1** (antisynthetase syndrome → ILD, mechanic's hands, fever).
- **Dermatomyositis** adds skin: **heliotrope rash** (violaceous eyelids), **Gottron's papules** (knuckles), shawl sign. ⚑ **Strong association with underlying malignancy (esp. dermatomyositis in adults)** → **malignancy screen**.
- Management: high-dose steroids + steroid-sparing immunosuppression.

##### Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD)
Overlap of SLE + scleroderma + myositis features with **high-titre anti-U1-RNP**; Raynaud's, puffy hands.

---

docs.title: Connective Tissue Disease, Vasculitis & Multisystem Rheumatology
docs.parent: Connective Tissue Disease, Vasculitis & Multisystem Rheumatology
docs.text:
##### Giant cell arteritis (GCA) *(emergency — sight-threatening)* ⚑
Granulomatous **large-vessel vasculitis** in the **over-50s**, affecting branches of the external carotid.
- **Clinical: new headache (temporal), scalp tenderness, jaw claudication** (highly suggestive), **visual disturbance/amaurosis fugax → permanent monocular blindness** (anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy), temporal artery tenderness/thickening/pulselessness; **raised ESR (often >50) and CRP**; ~40–50% overlap with **polymyalgia rheumatica**.
- **Investigation:** ESR/CRP, **temporal artery biopsy** (granulomatous inflammation, giant cells — ⚑ **skip lesions → a negative biopsy does not exclude it**), and **temporal artery ultrasound "halo sign"** (increasingly a first-line, biopsy-sparing test in fast-track pathways).
- ⚑ **Management: start high-dose glucocorticoids IMMEDIATELY on clinical suspicion — do NOT wait for the biopsy** (biopsy stays positive for ~1–2 weeks after starting steroids). **Visual symptoms → IV methylprednisolone; no visual symptoms → high-dose oral prednisolone (~40–60 mg).** Add **low-dose aspirin**; **tocilizumab (IL-6 inhibitor)** as a **steroid-sparing agent** (2021 ACR/VF) for relapsing or high-steroid-burden disease. Bone/GI protection with long steroid course.

##### Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR)
- **Bilateral shoulder and pelvic-girdle pain and stiffness** in the over-50s, **profound early-morning stiffness**, raised ESR/CRP; **NO true muscle weakness** (pain limits, CK normal — the discriminator from myositis).
- **Dramatic response to low-dose prednisolone (~15 mg)** — a near-diagnostic feature. Overlaps with GCA; always **ask about GCA symptoms** in a PMR patient.

##### Takayasu arteritis & polyarteritis nodosa
- **Takayasu** ("pulseless disease") — large-vessel (aorta/branches) vasculitis in **young Asian women**; absent pulses, BP discrepancy, bruits, claudication.
- **Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)** — **medium-vessel** necrotising vasculitis; **spares the lungs**; **hepatitis B** association; renal, GI, skin, mononeuritis multiplex; **"rosary-bead" microaneurysms** on angiography; **ANCA-negative**.

---

docs.title: Connective Tissue Disease, Vasculitis & Multisystem Rheumatology
docs.parent: Connective Tissue Disease, Vasculitis & Multisystem Rheumatology
docs.text:
**ANCA-associated vasculitides (AAV)** — small-vessel, the **pulmonary–renal** disease group:

| Disease | ANCA | Signature |
|---|---|---|
| **Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)** (Wegener's) | **c-ANCA / PR3** | **ENT (saddle-nose, sinusitis, otitis), lungs (nodules/haemorrhage), kidney (RPGN)**; the "**E-L-K**" trio |
| **Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA)** (Churg–Strauss) | **p-ANCA / MPO** (~40%) | **Asthma + eosinophilia + vasculitis**; nasal polyps, mononeuritis multiplex |
| **Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA)** | **p-ANCA / MPO** | **Pulmonary–renal** (glomerulonephritis + alveolar haemorrhage), no granulomas |

- **Presentation clues:** constitutional symptoms + **glomerulonephritis (blood + protein + red-cell casts)** ± **pulmonary haemorrhage** (haemoptysis) + **mononeuritis multiplex** + skin purpura/ENT.
- ⚑ **Management (2021 ACR/VF):** **remission induction with rituximab (or cyclophosphamide) + high-dose glucocorticoids** (± plasma exchange for severe renal/pulmonary haemorrhage); then maintenance (rituximab/azathioprine). A rheumatology/nephrology emergency when rapidly progressive.

**Other vasculitides / mimics:**
- **IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura)** — children after URTI: **palpable purpura (buttocks/legs) + arthralgia + abdominal pain + IgA nephropathy**; usually self-limiting.
- **Behçet's disease** — **recurrent oral + genital ulcers + uveitis**, pathergy, Silk-Road distribution; variable-vessel.
- **Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis** — hepatitis C association; purpura, arthralgia, neuropathy, low C4.

---

docs.title: Connective Tissue Disease, Vasculitis & Multisystem Rheumatology
docs.parent: Connective Tissue Disease, Vasculitis & Multisystem Rheumatology
docs.text:
##### Fibromyalgia
**Chronic widespread pain** with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive "fog", multiple tender points — **normal inflammatory markers, normal imaging, no synovitis**. ⚑ **The key contrast:** it is a **non-inflammatory** central pain-sensitisation syndrome — the giveaway is *lots of symptoms, normal bloods*. Management is non-pharmacological first (graded exercise, CBT, education), then adjuncts (amitriptyline, duloxetine, pregabalin); **NSAIDs/steroids don't help**.

##### Others in brief
- **Adult-onset Still's disease** — spiking (quotidian) fevers, **salmon-pink evanescent rash**, arthritis, sore throat, **very high ferritin**, raised WCC, seronegative.
- **Sarcoid arthropathy** — **Löfgren's syndrome** (erythema nodosum + bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + ankle arthritis) is the acute, good-prognosis form.
- **Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)** — arthritis <16 yrs, ≥6 weeks; subtypes (oligoarticular — **uveitis risk, ANA-positive**; polyarticular; **systemic/Still's**); watch for uveitis screening.

docs.title: Connective Tissue Disease, Vasculitis & Multisystem Rheumatology
docs.parent: Connective Tissue Disease, Vasculitis & Multisystem Rheumatology
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Young woman, malar rash, non-erosive arthritis, ANA + | **SLE** |
| Specific SLE antibodies / activity marker | **Anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm** / **low C3/C4** |
| Prolonged APTT + thrombosis + miscarriage | **Antiphospholipid syndrome** |
| Anti-histone antibodies after hydralazine | **Drug-induced lupus** |
| Anti-centromere / limited scleroderma risk | **CREST** / pulmonary hypertension |
| Anti-Scl-70 / diffuse scleroderma risks | ILD + **scleroderma renal crisis** (Rx **ACE inhibitor**) |
| Dry eyes + dry mouth + anti-Ro/La; lymphoma risk | **Sjögren's** |
| Proximal weakness + raised CK + heliotrope rash | **Dermatomyositis** (+ malignancy screen) |
| High-titre anti-U1-RNP | **Mixed connective tissue disease** |
| >50, headache, jaw claudication, ESR >50, visual loss | **Giant cell arteritis** → **immediate steroids** ⚑ |
| Shoulder/pelvic-girdle stiffness, normal CK, steroid-responsive | **Polymyalgia rheumatica** |
| c-ANCA/PR3, saddle nose + lung + kidney | **GPA** |
| Asthma + eosinophilia + vasculitis (p-ANCA) | **EGPA (Churg–Strauss)** |
| Medium-vessel, spares lungs, hepatitis B, ANCA-negative | **Polyarteritis nodosa** |
| Child, palpable purpura on buttocks + abdo pain + haematuria | **IgA vasculitis (HSP)** |
| Widespread pain, fatigue, **normal bloods and imaging** | **Fibromyalgia** |
| Salmon-pink rash, spiking fever, sky-high ferritin | **Adult-onset Still's** |

##### Sources
Kumar & Clark; Robbins; StatPearls (SLE, APS, systemic sclerosis, GCA, ANCA vasculitis, fibromyalgia). **2019 EULAR/ACR SLE classification criteria** (ANA ≥1:80 obligatory entry; weighted additive criteria; ≥10 points) verified against the published criteria. **2021 ACR/Vasculitis Foundation guidelines** for GCA (immediate high-dose glucocorticoids; tocilizumab as steroid-sparing) and for ANCA-associated vasculitis (rituximab or cyclophosphamide + glucocorticoids ± plasma exchange). Chapel Hill Consensus nomenclature for the vasculitis vessel-size classification. GCA ESR threshold, temporal-artery biopsy skip-lesion caveat, and PMR steroid-responsiveness cross-checked in ≥2 sources. Scleroderma renal crisis → ACE inhibitor confirmed in Kumar & Clark and StatPearls.

docs.title: Metabolic Bone Disease
docs.h: MSK & Rheumatology Notes — Metabolic Bone Disease
docs.text: *(MSK/fragility-fracture angle — the calcium-axis biochemistry lives in the endocrine notes.)*

docs.title: Metabolic Bone Disease
docs.text:
**Reduced bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration → fragility fractures.** Bone **quantity** falls but **quality (mineralisation) is normal** — contrast with osteomalacia below.

**A fragility fracture = a fracture from a fall from standing height or less** (classic sites: **vertebrae, hip/NOF, distal radius/wrist, proximal humerus**). ⚑ *Any fragility fracture in an older adult should trigger osteoporosis assessment, whatever the DEXA.*

**Risk factors — "SHATTERED FAMILY":** **S**teroids, **H**yperthyroid/hyperparathyroid, **A**lcohol/smoking, **T**hin (low BMI), **T**estosterone low, **E**arly menopause, **R**enal/liver failure, **E**rosive/inflammatory disease (RA), **D**iabetes/**D**ietary calcium low; plus age, female, family history, prior fracture.

**Diagnosis:** **DEXA** scan → **T-score** (SD vs young adult):

| T-score | Category |
|---|---|
| ≥ −1.0 | Normal |
| −1.0 to −2.5 | **Osteopenia** |
| **≤ −2.5** | **Osteoporosis** |
| ≤ −2.5 + fragility fracture | Established (severe) osteoporosis |

**FRAX** (or QFracture) estimates **10-year fracture probability** to guide who to treat/scan.
**Bloods are typically normal** (Ca, PO₄, ALP all normal) — abnormal bone biochemistry points elsewhere (osteomalacia, Paget's, myeloma, hyperparathyroidism).

**Management:** lifestyle (weight-bearing exercise, stop smoking, reduce alcohol, calcium/vitamin D repletion, falls prevention). **First-line pharmacological: oral bisphosphonate (alendronate/risedronate)**. ⚑ Anabolic options for severe/very-high-risk disease: **romosozumab** (anti-sclerostin, builds bone) and **teriparatide** (PTH analogue); **denosumab** (anti-RANKL) as an alternative — ⚑ **do not stop denosumab abruptly** (rebound vertebral fractures — transition to a bisphosphonate). HRT/raloxifene in selected women. (Drug detail in Section 8.3.)

docs.title: Metabolic Bone Disease
docs.text:
**Defective mineralisation of osteoid** (soft bones), usually from **vitamin D deficiency** (or hypophosphataemia). **Rickets** is the same process in the growing child (before physeal fusion).
- **Clinical:** **bone pain and tenderness, proximal myopathy (waddling gait), fragility fractures**; children → bowed legs, costochondral "rickety rosary", growth failure.
- **Biochemistry (contrast to osteoporosis):** **low vitamin D, low/normal calcium, low phosphate, HIGH ALP, high PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism)**.
- **Radiology:** **Looser's zones (pseudofractures)** — the buzz finding.
- **Management:** vitamin D (± calcium) replacement; treat the cause.

docs.title: Metabolic Bone Disease
docs.text:
**Disordered, accelerated bone turnover** (overactive osteoclasts then chaotic osteoblasts) → structurally weak, enlarged, deformed bone. Older patients; often **asymptomatic, found via isolated raised ALP**.
- **Clinical:** **bone pain, deformity (bowed tibia, skull enlargement — "hat no longer fits"), warmth over bone, fractures, deafness** (VIII compression), **secondary OA**; rarely **high-output cardiac failure** and **osteosarcoma** (sudden pain increase).
- **Biochemistry:** ⚑ **isolated markedly raised ALP with NORMAL calcium and phosphate** (the classic pattern). X-ray/bone scan: lytic + sclerotic, cortical thickening.
- **Management:** **bisphosphonates** (esp. IV zoledronate) for pain/active disease; analgesia.

docs.title: Metabolic Bone Disease
docs.text:
**Death of bone from interrupted blood supply.** Sites/causes to know:
- **Femoral head** (after **displaced intracapsular NOF fracture**, steroids, alcohol, **sickle cell disease**, SLE, the "bends"), **scaphoid proximal pole**, **talus**, humeral head, femoral condyles.
- **Investigation:** X-ray may be normal early → **MRI is the most sensitive test**; later X-ray shows sclerosis, subchondral collapse ("crescent sign").
- ⚑ **Bisphosphonate/denosumab-related osteonecrosis of the jaw** and atypical femoral fractures — a drug-related form to be aware of when counselling.

docs.title: Metabolic Bone Disease
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Fragility fracture + T-score ≤ −2.5, **normal Ca/PO₄/ALP** | **Osteoporosis** |
| Bone pain + proximal myopathy + **low Ca/PO₄, high ALP/PTH**, Looser's zones | **Osteomalacia** |
| **Isolated raised ALP, normal Ca/PO₄**, bowed tibia, deafness | **Paget's disease** |
| Hip/scaphoid/talus pain, X-ray normal, MRI shows necrosis | **Avascular necrosis** |
| First-line osteoporosis drug / anabolic options | **Bisphosphonate** / romosozumab, teriparatide ⚑ |
| Drug you must not stop abruptly (rebound fractures) | **Denosumab** ⚑ |

---

docs.text:
##### 2.1 The spine and the neuro-emergency landmarks

The vertebral column: **7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, sacrum (5 fused), coccyx**. The **spinal cord terminates at ~L1/L2** (conus medullaris); below that the lumbosacral nerve roots run as the **cauda equina** ("horse's tail"). **This single fact underlies two emergencies:**
- A lesion **above L1/L2** compresses the **cord** → **spinal cord compression** (UMN signs below the level, a sensory level).
- A lesion **below L1/L2** compresses the **cauda equina** (roots) → **cauda equina syndrome** (LMN signs, saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel).

**Dermatomes/myotomes worth memorising for OSCEs:**

| Level | Sensory landmark | Motor / reflex |
|---|---|---|
| C5 | Lateral upper arm | Shoulder abduction; biceps reflex |
| C6 | Thumb | Wrist extension / elbow flexion; **supinator reflex** |
| C7 | Middle finger | Elbow extension / finger extension; **triceps reflex** |
| C8/T1 | Little finger / medial forearm | Finger flexion / intrinsics |
| T4 / T10 | Nipple / umbilicus | (sensory level landmarks) |
| L3/L4 | Medial knee / medial shin | Knee extension; **knee jerk (L3/4)** |
| L5 | Dorsum of foot, big toe | **Big-toe dorsiflexion (EHL)**, foot drop |
| S1 | Lateral foot / sole | Plantarflexion; **ankle jerk (S1)** |
| S2–S4 | Perineum / **saddle** | Anal tone, bladder — **the cauda equina territory** |

**Nerve root (radiculopathy) vs peripheral nerve** — root lesions follow a dermatome/myotome and often a reflex; peripheral nerve lesions follow that nerve's cutaneous + motor territory.

##### 2.2 Shoulder and upper limb

**Rotator cuff (SITS)** — the dynamic stabilisers of the glenohumeral joint:

| Muscle | Action | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **S**upraspinatus | Initiates **abduction** (0–15°) | Empty-can test; **most commonly torn/impinged** |
| **I**nfraspinatus | External rotation | Resisted ER |
| **T**eres minor | External rotation | — |
| **S**ubscapularis | Internal rotation | Gerber's lift-off |

The **subacromial space** (between the acromion above and the cuff/humeral head below) is where **impingement** and subacromial bursitis occur.

**The signature peripheral nerve palsies** (very high yield):

| Nerve | Roots | Common injury | Deficit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Axillary** | C5–6 | Shoulder dislocation, surgical neck of humerus | Deltoid weakness, **regimental-badge** sensory loss |
| **Radial** | C5–T1 | **Mid-shaft humerus** fracture, "Saturday night palsy" | **Wrist drop**, sensory loss dorsal hand |
| **Median** | C6–T1 | **Carpal tunnel** (wrist), supracondylar # | Thenar wasting, LOAF muscles, **thumb/index/middle** sensory loss |
| **Ulnar** | C8–T1 | Medial epicondyle, elbow | **Claw hand**, wasting of interossei/hypothenar, medial 1½ digits |

##### 2.3 Hip, knee and lower limb

**Hip** — a ball-and-socket joint with a clinically critical blood supply: the femoral head is fed largely by the **medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries running retrograde up the femoral nec

docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Cord ends at which level; what's below | **L1/L2**; cauda equina (roots) |
| Saddle anaesthesia + bladder dysfunction localises to | **Cauda equina** (S2–S4 roots) |
| Rotator cuff muscle usually torn / initiates abduction | **Supraspinatus** |
| Wrist drop after mid-shaft humerus fracture | **Radial nerve** |
| Foot drop after fibular neck injury | **Common peroneal nerve** (mimics L5) |
| RA joint distribution vs OA distribution | RA: **MCP/PIP, spares DIP, symmetrical**; OA: **DIP/PIP/1st CMC** |
| Snuffbox tenderness after FOOSH, normal X-ray | Treat as **scaphoid fracture** (AVN/non-union risk) |
| Displaced intracapsular NOF fracture risk | **AVN** (retrograde femoral head supply) |

##### Sources
Guyton & Hall *Textbook of Medical Physiology* (bone, cartilage, muscle); Robbins & Cotran *Pathologic Basis of Disease* (RANKL/OPG, joint pathology); Kumar & Clark *Clinical Medicine*; Gray's Anatomy / Last's Anatomy (spine, limb, nerve courses); StatPearls (rotator cuff, scaphoid, cauda equina anatomy). No numeric thresholds requiring web verification in this section; the RANKL/OPG, sclerostin and collagen-type facts are stable and consistent across sources.

docs.title: MSK & Connective-Tissue Physiology
docs.h: MSK & Rheumatology Notes — MSK & Connective-Tissue Physiology
docs.text:
##### 1.1 Bone biology and remodelling

Bone is a living composite: an **organic** matrix (mostly **type I collagen** = osteoid, giving tensile strength) mineralised by **hydroxyapatite** (calcium phosphate, giving compressive strength). Two macroscopic types:

| Type | Also called | Where | Feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cortical** | Compact | Shafts (diaphysis), outer shell | ~80% of skeletal mass, dense, slow turnover |
| **Trabecular** | Cancellous / spongy | Ends of long bones, vertebrae, pelvis | Metabolically active, high surface area → **fractures/osteoporosis show here first** (vertebrae, NOF) |

**The three cells (know their lineage — it explains the drugs):**

| Cell | Lineage | Job | Drug relevance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Osteoblast** | Mesenchymal | Lays down osteoid, then mineralises it | Stimulated by **Wnt** signalling; **teriparatide** (PTH analogue) and **romosozumab** boost this |
| **Osteoclast** | Haematopoietic (macrophage/monocyte line) | Resorbs bone | Activated by **RANKL**; blocked by **bisphosphonates** and **denosumab** |
| **Osteocyte** | Terminally differentiated osteoblast, buried in matrix | Mechanosensor; secretes **sclerostin** | Sclerostin inhibits bone formation → **romosozumab** is an anti-sclerostin antibody |

**The RANKL–RANK–OPG axis** — the single most exam-relevant piece of bone physiology:
- Osteoblasts express **RANKL**, which binds **RANK** on osteoclast precursors → osteoclast activation → resorption.
- Osteoblasts also secrete **OPG (osteoprotegerin)**, a decoy receptor that mops up RANKL → protects bone.
- **Memory hook:** *RANKL Ruins bone, OPG is On your side (Protects).* **Denosumab is a monoclonal anti-RANKL antibody** — it mimics OPG.

**Calcium/phosphate & the bone loop** (cross-links to endocrine): PTH raises calcium (bone resorption, renal Ca reabsorption, activates vitamin D); **active vitamin D (calcitriol)** raises calcium and phosphate by gut absorption; calcitonin lowers calcium (minor in humans). This loop underlies osteomalacia, renal bone disease and hyperparathyroid bone disease (Section 6 / endocrine notes).

**Fracture healing (four overlapping stages):**

1. **Haematoma / inflammation** (hours–days) — clot, cytokines, inflammatory cells.
2. **Soft callus** (days–weeks) — fibrocartilage bridges the gap.
3. **Hard callus** (weeks) — woven bone replaces cartilage (endochondral ossification).
4. **Remodelling** (months–years) — woven bone → lamellar bone along stress lines.

⚑ *Anything that starves any stage delays or prevents union: poor blood supply (scaphoid, NOF), movement/instability, infection, smoking, NSAIDs (theoretical), diabetes, malnutrition.*

##### 1.2 Cartilage, synovium and the joint

**Hyaline articular cartilage** covers joint surfaces: **type II collagen** + proteoglycan (aggrecan) holding water. **It is avascular, aneural and alymphatic** → nourished by synovial fluid diffusion → **poor intrinsic healing** (the reason OA is progressive and cartilage injuries do

| Collagen type in bone/tendon vs cartilage | **Type I** (bone, tendon, skin) vs **type II** (hyaline cartilage) |
| Cell that resorbs bone / its master activator | **Osteoclast** / **RANKL** |

| Fibrillin-1 defect / type I collagen defect (brittle bones) | **Marfan** / **osteogenesis imperfecta** |

docs.title: MSK & Rheumatology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
**NSAIDs** — inhibit **cyclo-oxygenase (COX)** → less prostaglandin → analgesia/anti-inflammation.
- ⚑ **The three big harms:** **GI** (ulcer/bleed — co-prescribe a **PPI** for at-risk patients), **renal** (AKI, fluid retention — avoid in CKD/hypovolaemia; part of the nephrotoxic "triple whammy" with ACEi + diuretic), **cardiovascular** (raised MI/stroke risk, esp. high-dose diclofenac and COX-2 selectives). Also bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma.
- **COX-2 selectives (celecoxib, etoricoxib):** less GI risk, but **cardiovascular risk persists**; avoid in established cardiovascular disease.

**Corticosteroids** — potent anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressant; oral (prednisolone), **intra-articular** (flares of OA/RA/crystal), IV pulsed (severe vasculitis/GCA visual loss).
- ⚑ **Harms of chronic use:** osteoporosis (co-prescribe bone protection with long courses), hyperglycaemia, hypertension, weight gain/Cushingoid, infection, adrenal suppression (**never stop abruptly — sick-day rules**), cataracts, skin thinning, mood.

docs.title: MSK & Rheumatology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
##### Conventional synthetic (csDMARDs)

| Drug | Notes / monitoring | Key toxicity |
|---|---|---|
| **Methotrexate** ⚑ | **Anchor DMARD for RA**; weekly; **co-prescribe folic acid**; FBC/LFT/U&E monitoring | **Myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, pneumonitis; teratogenic** (stop ≥3–6 months pre-conception, both sexes advised); avoid with trimethoprim (marrow) |
| **Sulfasalazine** | Useful in RA and peripheral spondyloarthropathy; relatively pregnancy-safe | Rash, GI upset, reversible ↓sperm, myelosuppression |
| **Hydroxychloroquine** | RA (mild), **SLE backbone** | ⚑ **Retinopathy → baseline + annual retinal screening**; relatively pregnancy-safe |
| **Leflunomide** | RA/PsA | Hypertension, hepatotoxicity, **teratogenic (long half-life — needs washout)** |

##### Biologic (bDMARDs) — the cytokine/cell targets

| Class | Examples | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **TNF-α inhibitors** | infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept, golimumab | RA, axSpA, PsA, IBD — ⚑ **screen for latent TB and hepatitis B before starting** (reactivation) |
| **IL-6 inhibitor** | **tocilizumab** | RA, **GCA**, JIA |
| **Anti-CD20 (B cell)** | rituximab | RA, **ANCA vasculitis**, SLE |
| **T-cell co-stim** | abatacept | RA |
| **IL-17 / IL-23** | secukinumab / ustekinumab, guselkumab | **PsA, axSpA, psoriasis** |
| **Anti-BLyS** | belimumab | SLE |

##### Targeted synthetic (tsDMARDs)
- **JAK inhibitors** (tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib) — oral, block intracellular JAK–STAT.
- ⚑ **Safety signal (ORAL Surveillance):** increased **MACE, VTE, serious infection (incl. herpes zoster) and malignancy** vs TNF inhibitors — reserved for patients who fail/can't take a TNF inhibitor, and used cautiously in **≥65 yrs, smokers and those with cardiovascular/thrombotic risk**.

docs.title: MSK & Rheumatology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
##### Gout drugs *(the acute-vs-chronic split is the exam point)*

| Phase | Drugs |
|---|---|
| **Acute attack** | **NSAID**, **colchicine** (⚑ low-dose regimen now; caution in renal impairment — diarrhoea is the dose-limiting effect), **corticosteroid** (oral or intra-articular — good when NSAID/colchicine contraindicated) |
| **Urate-lowering (ULT)** | **Allopurinol** (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) — ⚑ **start low (100 mg/day; 50 mg if CKD) and titrate to target urate <0.36 mmol/L (<0.30 if tophi)**; cover initiation with **NSAID/colchicine prophylaxis 3–6 months**; ⚑ **HLA-B*5801 testing in high-risk ethnicities** (SJS/TEN risk). **Febuxostat** second-line. **Don't start ULT during an acute flare, and don't stop it if already established.** |

##### Bone-targeted agents

| Drug | Mechanism | Key point |
|---|---|---|
| **Bisphosphonates** (alendronate, risedronate, IV zoledronate) | Inhibit osteoclasts | ⚑ Oral: **take fasting, upright, with water, stay upright 30 min** (oesophagitis); rare **osteonecrosis of the jaw / atypical femoral fracture**; renal caution |
| **Denosumab** | **Anti-RANKL** monoclonal | 6-monthly SC; ⚑ **rebound vertebral fractures if stopped** → transition to bisphosphonate; hypocalcaemia risk |
| **Romosozumab** ⚑ | **Anti-sclerostin** (anabolic) | Builds bone; cardiovascular caution |
| **Teriparatide** | **PTH analogue** (anabolic) | Daily SC, limited duration |

##### Other
- **Neuropathic/central pain adjuncts** (amitriptyline, duloxetine, pregabalin) for fibromyalgia and neuropathic MSK pain; **NSAIDs/steroids do not help fibromyalgia**.

docs.title: MSK & Rheumatology Pharmacology & Prescribing
docs.text:
- **Before starting biologics/DMARDs:** screen for **latent TB, hepatitis B/C, HIV**; check vaccinations (⚑ **no live vaccines on biologics/high-dose immunosuppression**); baseline FBC/LFT/U&E.
- **Monitoring:** regular FBC/LFT/U&E on methotrexate/leflunomide/sulfasalazine/azathioprine (shared-care bloods); annual retinal screen on hydroxychloroquine.
- **Steroids:** bone protection + PPI on long courses; **sick-day rules**; taper — never stop abruptly.
- **Pregnancy:** ⚑ **safe(r): hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, azathioprine, low-dose prednisolone, certolizumab**; **teratogenic/avoid: methotrexate, leflunomide, cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate, and (in APS) warfarin in the first trimester** (switch to LMWH).
- ⚑ **Azathioprine + allopurinol** is a dangerous combination (allopurinol blocks azathioprine metabolism → marrow toxicity); check **TPMT** before azathioprine.

Kumar & Clark; Robbins; StatPearls (osteoporosis, osteomalacia, Paget's, AVN); NICE/NOGG osteoporosis guidance (DEXA T-score thresholds, FRAX, bisphosphonate first-line) — WHO T-score ≤ −2.5 cross-checked with the endocrine build; BNF (NSAID/steroid/DMARD/bisphosphonate cautions, methotrexate–trimethoprim and azathioprine–allopurinol interactions, TPMT). Drug sequencing anchored to the **2020 ACR gout** (start-low allopurinol, target <6 mg/dL [<0.36 mmol/L], HLA-B*5801), **2021 ACR RA** (methotrexate anchor; JAK-inhibitor MACE/VTE/malignancy warning) and **2022 ASAS-EULAR axSpA** guidance. Denosumab rebound-fracture warning and bisphosphonate ONJ/atypical-fracture cautions confirmed in ≥2 sources. Isolated raised ALP with normal calcium/phosphate as the Paget's signature verified in Kumar & Clark and StatPearls.

docs.title: Regional MSK, Soft Tissue, Trauma & Orthopaedic Emergencies
docs.h: 4.2 Mechanical back and neck pain (and the red flags)
docs.parent: Regional MSK, Soft Tissue, Trauma & Orthopaedic Emergencies
docs.text:
**Most acute low back pain is mechanical and self-limiting** — the job in an exam is to **screen for the sinister causes**. NICE (NG59) advocates staying active, avoiding routine imaging, and using the STarT Back-type risk stratification.

**Radiculopathy / sciatica:** nerve-root pain radiating down the leg in a dermatomal pattern (commonly L5/S1 from a disc prolapse); positive **straight-leg raise**. **Spinal (canal) stenosis:** older patient, **neurogenic claudication** — leg pain on walking, **relieved by leaning forward/sitting** (vs vascular claudication relieved by simply stopping).

**⚑ RED FLAGS in back pain — the "don't miss" list:**

| Red flag | Points to |
|---|---|
| **Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral sciatica** | **Cauda equina syndrome** (emergency MRI) |
| **Thoracic pain, new severe pain in >50s, known cancer, weight loss** | **Malignancy / metastatic cord compression** |
| **Fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression, recent bacteraemia** | **Discitis / epidural abscess / vertebral osteomyelitis** |
| **Age <20 or >55 new onset; night pain; systemic upset** | Sinister cause / spondyloarthropathy (young + inflammatory) |
| **Progressive neurological deficit, UMN signs** | **Cord compression** |
| **Significant trauma / osteoporosis / steroid use** | **Vertebral fracture** |

---

docs.title: Regional MSK, Soft Tissue, Trauma & Orthopaedic Emergencies
docs.parent: Regional MSK, Soft Tissue, Trauma & Orthopaedic Emergencies
docs.text:
##### Describing a fracture (the systematic OSCE answer)
Site (which bone, which part), **pattern** (transverse/oblique/spiral/comminuted/greenstick), **displacement** (translation, angulation, rotation, shortening), **intra- vs extra-articular**, **open vs closed**, and any **complications** (neurovascular, skin).

##### Management principle: **Reduce – Hold – Rehabilitate** (the "3 Rs")
Reduce (closed or open), hold (cast, splint, internal/external fixation), rehabilitate (mobilise, physio). Overarching aims: restore anatomy, achieve union, preserve function.

##### Fracture complications
- **Immediate:** neurovascular injury, haemorrhage, skin/soft-tissue.
- **Early:** compartment syndrome, infection, fat embolism, VTE.
- **Late:** **malunion, non-union, avascular necrosis** (scaphoid, femoral head, talus), stiffness, **complex regional pain syndrome**, post-traumatic OA, myositis ossificans.

##### The must-know specific fractures

| Fracture | Mechanism / clue | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| **Neck of femur (NOF)** | Elderly, fall, **shortened + externally rotated** leg | **Garden I–IV; intracapsular vs extracapsular determines implant** (below) |
| **Distal radius — Colles'** | FOOSH, **"dinner-fork" deformity**, dorsal displacement | Smith's = reverse (volar) |
| **Scaphoid** | FOOSH, **anatomical snuffbox tenderness** | ⚑ **AVN + non-union** (retrograde supply); if X-ray normal but tender → **immobilise & re-image / MRI** |
| **Ankle** | Inversion/eversion; Weber A/B/C (relative to syndesmosis) | Ottawa ankle rules to guide X-ray |
| **Supracondylar humerus** | **Child**, FOOSH | **Brachial artery / median (AIN) nerve** injury; check pulse |
| **Distal radius (child) / greenstick** | Incomplete cortical break | Paediatric plasticity |
| **Salter–Harris** | Physeal (growth-plate) fractures, grades I–V | **SALTR**: Slip, Above, Lower, Through, cRush |

**NOF implant logic (a classic viva):**

| Fracture | Blood-supply risk | Typical management |
|---|---|---|
| **Intracapsular, displaced** | **High AVN risk** (retrograde head supply torn) | **Replace**: hemiarthroplasty, or **total hip replacement** if fit/active/independent |
| **Intracapsular, undisplaced** | Lower | Internal fixation (cannulated screws) in selected patients |
| **Extracapsular — intertrochanteric** | Head supply intact | **Fix**: **dynamic hip screw (DHS)** |
| **Extracapsular — subtrochanteric** | — | **Intramedullary nail** |

---

docs.title: Regional MSK, Soft Tissue, Trauma & Orthopaedic Emergencies
docs.h: 4.4 Orthopaedic & spinal emergencies *(can't-miss — highest yield in the section)*
docs.parent: Regional MSK, Soft Tissue, Trauma & Orthopaedic Emergencies
docs.text:
##### Compartment syndrome ⚑
Raised pressure within a closed fascial compartment → ischaemia. Classic after **tibial fracture, forearm fracture, crush, reperfusion, tight casts**.
- **Cardinal sign: pain out of proportion to the injury, and pain on passive stretch of the muscles in the compartment.**
- ⚑ **It is a clinical diagnosis — do NOT wait for the late "6 Ps" (pulselessness/paralysis are late and signify irreversible damage).** Pulses are usually **present** early.
- **Management: remove all constricting casts/dressings, keep limb at heart level, urgent surgical fasciotomy.** Compartment pressures (or ΔP = diastolic − compartment pressure <30 mmHg) support the diagnosis but should not delay surgery.

##### Cauda equina syndrome ⚑
Compression of the lumbosacral roots below L1/L2 (usually a large central disc prolapse; also tumour, abscess, haematoma).
- **Red flags: bilateral sciatica, saddle (perineal) anaesthesia, urinary retention/overflow incontinence, faecal incontinence/loss of anal tone, reduced sexual sensation.**
- **Immediate MRI whole spine; urgent surgical decompression.** Delay → permanent bladder/bowel/sexual dysfunction. **Do a PR and check post-void residual — don't be reassured by "just back pain".**

##### Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) ⚑
Compression of the **cord** (above L1/L2) — cancer patient (breast, prostate, lung, myeloma, renal) with back pain + UMN signs, a sensory level, sphincter disturbance.
- **Urgent MRI whole spine; high-dose dexamethasone; oncology/spinal referral for radiotherapy or surgical decompression within ~24 h.** (NICE MSCC pathway.)

##### Open (compound) fracture ⚑
Skin breached over a fracture → contamination.
- **Gustilo–Anderson classification** (I–IIIC by wound size/soft-tissue/vascular injury).
- **Management (BOAST): early IV antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, remove gross contamination, photograph and cover with saline-soaked dressing, splint, neurovascular assessment, urgent debridement and combined ortho-plastics fixation.**

##### Septic arthritis (cross-reference — full detail in Section 5.5) ⚑
Any acute **hot, swollen, immobile joint** = septic arthritis until excluded → **aspirate before antibiotics**. Covered in the arthritides section.

##### Other acute presentations
- **Cervical spine injury:** immobilise; image (CT) per **Canadian C-spine / NEXUS** rules; beware neurogenic shock in high lesions.
- **Fat embolism syndrome:** 24–72 h after long-bone/pelvic fracture → **respiratory distress, confusion, petechial rash** (the triad). Supportive care; early fracture fixation reduces risk.
- **Dislocations** (shoulder, hip): reduce promptly; check neurovascular status before and after; hip dislocation of a prosthesis is common, native hip dislocation implies high energy + AVN risk.

Garden and Gustilo–Anderson classifications and the intracapsular→arthroplasty / extracapsular→DHS implant logic are consistent across Apley and BOA guidance. Compartment syndrome as a clinical diagnosis where pulses are typically preserved is cross-checked in StatPearls and BOAST.

docs.title: The Arthritides — Degenerative, Inflammatory, Crystal & Septic
docs.parent: The Arthritides — Degenerative, Inflammatory, Crystal & Septic
docs.text:
The commonest joint disease — a **degenerative "wear-and-repair" disorder of cartilage** with secondary bone response, not purely "wear and tear" (there is an active, if failed, repair process).

**Risk factors:** age, female, obesity (knees), previous joint injury/surgery, occupation, genetics, malalignment.

**Distribution (a diagnosis in itself):** **DIP (Heberden's nodes), PIP (Bouchard's nodes), first carpometacarpal (thumb-base squaring), hips, knees, cervical/lumbar spine.** Typically **asymmetrical**, **mechanical** pain (worse with use, better with rest), **short-lived** morning stiffness (<30 min), bony (not soft) swelling, crepitus, reduced range.

**Radiograph — "LOSS":** **L**oss of joint space (asymmetric), **O**steophytes, **S**ubchondral **S**clerosis, subchondral cysts. (Contrast with RA below.)

**Management (ladder):** education, weight loss, exercise/physiotherapy → topical NSAIDs (esp. knee/hand) and paracetamol (limited efficacy) → oral NSAIDs (lowest dose, gastroprotection) → intra-articular steroid for flares → **joint replacement** for end-stage disease refractory to conservative measures. ⚑ *Newer guidance de-emphasises paracetamol monotherapy (small effect) and prioritises exercise and topical NSAIDs.*

---

docs.title: The Arthritides — Degenerative, Inflammatory, Crystal & Septic
docs.parent: The Arthritides — Degenerative, Inflammatory, Crystal & Septic
docs.text:
A **chronic, symmetrical, inflammatory synovitis** driven by autoimmunity; the synovium proliferates into an erosive **pannus**.

**Presentation:** insidious, **symmetrical polyarthritis of the small joints (MCP, PIP, wrists), sparing the DIPs**, with **prolonged early-morning stiffness (>30–60 min)**, soft-tissue (boggy) swelling, fatigue. Later **deformities:** ulnar deviation, **swan-neck**, **boutonnière**, Z-thumb, subluxation.

**Investigations:** **anti-CCP (specific, erosive-predictive)** and **RF**; raised ESR/CRP; anaemia of chronic disease; X-rays show **periarticular osteopenia, soft-tissue swelling, marginal erosions, symmetrical joint-space loss** (mnemonic contrast to OA). Ultrasound/MRI detect early synovitis/erosions.

**Classification — 2010 ACR/EULAR** (score ≥6/10 → definite RA): points from **joint involvement** (number/size of joints), **serology** (RF/anti-CCP), **acute-phase reactants** (CRP/ESR), and **symptom duration ≥6 weeks**. (Classification, not a bedside diagnostic rule — but the components are examinable.)

**Extra-articular / systemic RA (higher-yield than students expect):** rheumatoid nodules, **ILD** and pleural effusion (low glucose exudate), pericarditis, **anaemia**, secondary Sjögren's, scleritis/episcleritis, **Felty's syndrome** (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia), **AA amyloidosis**, accelerated cardiovascular disease, carpal tunnel. ⚑ **Atlantoaxial subluxation** — cervical instability from erosion of the transverse ligament; **flag before intubation/anaesthesia** (risk of cord compression on neck extension).

**Management — treat-to-target (2021 ACR):**
- **Start a DMARD early** ("window of opportunity"); target **remission or low disease activity**, escalating until met.
- ⚑ **Methotrexate is the anchor DMARD** — first-line monotherapy for most (weekly, with **folic acid**; monitor FBC/LFTs; teratogenic, hepatotoxic, pneumonitis risk). Alternatives/additions: sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide.
- **Short-term glucocorticoids** as a bridge only.
- If target not met → **biologic (TNF inhibitor first-line class; also IL-6/tocilizumab, rituximab, abatacept)** or **targeted synthetic (JAK inhibitor)**.
- ⚑ **JAK-inhibitor safety signal (ORAL Surveillance trial):** increased **major adverse cardiovascular events, venous thromboembolism, serious infection (incl. herpes zoster) and malignancy** vs TNF inhibitors, especially in **older patients (≥65) and those with cardiovascular risk factors** — reserve accordingly. (Full pharmacology in Section 7.)

---

docs.title: The Arthritides — Degenerative, Inflammatory, Crystal & Septic

docs.text:
A family sharing: **RF-negative**, **HLA-B27** association, **enthesitis** (not synovitis) and **dactylitis** ("sausage digit"), **axial ± asymmetrical lower-limb** involvement, and extra-articular overlap — the **"SPINE-ACHE"** features: **anterior uveitis, psoriasis/skin, IBD/gut, aortic regurgitation, apical lung fibrosis, achilles enthesitis**. **Memory hook — the shared "A"s:** *Axial, Asymmetrical, Anterior uveitis, Aortic regurgitation, Apical fibrosis, Achilles enthesitis.*

##### Ankylosing spondylitis / axial spondyloarthritis
- **Young man, inflammatory back pain** (insidious, <45 yrs, morning stiffness, **better with exercise/worse with rest, night pain, buttock pain**), progressive spinal stiffness, **reduced chest expansion**, **reduced lumbar flexion (Schober's test)**.
- ⚑ **Nomenclature (2022 ASAS-EULAR):** **radiographic axial SpA (r-axSpA = classic ankylosing spondylitis)** when sacroiliitis is visible on X-ray, vs **non-radiographic axial SpA (nr-axSpA)** where MRI shows sacroiliitis but the X-ray is normal — same disease spectrum, MRI catches it earlier.
- **X-ray:** **sacroiliitis**, **"bamboo spine"** (syndesmophytes, squaring of vertebrae), enthesophytes.
- **Complications:** anterior uveitis (commonest extra-articular), aortic regurgitation, apical pulmonary fibrosis, atlantoaxial subluxation, osteoporosis/fracture.
- **Management (2022 ASAS-EULAR):** exercise/physiotherapy + **NSAIDs first-line**; if inadequate → **biologics: TNF inhibitor or IL-17 inhibitor**; **JAK inhibitor** an option. (No role for conventional DMARDs in purely axial disease.)

##### Psoriatic arthritis (PsA)
- Occurs in ~10–30% of psoriasis patients; **5 patterns:** asymmetrical oligoarthritis, symmetrical (RA-like), **DIP-predominant**, **arthritis mutilans** ("telescoping"/pencil-in-cup), and axial/spondylitic.
- **Nail disease (pitting, onycholysis)**, **dactylitis**, enthesitis; skin psoriasis may be subtle (scalp, umbilicus, natal cleft). X-ray: **"pencil-in-cup"** deformity, DIP erosions with new bone.
- Management: NSAIDs → csDMARDs (methotrexate, esp. with skin disease) → biologics (TNF, **IL-17, IL-23/IL-12-23**).

##### Reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter's)
- **Sterile** arthritis **1–4 weeks after** a **GI (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia)** or **GU (Chlamydia)** infection.
- Classic triad: **"can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree"** — **conjunctivitis/uveitis + urethritis + arthritis**; also keratoderma blennorrhagicum, circinate balanitis. Usually self-limiting; NSAIDs, treat underlying infection.

##### Enteropathic arthritis
- Peripheral (parallels IBD activity) or axial (independent) arthritis in **inflammatory bowel disease**.

docs.text:
##### Gout ⚑
Deposition of **monosodium urate (MSU)** crystals from **hyperuricaemia**.
- **Acute:** sudden, exquisitely painful **monoarthritis**, classically **first MTP joint = podagra**; also mid-foot, ankle, knee. Triggers: alcohol, purine-rich food, dehydration, diuretics, starting/stopping urate-lowering therapy, trauma, illness.
- **Diagnosis:** **needle-shaped, negatively birefringent MSU crystals** on polarised microscopy of aspirate. Serum urate may be **normal during an acute attack** — recheck after it settles. Chronic → **tophi** (ear, joints, tendons) and erosions with **overhanging edges/"rat-bite"**.
- **Acute management:** **NSAID, colchicine, or corticosteroid** (choose by comorbidity — e.g. steroid or colchicine if renal impairment/PUD). ⚑ **Colchicine now dosed low** (e.g. 1 mg then 0.5 mg an hour later, then 0.5 mg 2–4×/day) — the old high-dose-to-diarrhoea regimen is abandoned. **Don't stop existing urate-lowering therapy during a flare.**
- **Urate-lowering therapy (ULT) — treat-to-target (2020 ACR):** ⚑ **indications: ≥2 flares/year, tophi, radiographic damage, or urate nephrolithiasis.** First-line **allopurinol** (xanthine oxidase inhibitor), **start low (100 mg/day; 50 mg if CKD) and titrate up**, with **NSAID/colchicine prophylaxis for the first 3–6 months** to prevent flare on initiation. **Target serum urate <0.36 mmol/L (<6 mg/dL)**, or **<0.30 mmol/L (<5 mg/dL) in tophaceous/severe disease**. ⚑ Consider **HLA-B*5801 testing before allopurinol** in high-risk groups (Han Chinese, Thai, Korean with CKD) — risk of severe cutaneous reaction (SJS/TEN). Second-line **febuxostat**.

##### Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition, CPPD)
- **Calcium pyrophosphate** crystals → **rhomboid, positively birefringent**.
- Older patients; **knee and wrist** commonest; **chondrocalcinosis** (linear cartilage calcification) on X-ray. Associations: ⚑ **haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia, hypophosphatasia** (screen young/recurrent cases).
- Management: NSAIDs/colchicine/steroid for the acute attack; treat the underlying metabolic cause; no urate-lowering role.

**Gout vs pseudogout, side by side:**

| | **Gout** | **Pseudogout** |
|---|---|---|
| Crystal | Monosodium urate | Calcium pyrophosphate |
| Shape | **Needle** | **Rhomboid** |
| Birefringence | **Negative** | **Positive** |
| Classic joint | **1st MTP (podagra)** | **Knee, wrist** |
| X-ray | Erosions, overhanging edges, tophi | **Chondrocalcinosis** |
| Underlying | Hyperuricaemia, diuretics, alcohol | Age, **haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, low Mg** |

---

docs.parent: The Arthritides — Degenerative, Inflammatory, Crystal & Septic
docs.text:
##### Septic arthritis *(emergency — the acute hot joint)* ⚑
Infection within a joint → cartilage destroyed within **days** if untreated.
- **Presentation:** acutely **hot, swollen, red, exquisitely painful joint the patient won't move**, ± fever; usually **monoarticular (knee > hip)**. Any acute hot joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — **including in a patient with known gout or RA** (crystal and infection coexist; an RA flare and joint sepsis look alike).
- **Organisms:** **Staphylococcus aureus** commonest overall; **Neisseria gonorrhoeae** in young sexually active adults (migratory arthritis, tenosynovitis, pustular rash); Gram-negatives in elderly/immunocompromised/IVDU; **Streptococci**.
- **Investigation:** ⚑ **urgent joint aspiration BEFORE antibiotics** — Gram stain, culture, WCC (>50,000 supports, but no count excludes), crystals; blood cultures; FBC/CRP/ESR/urate.
- **Management:** **IV antibiotics** (empirical anti-staph, e.g. flucloxacillin; per local policy and Gram stain) for ~2 weeks IV then oral (total ~4–6 weeks), plus **joint drainage/washout** (arthroscopic or open); analgesia; do not delay for imaging. **Prosthetic joint → refer to orthopaedics, do not aspirate in ED.**

##### Osteomyelitis
Infection of **bone**. **Acute** (haematogenous in children — metaphysis of long bones; *S. aureus*) or **chronic** (contiguous spread, diabetic foot, post-traumatic; may form a **sequestrum** [dead bone] and **involucrum** [new bone shell]).
- **Diabetic foot osteomyelitis:** suspect if **ulcer probes to bone** or is chronic/large; **MRI** is the imaging of choice; bone biopsy/culture guides therapy.
- **Vertebral osteomyelitis / discitis:** back pain, fever, raised inflammatory markers; **MRI**; think **IVDU, bacteraemia, TB (Pott's disease)**.
- **Management:** prolonged targeted antibiotics ± surgical debridement.

##### Prosthetic joint infection
Early (perioperative) vs late (haematogenous); pain, loosening, sinus; needs specialist debridement/revision + prolonged antibiotics.

##### Sources
Kumar & Clark; Robbins; StatPearls (RA, spondyloarthropathies, gout, septic arthritis). **2010 ACR/EULAR RA classification criteria**; **2021 ACR guideline for the treatment of RA** (methotrexate as first-line anchor DMARD; the ORAL Surveillance-derived JAK-inhibitor cardiovascular/malignancy/VTE warning); **2022 ASAS-EULAR axial SpA recommendations** (r-axSpA vs nr-axSpA nomenclature; NSAID→TNFi/IL-17i sequencing); **2020 ACR gout guideline** (treat-to-target, start-low allopurinol with prophylaxis, serum-urate target <6 mg/dL [<0.36 mmol/L], ULT indications, HLA-B*5801 testing) — urate target and ULT indications cross-checked against EULAR gout guidance. Crystal birefringence directions verified in ≥2 sources. Septic-arthritis "aspirate before antibiotics" and organism spectrum from BSR/StatPearls.

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
*Sources: AHA/ASA 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients with Acute Ischemic Stroke; NICE NG128 (stroke and TIA); European Stroke Organisation guidelines; AHA/ASA spontaneous ICH guideline (2022); AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH guideline (2023); Kumar & Clark; Merck Manual Professional; StatPearls. Scope: the highest-yield acute section. ⚑ marks guidance that has moved since older textbooks.*

---

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**Stroke** — an acute focal neurological deficit of vascular origin lasting >24 hours or with imaging evidence of infarction/haemorrhage. **TIA** — transient focal neurological dysfunction of vascular origin **without infarction on imaging**; ⚑ the definition is now *tissue-based*, not the old "resolves within 24 hours" time-based one.

Roughly **85% ischaemic, 15% haemorrhagic** (of which about two-thirds intracerebral and one-third subarachnoid).

**Modifiable risk factors:** hypertension (the single biggest), atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking, hyperlipidaemia, obesity, alcohol, obstructive sleep apnoea, physical inactivity, combined oral contraceptive with migraine with aura. **Non-modifiable:** age, male sex, family history, prior stroke/TIA, ethnicity (higher risk in South Asian, African and Caribbean populations).

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
Symptoms usually last minutes (typically <1 hour). Distinguish from mimics: migraine aura (positive symptoms, slow march), focal seizure (positive symptoms, seconds, post-ictal), syncope (global, not focal), hypoglycaemia, functional.

**Management (NICE NG128):**

- Give **aspirin 300 mg immediately** unless contraindicated.
- **Specialist assessment within 24 hours** for anyone with a suspected TIA in the last 7 days. ⚑ NICE has **abandoned the ABCD² score** for deciding urgency — everyone gets seen within 24 hours.
- Do **not** do CT routinely; MRI (with diffusion-weighted imaging) is the test of choice, ideally on the day of assessment.
- Carotid imaging urgently if the patient is a candidate for carotid intervention.
- Start secondary prevention immediately (see 4.9). **Crescendo TIAs** (≥2 in a week) or TIA on anticoagulation → admit.
- Driving: in the UK, no driving for **1 month** after a TIA or stroke (Group 1 licence), longer and with notification for Group 2.

**Amaurosis fugax** — painless transient monocular visual loss, classically "curtain descending"; think ipsilateral carotid disease or cardiac embolus, and treat as a TIA.

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**TOAST aetiologies:** large-artery atherosclerosis; cardioembolism (AF, endocarditis, recent MI, prosthetic valve, patent foramen ovale); small-vessel occlusion (lacunar); other determined (dissection, vasculitis, thrombophilia, sickle cell, CADASIL, moyamoya); undetermined (cryptogenic).

**Bamford / Oxford (OCSP) classification** — clinical, done at the bedside, predicts prognosis.

| Class | Criteria | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **TACS** — total anterior circulation | **All three**: (1) higher cortical dysfunction (aphasia/neglect), (2) homonymous hemianopia, (3) motor and/or sensory deficit of ≥2 of face/arm/leg | Worst prognosis; large MCA ± ACA |
| **PACS** — partial anterior circulation | **Two of the three**, or higher cortical dysfunction alone, or a limited motor/sensory deficit | Highest early recurrence risk |
| **LACS** — lacunar | **No** cortical signs, no visual field defect: pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, or ataxic hemiparesis | Best prognosis; small perforator |
| **POCS** — posterior circulation | Cranial nerve palsy with contralateral deficit, bilateral deficits, disordered conjugate eye movement, cerebellar signs, **isolated homonymous hemianopia** | Easily missed |

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
| Presentation | Territory |
|---|---|
| Leg > arm weakness, abulia, incontinence | ACA |
| Face/arm > leg, aphasia or neglect, gaze towards lesion | MCA |
| Isolated homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing | PCA |
| Dense equal hemiparesis, no cortical signs, no field defect | Lacunar (internal capsule/pons) |
| Vertigo, ataxia, crossed sensory loss, Horner's, hoarseness | Lateral medullary — PICA/vertebral |
| Sudden reduced consciousness, quadriparesis, pinpoint pupils | Basilar occlusion / pontine |
| Preserved awareness, quadriplegia, vertical eye movement only | Locked-in (ventral pons) |
| Young patient, neck pain, Horner's, after neck trauma or chiropractic manipulation | **Carotid or vertebral dissection** |
| Young patient, migraine, recurrent subcortical strokes, family history, dementia | **CADASIL** (NOTCH3) |
| Stroke in pregnancy/puerperium, headache, seizures | Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, eclampsia, RCVS |

**Five lacunar syndromes:** pure motor hemiparesis (posterior limb of internal capsule — commonest), pure sensory stroke (VPL thalamus), sensorimotor stroke, ataxic hemiparesis (pons/internal capsule), clumsy-hand dysarthria.

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**Sequence:** ABC and glucose → NIHSS → **immediate non-contrast CT head** → decide reperfusion → CT angiography (± perfusion) if large-vessel occlusion possible → stroke unit.

**Thrombolysis**

- Agents: ⚑ the 2026 AHA/ASA guideline endorses **either alteplase or tenecteplase** within the 4.5-hour window; tenecteplase is a single bolus (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg) and is increasingly first-line, alteplase is 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg, 10% bolus then infusion over 1 hour). Older textbooks list alteplase only.
- **Window: within 4.5 hours of onset (or last known well)**, for disabling deficits ⚑ **regardless of NIHSS score**.
- **Extended/unknown-onset window:** selected patients **4.5–9 hours**, or wake-up stroke, using advanced imaging — perfusion core/penumbra mismatch (EXTEND) or **DWI–FLAIR mismatch** (WAKE-UP). ⚑ This did not exist in older texts.
- ⚑ For **non-disabling** deficits within 4.5 hours, dual antiplatelet therapy is now preferred over thrombolysis.
- **BP must be <185/110** before thrombolysis and kept **<180/105 for 24 hours** afterwards.
- **Absolute contraindications:** intracranial haemorrhage on imaging, previous ICH, active bleeding, known AVM/aneurysm/intracranial neoplasm at risk, recent significant head injury or intracranial/spinal surgery (<3 months), suspected SAH, GI haemorrhage <21 days, platelets <100, INR >1.7 or therapeutic anticoagulation, DOAC within 48 hours (unless assays normal), **glucose <2.8 mmol/L uncorrected**, uncontrolled BP above the threshold.
- **Complications:** symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (~2–6%), angio-oedema (especially with ACE inhibitors), systemic bleeding.

**Mechanical thrombectomy**

- For **large-vessel occlusion** (intracranial ICA, M1, and selected M2/basilar).
- **Within 6 hours** on standard criteria; **6–24 hours** with perfusion/clinical mismatch selection (DAWN, DEFUSE-3).
- ⚑ Now also offered to patients with **large established ischaemic cores** (SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT, RESCUE-Japan LIMIT) — the old rule "ASPECTS <6 excludes thrombectomy" no longer holds.
- ⚑ **Basilar artery occlusion: thrombectomy within 24 hours with NIHSS ≥10** (ATTENTION, BAOCHE) — a strong recommendation in the 2026 guideline.
- Thrombolysis and thrombectomy are not alternatives: if eligible for both, give thrombolysis and proceed to thrombectomy without waiting for a response.

**Other acute measures**

- **Aspirin 300 mg** as soon as haemorrhage is excluded, or at **24 hours** if thrombolysed (after repeat imaging); continue 300 mg for 2 weeks then switch to long-term antithrombotic.
- **Do not lower BP acutely** in ischaemic stroke unless thrombolysing, or BP >220/120, or another indication (aortic dissection, heart failure, hypertensive encephalopathy). ⚑ Intensive lowering to <140 systolic is **not** recommended even after successful reperfusion.
- Glucose 4–11 mmol/L; treat fever; nil by mouth until swallow screened; VTE prophylaxis with **intermittent pneumatic compression** (not routine heparin); ea

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**Causes:** hypertension (deep — basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum), **cerebral amyloid angiopathy** (lobar, elderly, recurrent, microbleeds on SWI), anticoagulation, AVM/aneurysm, tumour, sympathomimetic drugs (cocaine, amphetamine), venous thrombosis.

**Management:**

- ⚑ **Rapid BP lowering to a systolic target of 130–140 mmHg within the first hour**, sustained — as part of a care bundle (INTERACT3, which showed reduced mortality/disability). Avoid dropping >70 mmHg from baseline.
- **Reverse anticoagulation urgently:** warfarin → **IV vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate**; dabigatran → **idarucizumab**; factor Xa inhibitors → **andexanet alfa** (or PCC where unavailable) ⚑.
- Neurosurgery for **cerebellar haemorrhage >3 cm** or with brainstem compression/hydrocephalus (this one is exam-standard), for hydrocephalus (EVD), and for selected lobar clot evacuation (minimally invasive approaches increasingly used ⚑).
- Reverse the reversible: glucose, temperature, seizures (treat, do not prophylax), head up 30°.
- Stop antithrombotics; the timing of restarting is individualised (often ~4–8 weeks if a strong indication such as a mechanical valve or high-risk AF).

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**Presentation:** **thunderclap headache** — maximal within seconds, "worst ever", often occipital; ± vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, reduced consciousness, seizure, **subhyaloid/vitreous (Terson's) haemorrhage** on fundoscopy, third nerve palsy (PCom aneurysm), sudden death.

**Causes:** ruptured **saccular (berry) aneurysm** (~85%) — commonest sites: anterior communicating artery, posterior communicating artery, MCA bifurcation; perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal (benign, ~10%); AVM, dissection, trauma.

**Associations:** autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers–Danlos type IV, coarctation, family history, smoking, hypertension, alcohol.

**Diagnosis:** immediate **non-contrast CT** — sensitivity is >98% within 6 hours of onset and falls thereafter; if negative and the story is convincing, **LP at ≥12 hours** for **xanthochromia** (spectrophotometry). Then **CT angiography** to define the aneurysm.

**Management:**

- Neurosurgical/neuroradiology referral; **endovascular coiling is preferred to clipping** where the aneurysm is suitable (ISAT), ideally within 24–72 hours.
- **Nimodipine 60 mg orally 4-hourly for 21 days** — reduces poor outcome from delayed cerebral ischaemia. (Note: it is neuroprotective; it does not simply "prevent vasospasm on angiography".)
- Bed rest, analgesia, laxatives, careful BP control (avoid hypotension), euvolaemia, VTE prophylaxis mechanical initially.

**Complications and their timing:**

| Complication | Timing | Clue |
|---|---|---|
| Rebleeding | First 24–48 h (highest risk) | Sudden deterioration — secure the aneurysm early |
| **Delayed cerebral ischaemia / vasospasm** | **Days 4–14 (peak 7–10)** | New focal deficit or reduced GCS; treat with induced euvolaemia/hypertension, nimodipine, angioplasty |
| Hydrocephalus | Any time; early or late | Deteriorating consciousness; EVD/shunt |
| **Hyponatraemia** | Days | SIADH vs **cerebral salt wasting** (hypovolaemic — treat with salt and fluid, **not** fluid restriction) |
| Seizures | Any | Treat, don't prophylax |
| Neurogenic pulmonary oedema, stunned myocardium | Early | ECG changes mimicking ischaemia |

**Grading:** Hunt and Hess or WFNS (based on GCS and focal deficit) clinically; **modified Fisher** on CT (blood load predicts vasospasm).

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**Suspect when:** headache (often progressive over days, worse lying flat or on Valsalva), papilloedema, seizures, focal deficits **crossing arterial territories**, haemorrhagic infarcts in unusual places (parasagittal, temporal), or isolated intracranial hypertension.

**Risk factors:** pregnancy and puerperium, combined oral contraceptive, thrombophilia, dehydration, malignancy, local sepsis (mastoiditis, sinusitis), head injury, nephrotic syndrome, and (rarely) vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia.

**Diagnosis:** **CT or MR venography**. Plain CT may show a dense cord/delta sign but is often normal. D-dimer is unhelpful if negative in isolated headache.

**Treatment:** ⚑ **anticoagulate — with low-molecular-weight heparin — even in the presence of haemorrhagic infarction**, then oral anticoagulation for 3–12 months. Treat raised ICP; decompressive surgery in severe cases. Warfarin remains standard; DOACs are a reasonable alternative in stable patients (RE-SPECT CVT, ACTION-CVT) ⚑ but not where VITT or antiphospholipid syndrome is present.

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
| Setting | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Ischaemic stroke or TIA, non-cardioembolic | **Clopidogrel 75 mg daily** long term (aspirin + dipyridamole if intolerant) |
| **Minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3–5) or high-risk TIA** | ⚑ **Dual antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 21 days**, then clopidogrel alone (CHANCE, POINT, THALES). Loading doses used; do not continue DAPT long term — bleeding risk |
| Atrial fibrillation | **DOAC** (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran); warfarin if mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis. Timing: ⚑ **early initiation (within days) is safe and is now supported** by ELAN/OPTIMAS; the old "1-3-6-12 day rule" is being superseded |
| Lipids | High-intensity statin (e.g. atorvastatin 80 mg) — target LDL <1.8 mmol/L (some guidance <1.4) |
| Blood pressure | Long-term target <130/80 in most; start once stable (usually after ~2 weeks) |
| **Symptomatic carotid stenosis 50–99% (NASCET)** | **Carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks** of the event — benefit falls sharply with delay. Stenting in selected younger patients or high surgical risk |
| Asymptomatic carotid stenosis | Best medical therapy; surgery only in selected cases |
| **Patent foramen ovale** in cryptogenic stroke, age <60, high-risk PFO | ⚑ **PFO closure** (CLOSE, REDUCE, RESPECT) plus antiplatelet |
| Lifestyle | Smoking cessation, alcohol reduction, exercise, diabetes control, AF screening |

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
**Acute complications:** aspiration pneumonia (swallow screen before anything by mouth), malignant cerebral oedema (day 2–5 after large MCA infarct), haemorrhagic transformation, seizures, DVT/PE, pressure ulcers, depression, urinary retention/infection, malnutrition.

**Rehabilitation** is multidisciplinary from day one: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy (both for aphasia and swallowing), dietitian, psychology, stroke nurse specialists. **Post-stroke complications to actively look for:** spasticity (physiotherapy, botulinum toxin), shoulder subluxation and pain, central post-stroke (thalamic) pain, emotional lability, post-stroke depression (common, treatable), fatigue, cognitive impairment/vascular dementia.

**Prognostic notes:** TACS carries the worst outcome (~60% dead or dependent at 1 year); LACS the best. Most functional recovery occurs in the first 3 months.

---

docs.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
docs.text:
| Clue / question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Current definition of TIA | Tissue-based — transient symptoms **without infarction on imaging** ⚑ |
| Score NICE no longer recommends for TIA triage | ABCD² — all suspected TIAs are seen within 24 hours ⚑ |
| Thrombolysis window | 4.5 hours (extended 4.5–9 h or wake-up with imaging mismatch) ⚑ |
| Thrombolysis agents endorsed in 2026 | Alteplase **or tenecteplase** ⚑ |
| Tenecteplase stroke dose | 0.25 mg/kg single bolus, max 25 mg |
| BP required before thrombolysis | <185/110 (then <180/105 for 24 h) |
| Thrombectomy window | 6 h standard; up to 24 h with mismatch imaging; basilar up to 24 h if NIHSS ≥10 ⚑ |
| Does a large core exclude thrombectomy? | No longer — SELECT2/ANGEL-ASPECT ⚑ |
| When to give aspirin after thrombolysis | 24 hours, after repeat imaging |
| BP threshold to treat in non-thrombolysed ischaemic stroke | >220/120 |
| All three of hemianopia, cortical signs and hemiparesis | TACS |
| Pure motor hemiparesis with no cortical signs | LACS — internal capsule |
| Commonest lacunar syndrome and its site | Pure motor; posterior limb of internal capsule |
| Lobar haemorrhage with microbleeds in an 80-year-old | Cerebral amyloid angiopathy |
| BP target in acute ICH | Systolic 130–140 mmHg within the hour ⚑ |
| Reversal for dabigatran / for factor Xa inhibitors | Idarucizumab / andexanet alfa (or PCC) |
| Cerebellar haemorrhage size prompting surgery | >3 cm (or brainstem compression/hydrocephalus) |
| Sensitivity of CT for SAH within 6 hours | >98% |
| Timing of LP after thunderclap headache | ≥12 hours, for xanthochromia |
| Commonest aneurysm site in SAH | Anterior communicating artery |
| Drug and duration for SAH | Nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days |
| Peak timing of delayed cerebral ischaemia after SAH | Days 4–14 (peak 7–10) |
| Hyponatraemia after SAH that is hypovolaemic | Cerebral salt wasting — give salt and fluid, do not fluid restrict |
| Infarct crossing arterial territories, often haemorrhagic | Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis |
| Anticoagulation in CVST with haemorrhage | Still anticoagulate ⚑ |
| DAPT after minor stroke/high-risk TIA | Aspirin + clopidogrel for **21 days**, then clopidogrel ⚑ |
| Long-term antiplatelet of choice after ischaemic stroke | Clopidogrel 75 mg |
| Symptomatic carotid stenosis threshold and timing | 50–99% (NASCET); endarterectomy within 2 weeks |
| Cryptogenic stroke under 60 with a PFO | Consider percutaneous closure ⚑ |
| Young stroke with neck pain and Horner's | Arterial dissection |
| Recurrent subcortical strokes, migraine, family history, dementia | CADASIL (NOTCH3) |

docs.title: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.parent: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.text:
**Pathology:** chronic immune-mediated inflammatory demyelination of the CNS with axonal loss. Plaques are perivenular and favour the periventricular white matter, corpus callosum, juxtacortical region, optic nerves, brainstem/cerebellar peduncles and spinal cord. **Prevalence rises with distance from the equator**; peak onset 20–40 years; female:male ~3:1; risk factors include low vitamin D, **Epstein–Barr virus infection** (now regarded as a near-necessary prerequisite ⚑), smoking, adolescent obesity, and HLA-DRB1*15:01.

**Phenotypes:**

| Phenotype | Course |
|---|---|
| **Clinically isolated syndrome** | First demyelinating episode; may or may not go on to MS |
| **Relapsing–remitting (~85% at onset)** | Discrete relapses with partial or full recovery |
| **Secondary progressive** | Steady progression after an initial relapsing course (most RRMS eventually) |
| **Primary progressive (~10–15%)** | Progressive from onset; older, more male, more spinal cord |
| **Radiologically isolated syndrome** | Incidental typical MRI lesions without symptoms ⚑ — now diagnosable as MS in some circumstances |

**Common presentations:** **optic neuritis** (subacute painful monocular visual loss, pain on eye movement, red desaturation, RAPD), **partial transverse myelitis** (sensory level, Lhermitte's, bladder symptoms), brainstem syndromes (diplopia, **internuclear ophthalmoplegia**, vertigo, trigeminal neuralgia in a young person), cerebellar syndromes, fatigue, cognitive change. **Uhthoff's phenomenon** — transient worsening with heat.

**Diagnosis — dissemination in space (DIS) and time (DIT).** The 2017 McDonald criteria required lesions in ≥2 of four typical locations (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) for DIS, and either a new lesion over time, simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, or **CSF-specific oligoclonal bands** as a substitute for DIT.

⚑ **The 2024 revisions (published 2025) change several things:**
- The **optic nerve** is added as a **fifth topography** for dissemination in space (evidenced by MRI, OCT or visual evoked potentials).
- **Central vein sign** and **paramagnetic rim lesions** are incorporated as MS-specific imaging biomarkers.
- **Kappa free light chains** in CSF are accepted as an alternative to oligoclonal bands.
- When enough topographies are involved, **separate evidence of dissemination in time is no longer required**.
- MS can now be diagnosed in **asymptomatic** individuals (previously labelled radiologically isolated syndrome) when supportive biomarkers are present.
- The stated trade-off is a risk of **overdiagnosis** — the criteria are only valid once mimics have been excluded.

**Investigations:** MRI brain and whole spine with gadolinium (**"Dawson's fingers"** — ovoid periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles — are characteristic), CSF for oligoclonal bands unmatched in serum, visual evoked potentials, and blood tests to exclude mimics (**AQP4 and MOG antib

docs.title: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.h: 8.2 MS — relapse management and disease-modifying therapy
docs.parent: Demyelinating, Inflammatory and Infectious CNS Disease
docs.text:
**Relapse:** new or worsening symptoms lasting **>24 hours** in the absence of infection or fever, ≥30 days from the last relapse. **First exclude a pseudo-relapse** — infection (especially urinary), fever, metabolic upset unmasking old deficits; treating the infection is the treatment.

**Acute relapse treatment:** **methylprednisolone 500 mg orally for 5 days** (or 1 g IV daily for 3–5 days if severe or unable to take oral). Steroids shorten the relapse but do not change long-term disability. Plasma exchange for severe steroid-refractory relapse.

**Disease-modifying therapy** — for relapsing MS; the direction of travel is towards **earlier use of higher-efficacy agents** ⚑.

| Class/drug | Route | Key risk to remember |
|---|---|---|
| Interferon beta, glatiramer acetate | SC/IM | Modest efficacy; flu-like symptoms; injection reactions; safe in pregnancy |
| **Teriflunomide** | Oral | **Teratogenic** — needs washout with cholestyramine; hepatotoxicity |
| **Dimethyl fumarate** | Oral | Flushing, GI upset, **lymphopenia → PML risk** |
| **Sphingosine-1-phosphate modulators** (fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod) | Oral | **First-dose bradycardia**, macular oedema, VZV reactivation, **rebound disease on stopping** |
| **Cladribine** | Oral (short courses) | Lymphopenia, herpes zoster, contraception for 6 months |
| **Natalizumab** (anti-α4-integrin) | IV/SC | **Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy** — risk rises with **JC virus antibody positivity**, long duration and prior immunosuppression |
| **Anti-CD20** (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, rituximab, ublituximab) | IV/SC | Infusion reactions, hypogammaglobulinaemia, infections; **ocrelizumab is the only licensed DMT for primary progressive MS** |
| **Alemtuzumab** (anti-CD52) | IV | Powerful but **secondary autoimmunity — thyroid disease (~40%), ITP, anti-GBM nephritis**; needs 5 years of monthly monitoring |
| **Autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation** | — | For highly active disease failing therapy ⚑ |

**Progressive MS:** ⚑ **ocrelizumab** for early inflammatory PPMS; **siponimod** for active SPMS. Otherwise the focus is symptom control and rehabilitation.

**Symptomatic management:** spasticity — baclofen, tizanidine, gabapentin, botulinum toxin, **nabiximols** in refractory cases; **fatigue** — exercise, sleep, amantadine/modafinil (limited evidence); bladder — anticholinergics, intermittent self-catheterisation (check post-void residual first); neuropathic pain — gabapentinoids, amitriptyline, duloxetine; **fampridine** for walking speed in selected patients; depression, sexual dysfunction, osteoporosis, vitamin D.
